title: Evangeline
author: Eric Bush
synopsis:
Subtitle: From the award winning author of The Meaning of Androsia: A love story just slightly ahead of its time.

Etienne first met Evangeline when she was sitting on a park bench in the Public Garden, on an otherwise ordinary morning in late summer. He didn’t really meet her on that first encounter. His eyes met her. Everyone has a particular taste in the opposite gender, a set of features they find compelling, a vision they find it hard to turn away from. Evangeline hit this bullseye exactly. He couldn’t turn away.

As he got to know her bet

chapters.title: ONE
chapters.content:
ONE

The death of a beautiful woman, especially from the point of view of a bereaved lover, Edgar Allan Poe believed, is the most poetical topic in the world. His bereaved lovers struggled to make sense of the aftermath of many such women. They all were beautiful. They all died young. They all left a devastating impression on the lover who remained behind.

But the utter finality of death, at this inappropriate place in the blossoming story of a life, was not just a source of unbearable grief for the abandoned lover, but a source of incomprehension. Something had gone terribly wrong with the purposeful arc of the universe. This is not where death is supposed to happen. There can be no reconciliation, no rekindling of affection, no meeting again someday. It’s done. So Poe took poetic license, with the magical realism of his day, to restore some purpose to the universe by bringing some of the deceased lovers back in otherworldly forms.

Etienne, for his part, was not poetically inclined. So he wrote no verses or stories about the aftermath of Evangeline. But he was just as profoundly affected – perhaps more so. There was no reference in any literature that he knew to describe the kind of love he had with Evangeline – or to account for his kind of bereavement. She was unique, you see. Very unique. As unique as a woman could be.

He had not read Poe, but if he had, one line from “Annabel Lee” would have rung true: “We loved with a love that was more than love.”

Only it was also less than love. And it was, at times, different than love. In his time with Evangeline, the familiar contours of love had been stretched out of shape, remodeled, extended, refined, and ultimately rendered incoherent. Even the theme of dying young and beautiful didn’t quite fit their circumstances. Evangeline was undeniably beautiful, but her death was not the usual kind, and her youth was not the usual kind either.

Etienne first met Evangeline when she was sitting, attentively, on a park bench in the Public Garden, on an otherwise ordinary morning in late summer. It was already past ten, so the bankers and lawyers that shuttled past did so with some purpose, on their way to meetings where something of importance was likely to transpire. Places to go. People to meet. The ordinary aspect of their days had been experienced earlier, on their initial commutes. But Etienne was a professor, on his way to the train, over the river to Harvard. He enjoyed the more leisurely academic’s agenda. Things to read. Concepts to think about. Nothing of any urgency. So the ordinariness of his day was still intact.

He didn’t really meet Evangeline on that first encounter. His eyes met her. Her eyes were focused on the walking path nearest her, and she parceled out her attention equally to each person who approached from either side. She was waiting for someone. She wasn’t anxiously waiting for someone, or impatient, or worried. Just waiting, serenely undisturbed, as if it could take all day.

Etienne was on a different walkway, further afield from the one crossing in front of her bench, so she didn’t notice his passing. But he noticed her non-passing. Everyone has a particular taste in the opposite gender, a set of features they find compelling – a vision they find it hard to turn away from. Evangeline hit this bullseye exactly. He couldn’t turn away. He realized he was far enough away that it was unlikely she would notice him, and passersby on his walkway would only notice his attention locked on something to his far left, as his head slowly rotated in that direction while his body continued to progress ahead. A moment of social anonymity in which he could safely indulge this vision.

His piqued attraction to Evangeline was instinctive, of course. Not something premeditated, or reflected upon, or consciously evaluated. It was just suddenly experienced. Felt. He shared this purely visceral sense of attraction with all humans, of course, but it is usually fleeting. When the stimulus is gone, the impression fades. But this impression continued to take up residence in his mind after his head ran out of turning circumference to keep her in view. She had very large, dark eyes – impossibly large for an adult – but somehow set perfectly into her adult face under elegantly dense, dark, level eyebrows. The look was topped off with improbably long dark eyelashes, so long as to appear artificial, except that they matched the oversized geometry of her eyes and the density of her eyebrows, so it was easy to believe they were natural.

The eyes alone would have done it, even without a smile. Her look had been mostly one of anticipation as her wide eyes surveyed the passersby. But Etienne’s short clip of the scene had included a moment when no one was passing, and she briefly glanced down at the small brass statues of the ducklings following the statue of the mother duck – an iconic piece of outdoor art widely associated with the Public Garden. This pleased her, and a broad smile opened up across the whole of her lower face – a feature, again, outsized for an adult, but matching the outsized proportions of everything else on her perfectly balanced face.

Her hair was cut fashionably short, though not in any current style that one could easily identify. It was center-parted on the rear portion of the top of her head, then gracefully interrupted by a cross-cut part that sourced a short wave of bangs cresting gently over her forehead. The unique hairstyle nicely framed the face that carried all of these other unique features. It was easy to believe that it had been created for her face in particular. And indeed it was. Though he had no way of knowing this at the time.

And there was more. She had not only the delicate facial features that Etienne was so drawn to, but also the elegant, elongated body proportions that he had a soft spot for. The short hairstyle revealed a long, slim neck resembling that of a ballerina. In fact, her whole body was ballerina-like, even though she was sitting, and not wearing anything ballerina-like. It was easy to imagine this. For the remainder of his journey through the Common to Park Street Station, where he would catch the Red Line to Harvard Square, Etienne imagined this.

At Park Street, Etienne boarded the train in his customary fashion, crossing over underground to the outside platform of the outbound track because the doors opened on this side first, affording entering passengers a greater choice of seats. He preferred the western view out the windows when the train crossed the Longfellow Bridge over the Charles River into Cambridge. He boarded the car, and the segment of the car, that would stop closest to the underground stairway at Harvard Station, leading directly to the Johnson Gate at Harvard Yard. All of this would have perpetuated the ordinariness of his otherwise ordinary morning, except that the appearance of Evangeline had plucked it out of ordinariness and raised it several degrees into a morning of some note.

But he had been through this kind of moment before – this “some enchanted evening, you may see a stranger across a crowded room” kind of moment. Etienne’s mental life was one long, continuous soliloquy, you see. Ordinary people could zone out, and think of nothing at all. He was either working through some philosophical problem or other, or, like now, just letting his imagination wander through remarkably vivid stories about futures he would like to participate in. So he spun a short story about meeting her again, and all of the improbable ways they would just hit it off, etc., etc. But the follow-on from these first chance encounters never happens in the real world. It’s always one and done. He knew that.

So he was sanguine about this now, and had learned to keep his expectations low. Still, the appearance of Evangeline in the Public Garden this morning merited a certain amount of celebration. There was a real woman, at least temporarily in his own neighborhood, whom he found unusually compelling. This would have been step one, if he had actually met her under some socially acceptable circumstance. But he hadn’t. There had been no realistic chance of meeting her at that distance and in that briefest of intervals. So that she existed at all was irrelevant. She wouldn’t still be there when he came back this evening, he thought, so their lives would likely never intersect again. Still, they actually had intersected, so that event itself outweighed the qué será, será moment, and continued to buoy the morning a little above ordinariness.

When the train emerged from underground at Charles Street Station, at the base of the Longfellow Bridge, a second event occurred that would decrease the morning’s ordinariness further. The event would come to have a significant impact on Etienne, though at this point he did not know this, nor what the actual nature of the event was. He only saw some of its effects. The conductor announced that the train would be “standing by.” This was T-speak for “the train will be parked at this station for an indefinite amount of time.” All by itself, this was not out of the ordinary. It happened all the time on the T, for any number of unexplained reasons. But Etienne could see the traffic backed up on Storrow Drive on the south bank of the river, fully saturating the lanes, as far as the eye could see. He could hear police sirens, and see the distant flashes of emergency vehicle lights.

Such a collection of sights and sounds, at this point in the year, would also not automatically qualify as out of the ordinary. Etienne initially settled on this most likely of hypotheses. It was the end of August, after all, when students from all over the country, and all over the world, make the annual migration to Greater Boston, the quintessential college town. Some of the overpasses on Storrow Drive are too low for several sizes of U-Haul moving trucks. The out-of-towners didn’t know this, of course, so inevitably one of them would get stuck under an overpass and the annual extraction game would begin.

But this was possibly different, Etienne reflected (correctly as it turned out). There were more sirens and flashing lights than seemed necessary just to pull a moving truck out of captivity and tow it away. No one was typically injured in these mishaps, it just created a colossal traffic jam. But there were lots of lights and sirens, suggesting first responders and ambulances. Storrow Drive had another reputation for traffic mishaps that was quite a bit more serious. Its east- and westbound sides alternated between two and three lanes as the roadway curved, sometimes sharply, around river bends, entrance and exit ramps, bridges and tunnels. It resembled the German Autobahn for its excessive speeds, not because such speeds were permitted as with the Autobahn, but because it was habitual behavior for Boston drivers. There were no traffic lights – rare for a roadway in Boston – so drivers treated it like a California freeway.

This could lead to some horrific collisions, and even though the emergency rooms of some of the best hospitals in the world were just a stone’s throw from several of the exits, getting an ambulance to and from the crash site, through a saturated traffic jam on a roadway with no shoulders, was a logistical nightmare.

When your train is “standing by” on the T, all you can do is wait. There is never an estimate of how long you must wait. The conductor will typically open all of the doors during this period, presumably to allow you to bail out if you are going to miss your appointment somewhere. But few passengers actually leave. Instead, more and more of them arrive, thinking the train with the open doors is about to depart, some running frantically down the platform, afraid that the doors are about to close, only to discover that they are crammed into an overstuffed train with barely any standing room. Your signal for when the interminable wait is over is the beeping sound made by the closing doors.

Boston area commuters know that if you have to be somewhere by a given time, you do not take the T. You never know when this black hole might open up and swallow your plans beyond its event horizon. So experienced riders, like Etienne, have schedules that typically allow for some flexibility. The unpredictable arrival time is made up for by not having to fight for the very sparse parking opportunities at the other end.

But today, Etienne had a specific appointment at Harvard. He had already factored in his customary half hour of buffer time, just in case. As the half hour mark of standing by approached, he knew he would be late, but not by how much. So he texted ahead to the philosophy department administrator to let him know his situation. “I’ll text again when the train starts to move,” he added. Then he waited.

He was of two minds about the waiting, because this was not an appointment he really wanted to keep. It was with Richard Hornby, a writer for the New York Times who had reviewed one of his popular books on philosophy for the Times Literary Supplement. It was an OK review, but it perpetuated the myth, common among the New York literary/intellectual crowd, that modern philosophy had devolved into technical arcana from a once golden age when weighty, more substantial ideas were debated. But there never was such a golden age. Academic philosophy has always been about technical arcana that is not readily digested by non-professional readers. It was no different, in that regard, from academic science, or engineering, or mathematics. Etienne had tried to disabuse journalists of this myth before, and was growing tired of trying. So he was not looking forward to treading this path again.

This gave the interminable waiting a silver lining. Perhaps Hornby would have to reschedule. That would be a net positive. At around the full hour mark of the standing by, the beep finally sounded and the doors closed. The train started to roll. Etienne had already given up his winning seat from the earlier outbound platform maneuver to an elderly woman, so he was now packed against his fellow standing passengers, with one hand clinging to an overhead strap. The upside of this arrangement was that you couldn’t fall during sudden accelerations and decelerations. As his fellow sardines fretted about the consequences of missed schedules, he mentally settled back into the knowledge that there was even more time ahead to lose, because the next three stops would be overflowing with waiting passengers who had to exchange positions with the already packed passengers on the train who were trying to get off – a logistical impediment not unlike the ambulances trying to get into and out of Storrow Drive.

When Etienne finally reached Harvard Square Station, and jostled his way out of the train and up the stairs to the Johnson Gate, he took his time crossing the Yard to Emerson Hall. He already had a credible excuse for being very late, documented by text messages, so he might as well exploit it to the max, he reasoned. Maybe, just maybe, the engagement had been postponed. He went straight to the department office first, to inquire about the current status of the appointment. This was control central for the philosophy department, organized, coordinated, and administered with impeccable precision by their very affable administrative assistant, Mr. Morgan Decker. He had a superhuman ability for managing the affairs of the department – never missed a schedule, a due date, or an official correspondence. Everyone liked Morgan because his disposition was always pleasant and accommodating despite his machine-like precision at getting things done.

He glanced up, amiably, when Etienne entered the room. Before Etienne had a chance to inquire, Morgan volunteered, “The journalist is waiting for you in your office.”

Damn! he thought. “Did you explain why I was held up?”

“Yes, at each update.”

“And how was that received?”

“Didn’t seem to mind at all.”

Curious, Etienne thought. A native New Yorker, all the way up from the city this morning, and he doesn’t mind waiting. When he reached his office and opened the door, armored up in his professional academic demeanor ready for battle, he saw why. The waiting journalist was not a he, but a she. And a very attractive she. She immediately stood to introduce herself, extending her hand with an equal measure of deference and smiling invitation.

“Good morning, Professor Harris. I’m Britta. Britta Lindemann.”

Etienne was taken aback, but in a positive direction, quickly shedding his battle disposition and grasping her hand. “Well, I can see you are not Mr. Hornby,” he smiled. This just came out, with no forethought. It was meant as ironic repartee, but the way he said it, and his facial expression, betrayed a second, involuntary channel of meaning. She picked up on this immediately, and her own involuntary facial expression let him know that the compliment was graciously received, and it pleased her.

“I’m sorry you had to wait so long, after coming all the way up here from New York,” he said. He really was sorry, now that the character of the interview he had been avoiding had fundamentally changed.

“Oh, I didn’t come from New York. I’m local here in Cambridge. Mr. Hornby was unexpectedly taken ill yesterday, so the Times and your publisher arranged for me to fill in. I’m a Nieman Fellow for the coming academic year, so I live right down the street.”

Ordinarily, Etienne would have wanted to know more about this fortuitous triangle between the Times, his publisher, and the Nieman Foundation, but today it never entered his mind for some reason, as they took their respective seats. He was more interested in the journalist the triangle had produced. She was a natural blonde, right down to her eyebrows, with very blue eyes.

“If I had to guess, I’d say you were Swedish,” he offered.

“Is it that obvious?” she fretted.

“Well, your name, and your … ” – he searched for the right word – “… appearance are clues, but your accent is what really sealed the deal.”

She did have a distinctly Scandinavian accent, a lilting, sing-song way of pronouncing her words.

“That’s what I was referring to,” she confessed. “We all learn English as a second language from very early on in school. Everyone can speak it, and we hear plenty of it with British and American accents. But some people are able to shed their native accent, and speak it like foreigners right away. You know – to blend in. I guess I’m not one of those people.”

“I guess I am,” Etienne volunteered. “I imitate foreign accents very easily when I hear them. That’s how I recognized yours as Scandinavian.”

She perked up at this. “So you’ve been to Sweden? Can you speak it?”

“Have I been there? Yes, many times. Can I speak the language? No, not at all,” he smiled. “I can often get by reading it, on shop windows and street signs and menus, because I know German, and a lot of the words are cognates, or have similar spellings, but it doesn’t sound like German at all to me. So when I hear people speaking Swedish, I have no idea what they are saying, only that they are probably speaking Swedish. I’m afraid my talent is of very limited value.”

“So how would you compare Sweden to America? I haven’t been here very long yet.”

He had to think about this. “America is a very big and diverse country. It has many regions and many cultures, and nothing approaching a unified national attitude about anything. Sweden is smaller and a lot more homogeneous.”

“Then how about Sweden compared to, say, New England?”

“Ah,” he replied, “I sometimes think of Uppsala-Stockholm as the analog of Cambridge-Boston. Uppsala is the original university town and Stockholm is the nearby metropolitan center that hosts the latter day universities. I love Stockholm, particularly the old town. It is one of my favorite cities in the entire world.”

“Really?” she said, excitedly, in her lilting accent. “I’m from Uppsala! So Cambridge is the Uppsala of New England?”

“Well, the analogy only goes so far. Boston is right across the river. Uppsala is what, an hour away from Stockholm?”

Then Etienne confessed something he really hadn’t intended to. “You know, there’s nothing wrong with your accent. I really like it. I hope you don’t lose it too soon. I think it makes you more interesting – a woman from a different culture with different life experiences.”

There was a pause, as he belatedly realized he had possibly gone too far. Britta had an aspiration to lose her accent, so as to appear more professional and capable of adapting, but he was offering her a different route whose only benefit was to appear more appealing to him. Now that the sentiment had leaked out, there was no way to spin it into something more general or high-minded – something that applied to people in general, of any gender.

Britta, however, saw it for what it was. She had never thought of her accent this way – as appealing – even if the appeal was only in the eyes of one particular person. So she rescued him. “You know, I’ve never really thought of it that way,” she said in her endearing lilt. “That it might make one seem more interesting to someone from a different culture. That could be true for anyone, I suppose, male or female.”

“Yes, that’s what I meant,” Etienne hastily added.

“Yes, I know what you meant,” she said diplomatically, with a smile that told him everything he needed to know.

Eventually, they did get around to talking about philosophy. Britta volunteered that she didn’t know much about it, except for an introductory course she had taken at Uppsala, so she had researched Hornby’s review the night before to get up to speed. Etienne liked her fresh take on the topic – much better than Hornby’s, he thought.

She dug right in. “Do you think we have free will?”

“Yes,” he responded, with equal immediacy.

She waited for a moment. She was expecting more. Then she caught on that this was his dialectical style. It was incumbent upon her to drive the discussion in a direction she found relevant. Why was this, to her, not an adequate answer? “But isn’t there some sort of paradox about this and science? You know, ‘every event has a cause’ and all that?”

“You mean determinism?”

“Yes, determinism, that’s the term. If every event is determined by a prior cause – that’s what science says – including all of our decisions, how can we be said to have freely chosen them? And if we could not have chosen otherwise, how can we be held morally responsible for our actions?”

This perked Etienne up. “You’ve summarized the classic problem very nicely,” he said, clearly impressed.

“It was put this way in my course at Uppsala,” she smiled in return, slyly even, properly citing the source but letting him know she took credit for knowing when to use it.

“OK,” he said, “so now we have a classic paradox – two apparently contradictory beliefs that can’t both be true, yet it seems absurd to deny either. How can I believe in moral responsibility and scientific determinism?”

She waited again for more. Then she started to get the hang of this game. “Yes, how can you? Do you not believe in scientific determinism?”

“Well, most paradoxes are resolved by showing that the two beliefs are actually compatible. For a few thousand years, when science was much younger, this was resolved by having a special class of mental causes, the spontaneous acts of human souls. So there were all of these little islands in the landscape of cause and effect where the cascade of physical causes and effects paused at the borders of human souls, and new events were generated by free choice to continue the chain of events downstream. The universe, it was decided, was constantly receiving these new inputs from another realm to augment its initial starting events.”

“And now that science has lost its souls …?” she interjected. She was getting good at this game.

Well put, he thought. “Science has progressed by yanking more and more of these autonomous, soul-caused events back into the physical domain. So Thor pounding his hammer to cause thunder has been replaced by electrostatics. Evil spirits causing diseases have been replaced by viruses and bacteria. And human souls spontaneously making decisions have been replaced by the activity of 86 billion neurons in the average brain. The islands of free choice have been filled in with physical cause and effect. So we have our determinism at the neuron level, but the perception of freedom at the mental level. As the free choosers, we have no visibility into the micro causes of our decisions. That doesn’t mean there are none.”

“So free will is an illusion?”

“I wouldn’t put it that way. Is hunger an illusion? Is happiness an illusion? Is love an illusion? These are all experienced mental states in which we have no introspective visibility into the underlying neural causes. They aren’t any less real because of that. I would say, instead, that this is what these human experiences are.”

Now he was waiting for a response. It didn’t come. She was still digesting this with a studied look on her face. Finally she asked, in a quizzical way, “Do you think love is just an interaction of neurons?”

“Well, it’s a little more complicated than that. There are a lot of hormones involved as well.” He paused, but could see that the attempt at humor did not help the situation. “But I know what you mean. And I don’t think love is just neurons and hormones. It’s also sonnets, and aspirations, and sharing, and expectations, and tender moments, and faces that launch a thousand ships, and let me count the ways. It’s all of these things, and it is woven into our social fabric in ways we still don’t completely understand. All of this is part of love, and all of it is equally real.”

Her face brightened a little. That was better. She could sign on to that. “I suppose it’s obvious that we don’t know the underlying causes of love when we experience it. It just happens to us. We barely understand the more visible causes up at the people level. It’s much more complicated than just making a conscious decision, like choosing an ice cream flavor. We like to think that we are freely choosing, but it’s more like love chooses us when it happens.”

She was trending a little wistful at this point, but then managed to get her thought back on track. “So the experience of free will may be like this – our observation at the conscious level of a decision that is already being made at a much lower level. So if I fall in love with you, because of lower level causes that I don’t understand, it doesn’t make my love any less real. That makes sense. And by the same token, if I consciously choose a course of action because of lower level causes that I don’t understand, it doesn’t make my choosing any less real. Right? Love is what it always was, we just know a little more about its biology. And free will is what it always was, we just know a little more about its biology now as well.”

Etienne was stunned. “I feel like I should be interviewing you! Did you learn all of this at Uppsala as well?”

“No,” she demurred, smiling. “Not in philosophy class anyway.”

“Do you mind if I use your analogy to love in my lectures on free will? It’s very good.”

“No, not at all! Please do. As part of my Nieman Fellowship, I’m encouraged to audit as many Harvard courses as I like, and required to take at least one for credit. Maybe I’ll take one of yours.”

There was a brief pause for mutual admiration at this point in the interview. It had taken an unexpected turn for both of them and ended up in a place from which it was hard to naturally restart. But Britta’s journalist instinct kicked in just in time to keep it going. “OK, we’ve covered perception of freedom in the presence of determinism. What about the moral responsibility part of the paradox? Does the love analogy help at all here?”

Etienne had to think about this question, but not for too long. “Well … not love specifically, but the idea of the perception of love being essentially bound up in a larger social context of expectations and behaviors applies. We hold people responsible for their actions because we think there were no impediments to their freely choosing them. But we make exceptions for various degrees of impediments. Children are considered not sufficiently developed yet to comprehend the consequences of their actions. Insane or mentally incompetent persons get excused. If someone was holding a gun to your head, your freedom of choice was significantly constrained. So moral responsibility comes in degrees, to match the degrees of freedom in our choices.”

Britta tried this thought on, but was not completely satisfied. “But in just a pure cause and effect sense, in the exact moment that you make a decision, you couldn’t have chosen otherwise. Your action was already determined, no?

“Yes, that’s true,” Etienne replied, “but the moral responsibility derives from the whole history of things you have done prior to the actual decision point. Almost all of our decisions are conditioned by habit. We adopt certain policies of behavior, subscribe to certain moral principles, enter into agreements with others, remember the consequences of previous actions. These standing inclinations are what predetermine what we are likely to do at choice time. So we have no visibility into the final neuron firings, but we have plenty of visibility into how we formed these general inclinations in the past. We couldn’t have done otherwise at the last microsecond, but we could have done otherwise much earlier to put us in a different disposition than we are in now.”

Britta mulled this over, then formed a new analogy. “So I can’t control my own neurons at decision time, but I could have done things earlier to make it more likely that my neurons will fire in the direction I intend. Sort of like the CEO of a large company. The CEO is like the conscious person, and the employees are like the neurons. We hold the CEO responsible for the collective actions of the employees, even though they are the ones performing the actions. If they do something wrong, the CEO is powerless to prevent the action at the moment it occurs. But a good CEO would have put policies in place, and instituted training programs, and published a code of ethics, to make it less likely for these kinds of events to occur. So we judge the CEO based on prior, much larger actions over which he or she actually did have some control.”

“May I use that one in my lectures too? You are a natural at this.”

“Of course!” she smiled.

Just then, Morgan peeked in. “Sorry to interrupt, Professor Harris, but your conference with the Dean is in ten minutes.” Etienne had lost track of time and forgotten about this. He turned to Britta, trying to compose a proper ending to the interview that was nowhere near an actual conclusion.

She sized up the situation, graciously, and offered a deferred ending. “I could come back another time to finish up. I’m just down the street after all.”

“Would you?” he responded, gratefully. He turned to Morgan, who was already prepared for the situation.

“I’ll arrange a mutually agreeable time with Ms. Lindemann when your schedule is a little more open-ended.”

There were smiles all around.

On his return home later that evening, Etienne had all but forgotten about Evangeline from the morning encounter. His time with a certain journalist later that morning had pushed the earlier encounter further down the stack of current events. But as he walked across the Common on the way to his townhouse on Beacon Hill, the ambient views resurrected the memory of Evangeline’s earlier discovery. He lived on the actual Beacon Hill, not the so-called “Flat of the Hill” portion west of Charles Street, so the Public Garden was not on his direct route from home to Harvard. He had come through the Public Garden this morning because he had first gone for breakfast, as he often did, at a private dining club on Marlborough Street.

It was a pleasant evening, still warm, so he retraced his morning route through the Garden – not because he thought there was even the remotest chance that she might still be there, but just because it was a warm, pleasant evening. Nothing wrong with a little extra walking. So he took the path that passed the bench near the “Make Way for Ducklings” statues.

And she was still there.

Waiting for someone.

Serenely undisturbed.

As if it could take all evening.

He paused, before he was close enough for her to evaluate him as the waited-for candidate. She couldn’t possibly have been waiting all day, he thought. Maybe she had found whom she was waiting for, done whatever it was on their joint agenda, parted ways, but had arranged to meet up again in the evening at the same location. That made sense. Just an unlikely coincidence that he was present to observe the two waitings. But he didn’t know this, of course. He was only trying to construct a scenario that made sense. If she had been waiting all day, that was an entirely different matter. There must be something wrong here.

Now he had a whole handful of reasons to stop and talk to her. She might actually need his help. And if not, the two coincidental sightings were certainly worthy of a polite inquiry. So he started walking toward her bench. When she sighted him, he made a point to establish eye contact – and smile.

“Good evening. I can’t help noticing that you were sitting on this same bench this morning when I was passing in the other direction. Are you waiting for someone?” (Of course she was, but he needed a way to get the conversation started.)

She perked up, looked up at him, smiled her broad smile back, and said, “Yes.”

He needed a way to introduce the delicate topic without implying that she might have been waiting all day. So he came up with “It almost seems like you’ve been waiting here all day – I mean you’re exactly where I saw you this morning.”

“I have been waiting all day,” she said, still smiling, but not as broadly, and still without a hint of concern or distress. Though her expression showed that she was reflecting on this fact a little. She broke eye contact and looked straight ahead for a moment, then looked back up at him, as if she were waiting for him to speak again.

Etienne could see that he would have to take the lead, if he wanted to get to the bottom of this odd set of circumstances. So he invited himself in. “Do you mind if I sit?”

“Oh no, please do.” She moved her bag to the other side of the bench so as to imply that she expected him to sit right next to her. There still would have been plenty of bench space otherwise, so he could see the gesture was an invitation.

So he took his designated place beside her, and she turned toward him to make eye contact again. “You don’t really mean you have been sitting right here all day? You’ve had something to eat, haven’t you?”

She looked a little quizzical at this, as if she had to compose some proper explanation. She looked down again to think about it, then back up. “Oh, don’t worry. I took care of that.”

Completely opaque, he thought to himself. He would have to do the digging. “Do you know why this person you are waiting for didn’t show? Was there some sort of problem? Did he try to contact you – or she try to contact you?”

“He,” she smiled, seeing his awkward moment. “No, he didn’t contact me.”

“Did you try to contact him?”

“No, I don’t have a phone.”

The scenario was getting progressively harder for him to understand. “Here, you can use my phone.”

As he reached for it, she said, “I don’t know his number.”

Etienne could see there was a lot going on here that she didn’t necessarily want to talk about. How to crack this nut? “Look, I don’t mean to pry, but no one should have left you waiting here all day. How do you know this person, and why were you supposed to meet here this morning? Perhaps I can help.”

Now he could see that she really was conflicted. She took a while to answer.

“I was waiting for Mr. Collins. Marcus Collins.” She paused, but that clearly wasn’t enough. “We work together on … a project. We flew in from Switzerland. He has a conference in Boston. He was coming to pick me up.”

Finally, some context. “So he’s clearly not coming at this point – for whatever reason. You can’t be expected to just wait here. Did you have any plans? A hotel where you were staying?”

“No, no plans that I know of. He made all of the plans, I’m afraid. We flew in on the red-eye this morning. I was to wait here until he registered for the conference. Then there would be plans, I suppose, but I don’t know them.”

“Well, you can’t wait here all night!”

“No, I suppose you’re right. I can’t wait here all night, can I?” She said this with a little more seriousness than her previous “serenely waiting” disposition.

“Well, why don’t you stay with me tonight. I live right up the hill.” He pointed. “I have plenty of room. Then we could try to sort this all out in the morning.”

“That would be very kind of you. Thank you. That sounds like a proper plan.” Her disposition returned to serenity, as did her smile.

By now, Etienne had picked up on her accent. It was hard to place exactly. Vaguely British – upper-class British. But there were other elements mixed in. A little French, maybe. And some Netherlands influence. Dutch maybe. Whatever it was, it had an elegant harmony to it. Precise and well-articulated, but endearing and full of wonderment. Like her unique hairstyle and facial expressions, it seemed to be designed specifically for her.

But he resisted the urge to ask about or comment on it, for fear of disclosing its personal attraction for him. He didn’t want to make the same mistake twice in one day.

When they reached Etienne’s townhouse on the south slope of the Hill, he showed her around the three floors of his typical 19th-century, red-brick Federalist home, built shoulder to shoulder with the neighboring townhouses on either side, as was the row house custom back then. She looked in each room with curious pleasure, noticing the historical decor and the quaint period pieces. She didn’t say much, but her face, and very expressive eyes, said much.

Then she paused, as if she’d suddenly remembered something. She turned, flashed that broad smile and wide eyes, and said, “How rude of me. We haven’t been properly introduced. I’m Evangeline. And you?”

Evangeline, he thought. That’s a nice name. Evangeline who? he wondered. She hadn’t said, so he matched the protocol and dispensed with his own last name. “Pleased to meet you, Evangeline (he really was). I’m Etienne.” That seemed to satisfy her, so he just went with the flow.

When they reached the bedrooms, two of them, on the third floor, he showed her where she would sleep. Rooms in these row houses were typically laid out front to back on each floor. He had adopted the back bedroom as his own when he first moved in, he explained, because he liked to let the natural sunlight in to wake him in the morning. There wasn’t much visibility through the rear windows from the alley at the back, particularly on the top floor, so there was no particular need to close the Indian shutters, top or bottom.

She would have the guest bedroom at the front, which had much better street views, but she might want to close the bottom set of Indian shutters for privacy, he said, because the third floor windows in the houses on the other side of the narrow street had this same good view in reverse.

She thought about that for a moment, then walked over to take in the view from the windows, scanning the quaint, narrow streetscape with its faux gaslights and real cobblestones, and opposing row houses. Then she turned around to see where the bed was positioned relative to the windows. She walked gracefully over to sit on the bed and looked back toward the nearest window. She considered the view from there to the window for a moment, then not being satisfied, lay on the bed and reconsidered the view. Then walked back to the window, closed the lower shutters, and peeked out the window over them. Now satisfied, she re-opened the shutters, turned around and just smiled, without saying a word.

There was something about her enigmatic behavior, her moods, her way of walking, her way of communicating what was on her mind with her eyes in lieu of words that Etienne found both mystifying and endearing. He didn’t know it at the time, but this would often happen in their time together. This was quintessential Evangeline.

“I imagine you must be pretty jet-lagged,” he said, “if you just got off a red-eye this morning.”

She considered this for a moment, as if she’d been suddenly reminded of something, then said, “I guess I should be very tired by now, shouldn’t I?” Then, “No, I am very tired by now.” Then, as if correcting herself, “I am particularly tired right now.” She stifled a yawn, and closed her eyes, still standing there.

She looked for all the world like she might be falling asleep in front of the window. Etienne hurried over to catch her by the shoulders before she fell. Her head slumped onto his shoulder, and her arms hugged him as if he were a pillow.

“Let’s get you to bed,” he said, helping her navigate the distance to the bed. He eased her down gently into a sitting position. Without opening her eyes, she said, “Thank you very much. Delighted.”

She must be dreaming, he thought. That was quick. He nudged her a little. “Don’t fall asleep just yet. Let me get you something to sleep in first.”

“Can I have a silk nightgown with rosebuds on it?”

He couldn’t suppress a slight smile at this. “I’m afraid all I have is pajamas. I don’t wear them myself. Someone who was unaware gave them to me as a present.”

“Pajamas! I’ve always wanted to sleep in pajamas. Just the top half. Did you know there are people who sleep with absolutely nothing on at all?”

“That doesn’t surprise me.” Another half smile.

She looked down at her dress, then back up at him expectantly, eyes still open. “Will you help me get undressed please?”

Etienne was confused about this request, not sure what to do next. He guessed this was her half-sleep state talking. “Why don’t you get started and I’ll go get the pajamas.” With that, he made a quick, diplomatic exit.

When he returned with the pajamas, she had managed to unbutton her cuffs, but was fiddling a little unsuccessfully with the bottom buttons of her blouse. “I’ve never been alone with a man before, even with my dress on.” She pulled up her blouse out of her skirt. “With my dress off, it’s most unusual.” Then, smiling, she said, “Hm, I don’t seem to mind at all.” She looked up at him. “Do you?”

It was clear to Etienne that he wasn’t talking to a fully conscious person at this point. He didn’t have an answer. If this had been the fully conscious Evangeline, he would have been pleasantly surprised, but he wouldn’t have minded. Though he may have struggled with how to properly express that sentiment. Since she wasn’t fully present, he did mind. She may regret this later.

Then she stood up, as her skirt slid down to the floor. “You have my permission to withdraw,” she announced.

So he seized on the sudden opportunity, and withdrew.

He waited a while in his own bedroom, giving her time to complete the dressing transition to pajamas, he hoped, and then onto the transition to full sleep. When he returned, quietly, she was properly pajamaed – top and bottom – and sound asleep on top of the covers, lying diagonally to the bed frame as if she had literally fallen asleep. He picked her up gently and eased her under the covers. Then he went to the window nearest the bed and closed the lower shutters. He mimicked her routine in reverse, surveying the angle from the open, top-level shutters to the bed. This seemed to provide adequate privacy from any casual voyeur. The other window had no view to the bed at all.

He watched her for a moment, sleeping silently, becoming the voyeur himself. Then cautiously made his way to the door, so as not to cause the wide, pumpkin pine floorboards to squeak, and closed it with equal acoustic care.

It was still early evening in late August, so there was plenty of daylight left before Etienne would receive nature’s circadian signal for his own drowsiness. He hadn’t eaten yet, and it was pretty clear that the exhausted Evangeline was down for the count, so he considered going out to eat on Charles Street. But suppose she did wake up while he was gone, he thought. She would probably be disoriented and may be wondering where she was – or where he was. Couldn’t afford to let that happen. So he ordered out for delivery.

After dinner, he retired to his study on the second floor. It had been an eventful day, he reflected, ending with this most curious encounter with Evangeline. And her adventure was just beginning. It was not clear to him what he could propose tomorrow to help her with her apparent abandonment. How could they locate this Marcus Collins fellow? How long might she have to stay with him? How would he manage that? These practical concerns didn’t really compete with the overwhelming sentiment that he didn’t mind her being here at all. She was an inconvenience that he was happy to bear. There seemed to be several levels to her personality, and she would glide back and forth between them on a whim. She was thoughtful, then delighted, then serious, then naive and in need of help, then slyly revealing that she had been aware of the situation all along. She confronted each situation directly, saying what was on her mind as it occurred to her. There was no hint of duplicity, no sense that she was acting. You could read her present state of mind from her face, though you often couldn’t predict what would come next. It was both confusing and charming. She drew you in. You wanted to follow her even though you didn’t know where she was going.

He was not particularly tired yet, so he busied himself with tasks to take his mind off her. He read a little. He wrote a little. But nothing could dislodge his fascination with the extraordinary circumstance he found himself in. This sometimes happened to him – when his mind was too preoccupied to sleep. His solution was just to prepare for bed and hope for nature to take its course. Better to be already in bed when his mind eventually let go.

So he turned off the downstairs lights and retired to his bedroom. He customarily slept in just his briefs. It was a warm night, so he sat up in bed with just a top sheet covering him from the waist down. Sitting was just as good as lying down as long as his busy mind refused to yield.

Then he heard the faint squeak of the floorboards from Evangeline’s room. She was up, stirring. She cautiously opened the door to her room, peeked out, then crossed the hallway to his open doorway in her conscious, elegant, dancer’s style – not the staggering, half-asleep style from earlier. She leaned on his doorway with her head against her clasped hands, fully clad in the oversized pajamas.

“I suppose I am awake now,” she said plaintively. “I hope I’m not disturbing you.”

“Not at all. … Having trouble sleeping?”

“Yes … but I really shouldn’t be bothering you about that. Are you having trouble sleeping?”

“Yes.”

“Because of me?”

“Yes.”

“Then I am disturbing you.”

“Well, I wouldn’t call it ‘disturbing’ exactly. It’s not a bad thing. I’m just preoccupied – thinking about things. People like you and situations like this don’t come along every day.”

She reflected on this a moment, then said, “I suppose you’re right … but there’s nothing you can do about it right now. Thinking about the situation won’t solve it, so there’s nothing more you can do tonight, right? Perhaps if you were to lie down, instead of sitting up, it would be easier for you to fall asleep?”

She had a point, he thought, but she hadn’t walked across the hall just to help him sleep. Her insomnia had more legitimately disturbing causes than his. He should be helping her to sleep. “Would you like to talk about it – what’s on your mind, what you are feeling?”

It looked, at first, that this was just what she wanted to hear – the invitation she was hoping for. But before she could act on it, she caught herself with “No, I don’t want to burden you with this.”

“You are not a burden, believe me. Come. Sit down. We’ll talk about it.” He motioned toward the end of the bed.

“Only if you lie down. I’m not going to be the cause of you staying up all night.”

She had made her condition clear, so he pulled himself under the top sheet, and put his head up on the pillow. She hadn’t expected such an easy capitulation. So she walked over and sat at the foot of the bed. It was his invitation, so she waited for him to start.

“You’re right. We can’t solve this tonight. But it would be natural for a situation like this to take an emotional toll on you. It might help for you to let that out, to tell someone who is sympathetic to your plight – to tell me.”

Her face did show some relief, but her words were still cautious. “I suppose I’m feeling a little abandoned, right now … a little vulnerable … because I don’t know what I am to do about this.”

This was a good start, he thought. But he hadn’t expected her to open up so quickly. The onus was now on him to go next, but it was taking him a while to compose his response.

Sensing this, she reclaimed the initiative. “Do you mind if I just get in with you for a minute?” She didn’t wait for an answer. She just got under the top sheet with him, lay next to him, and rested her head on his shoulder. “It’s all right … really it is. We’re just friends, that’s all. We are friends, aren’t we?”

“Yes,” he replied, philosophically, suppressing his surprise. “I suppose we are.”

“Okay … now let’s don’t say another word … let’s just go to sleep.”

And with that, she closed her large eyes with the long lashes, and said nothing more. It took less than a minute for her to fall asleep.

There was nothing further for Etienne to do. This was clearly good therapy for Evangeline. The antidote to abandonment and vulnerability. It pleased Etienne no end, because he hadn’t really done anything at all except just being there. Without really thinking, he moved his arm gently around her waist to cuddle her slightly. It just seemed the natural extension of the larger comforting gesture – reclaiming her from abandonment and protecting her from vulnerability. The added warmth of their body heat extended the theme further in the desired direction. It caused her to stir slightly, then unconsciously extend her free arm around him to complete the hug.

This was certainly not the cure for Etienne’s insomnia. As his body relaxed into the warmth, his mind revved up into a higher gear. He wasn’t thinking of anything in particular, he was just hyper-aware of the situation he now found himself in. He didn’t need sleep to come right away. The waking state was just fine.

After a while, Evangeline stirred again, and began talking in her sleep. “But Mr. Collins … what if they discover me?”

She seemed agitated by the dream, so Etienne nudged her gently awake. “Evangeline! It’s just a dream.” She opened her eyes with a confused start and looked at him. “You were dreaming.”

“I was?”

“Yes. And you sounded very worried. You were talking about Mr. Collins, and something about being discovered. What was that all about?”

She looked at him with a sudden pout. “If we’re going to be friends, let’s get one thing straight right now! I hate snoops!”

As prepared as he was for her sudden mood shifts, he was not prepared for this. But the message was clear. This was a sensitive topic for her. He would not inquire about this further. So he just placed her head back on his shoulder where they had started. “Yes, let’s just be friends.” That seemed to work. Before long she was asleep again, and unconsciously resumed the comforting hug.

Now Etienne was ready for sleep.

chapters.title: TWO
chapters.content:
TWO

At the first hint of morning, Etienne, true to his circadian rhythm, awoke with the sun. It did not come streaming in through his shutterless windows because the sky held a slight overcast, so it was more of a gradual rolling in. His usual custom was to mentally acknowledge the new day at sunrise, then drift back to a shallower sleep until about 7:00. Then, just like clockwork (circadian clockwork in this case), he would become fully awake to start the day. This being the end of August, he estimated the half-sleep would last about an hour ten this morning.

But that was his routine for sleeping alone. This morning he found himself still comfortably nestled against Evangeline, in the same position they had been all night. Things would likely be different this morning.

He watched her at close range for a while, so as not to disturb her. He tried to shift his position a little so his arm wouldn’t fall asleep. That caused her to stir slightly, then she resumed her original position with her arm around him. “So happy …” she said in her sleep. Happy indeed, he thought to himself, smiling.

Now fully awake, his mind began to work on a plan for reuniting her with this Mr. Collins. Since they were incommunicado, and he and Evangeline were in the dark as to Collins’ whereabouts, they would just have to wait for some contact from him. So it only made sense for her to take up residence again on the same park bench. But he would wait with her this time, just in case Collins was still a no-show.

Eventually, Evangeline stirred again. This time she woke up. Her eyes opened first, taking in Etienne and their most intimate, close proximity. She raised her head a little to assess the room with a quizzical look. “Where am I?”

“At my house. In my bed. Don’t you remember what happened last night?”

“Should I?” She looked back at him, then down at the very comfortable proximity of their body positions.

“We’re just friends, remember?” He said this with a smile.

She turned back to him and matched the smile. “Yes, now I remember. And I’m wearing your pajamas.” She put her head back down on his shoulder, with her eyes at half-mast.

Then she opened them wide, as if she had suddenly remembered something. She reached down under the covers, feeling for the presence of pajama bottoms around her hips. Satisfied, she smiled again and put her head down again.

Etienne waited patiently for her to decide when to rise. There was no hurry, of course. But her eyes slowly assumed the half-mast position again, then eventually closed. She was asleep again. “So happy …” she murmured.

Etienne’s willingness to wait for Evangeline to make a full transition to consciousness eventually expired. If she was recovering from jet lag, this could take who knows how long. Also, he was beginning to wonder how he would make his own transition from almost naked to more fully dressed. Evangeline was hard to read. She was alternately uninhibited and a little modest the night before, so he didn’t know what version he might get this morning. He resolved to make his exit now so as not to have to deal with this. He slowly, carefully, and gently disengaged himself from her hug without waking her. Then he showered in the second floor bathroom, leaving the third floor bath undisturbed for her, dressed, and went about tidying up her now abandoned bedroom.

He had no idea whether she would require coffee, but he would. It was the mandatory first event of his morning ritual. It was an addiction, to be sure, but a benign addiction, he had decided. He always made it strong and black. His brain expected this before it turned on the switch to make him fully aware. If he missed his morning coffee, he would not experience any withdrawal symptoms, such as a headache. He would just be a little spacey until that first hit of caffeine was deposited.

So he made enough for two, just in case, and left her portion in the carafe on the warming plate. While his brain was powering up in response to the injection of awareness fuel, he heard the faint squeaking of floorboards upstairs. This was a feature of antique houses with their wide pine floorboards. You accepted the less-than-fully-level floors, and the aging joists that flex a little under weight, in return for the charm of the Federalist interiors and their warm, pumpkin pine colors. Eventually he heard the squeaks of the stairs, as Evangeline descended. She emerged fully awake and fully dressed, smiling as she entered.

“Coffee?” Etienne offered.

Her expression changed, ever so briefly, to one of deliberation, then quickly switched back to her characteristic wide smile. “Yes. Thank you. How very kind of you.” She sat at the table in her signature graceful-ballerina style. If she was still carrying the weighty concerns of abandonment and vulnerability from the previous evening, it did not show. She had returned to the sunny disposition he had first observed the previous morning on the park bench.

He waited for her to raise the subject of the missing Mr. Collins, because he did not want to disturb this oh-so-pleasant demeanor. They made light, inconsequential conversation about the strength of the coffee, the squeaking of floorboards, and the historical decor of his house. Seeing that he would have to introduce the subject himself, he began.

“I had thought that we might as well start back at the park bench this morning, because that’s the only location your Mr. Collins knows where to find you.”

“Oh, you don’t have to wait with me. That would be very kind of you, and I thank you for the offer, but I’m sure you have your own business to attend to.”

Etienne hadn’t had the chance to finish his now amended plan, so he added a prelude. “I don’t mind waiting with you at all. I’m a professor. I have a very relaxed schedule, shall we say. I have nothing pressing to attend to this morning. But I don’t think either of us will want to wait on the bench this morning because it is already starting to rain. I certainly couldn’t leave you alone in the rain all morning.”

“Oh!” she said, with raised eyebrows, considering the implications.

“So I have a better plan. You can stay here, and I’ll post a note on the park bench for Mr. Collins on my way to work, telling him that he can find you here. I’ll leave you a key to the house, in case you need to go out while I’m gone. When you’re here, keep the door locked, and answer it by checking who’s there first. If Collins finds you, just leave the key under the mat outside.”

She could agree to this version of the plan, she said. So he set about preparing the particulars. He found an index card, then began to write, “For Mr. Collins: …” He struggled a little with how to describe the situation as anonymously as possible, so others who saw the note on the bench wouldn’t learn anything they weren’t entitled to. He kept it brief, but when he got to the part about where to find her, he paused. He didn’t want to post his address publicly, so he settled on his phone number. That way, he could reveal the address only to Collins – if it was in fact he who called. Then he fretted again about publicly posting his personal phone number. Ah, he thought, when the perfect plan finally occurred to him. He would post the number of the philosophy department at Harvard – ‘ask for Professor Harris’. This was already an easily accessible public number, and his affiliation with Harvard was already an easily accessible fact. No new information revealed!

He found a pushpin to attach it to the bench, then paused again. It was raining. The ink would eventually run and become indecipherable. So he placed the card inside a clear, quart-sized plastic Ziplock bag, then sealed it. Now he was ready.

He got the spare key for Evangeline, gave it to her, grabbed his umbrella, then headed for the door. He paused, wondering if some sort of goodbye ritual was in order, given that he may never see her again. A hug was perhaps too personal at this point, even though they had shared one all night. A different mood was orchestrating events then. Now the mood was more formal. A handshake wasn’t appropriate at all. It would only serve to erase their previous connection. Lacking any alternative, he simply turned back to smile. Evangeline seemed equally conflicted, and matched this with the complementary smile. Then he left for the Public Garden.

On his way to Harvard this morning, Etienne marveled at how quickly the trip could take without any “standing bys.” Storrow Drive was clear, the trains were evenly spaced, and there was no conflict between the boarding and unboarding.

When he reached his office, he sat down at his desk for a moment of contemplation. He was under the impression this would be a light academic day. He taught on Tuesdays and Thursdays this semester, and today was Friday. He checked his calendar. Only some administrivia in the afternoon. His thoughts were naturally still centered on Evangeline and her unique plight. His departmental responsibilities, aside from the teaching part, were his least favorite part of being a tenured professor. They came with the territory, so they couldn’t be avoided, but the territory also included wide academic freedom, and a year’s sabbatical every seven years. So there was compensation.

Just then, Morgan peeked in. “Ah, Professor Harris. You’re in bright and early this morning.”

“Yes, sometimes the T just works.”

“I’ve rescheduled Ms. Lindemann for 1:00 this afternoon. I wanted to leave plenty of buffer so she wouldn’t have to wait in the morning, or leave prematurely, like yesterday.”

“Thank you for that, Morgan. Though of course today I have plenty of time in the morning. I wonder what the big holdup was on the T yesterday.”

“You haven’t heard?”

“No, is there some news? I was a little preoccupied with … a personal matter yesterday.”

“Big multi-car collision on Storrow Drive. Someone was killed. Someone named Marcus Collins. He was apparently an international expert of some note in robotics. He was here to give the keynote speech at a conference in Back Bay.”

Etienne was stunned, of course, but he tried not to show it. Morgan was good at reading facial expressions and body language, so this took some concerted acting. “Hm, never heard of him. Well, thanks again for the prescient scheduling of Ms. Lindemann. I’ll let you get back to work now.”

With that, Morgan popped back out, and Etienne immediately went to his computer for the news. He didn’t spend much time on Collins’ career or accolades. He was looking for any reference to Evangeline. The flight from Switzerland was mentioned, but she wasn’t.

So the near term mystery of her abandonment was solved. He was dead – probably killed on his way to pick her up when Etienne first saw her on the park bench. All of the other non-events, the no messages, no contact, fell into place.

His take on Collins shifted now to a more favorable impression. He had not abandoned her – not through any will of his own, anyway. But now, how to break this to Evangeline? Etienne was the only person she knew in Boston, and possibly the only person who knew she should be contacted. She was his responsibility now, and there was likely some grief to be dealt with.

Etienne hurried to the department office to find Morgan.

“Morgan, something of a personal nature has just come up, and I will need to go back to Boston for the morning.”

“Same personal matter as yesterday?”

“Yes, actually. I expect I’ll be back in time for Ms. Lindemann’s appointment. If not, I’ll let you know.”

With that, he made a beeline for the T.

All the way home, Etienne mulled how he should disclose the news to Evangeline. He had never dealt with a situation like this before. There was no generally accepted way to break this kind of thing to someone. It doesn’t come up very often. It helps if you know the person you are informing well, and perhaps something about what the deceased meant to them. But he didn’t know either of these things, so he had no context to fall back on.

When he reached his house, he still wasn’t any clearer on the matter. He turned his key in the lock, figuring that she would know it must be him (only other person with a key). He opened the door, and there she was, sitting in the front room, waiting – looking remarkably like he had first seen her on the park bench. She looked at him and flashed her wide smile. He loved that smile, and now regretted that he would be the one to break it.

How to proceed? Normally, people start by asking the receiver of bad news to sit down. Why, he wasn’t sure. But she was already sitting. He couldn’t just tell her from across the room, so he walked over and sat beside her, in case she would need some comforting. He tried to keep a neutral expression. Smiling was certainly not appropriate for him, but her smile remained.

“I have some … news. I’ve found out about Mr. Collins and why he didn’t meet you yesterday.”

She perked up. “That’s good news, isn’t it?”

“No, I’m afraid it’s not good news.” How to say it? People always say “passed away,” as if it was some slow, gradual, expected event. That was not the case here. So he came right out with it. “He died in a car accident yesterday morning on his way to pick you up.”

Then he watched her face carefully to see how she took it. The smile disappeared, for sure, but it was not replaced with any of the characteristic responses. No “Oh No!,” with hands placed over the mouth. No frightened disbelief. No crying. No slumping onto his shoulder. She looked serious, but it was not her usual eyes down, contemplate, then back up with a question-serious. She just looked straight ahead, at nothing in particular. She was clearly processing this, but it was more of a “what happens now” look than a “how can this happen?” look.

She finally looked directly at Etienne, with raised eyebrows and soulful eyes, and asked, “So whatever will become of me now?”

He was not expecting this. “Is there someone we should contact? Someone who knew you were coming to Boston? Someone in Switzerland, perhaps?”

Without any hesitation, she said, “No. No one knew I was coming. Here or in Switzerland.”

Now Etienne began to wonder if this had maybe been a secret affair. That might explain her earlier reluctance to talk about their association. But if that were true, where was the grief? It did not make sense. Perhaps she was in shock, suppressing the grief. He instinctively pushed her head onto his shoulder and gave her a comforting embrace. Maybe she needed an invitation to let it out. She willingly embraced him in return, but said nothing. There was no catharsis, no weeping, no evidence of grief at all. It was a replay of last night’s impromptu gesture – the antidote to abandonment and vulnerability.

Then, without looking up, she repeated her plaintive “Whatever will become of me now?” As she said this, she tightened her embrace a little. Etienne got the message, cryptic though it was. Marcus Collins was not her paramour. Whatever their association was would have to remain a mystery, for now. What was clear was that her abandonment had suddenly become a fait accompli. Last night he had provided a temporary reprieve for this. Now he would have to provide a more permanent one.

“You can stay right here with me. For however long it takes.”

Without looking up, she said, “Are you sure I won’t be a burden?”

“I’m sure.” He really was. As sure as he was about anything in his life so far. Whatever the circumstances that had brought her to his door would emerge in time, but they clearly didn’t matter now. She was here now. She had no place else to go. And, despite the morbid circumstances, he couldn’t be happier about this.

Etienne sat with her a while. They made polite small talk. But the shallowness of the conversation merely papered over private concerns they each had. Etienne was looking for some assurance that she was stable now – that there was no latent grief or sorrow or other kind of emotional upheaval that was being suppressed. Evangeline, for her part, was dealing with whatever she was dealing with. Etienne could never tell. She was still a complete enigma to him.

He could hardly go back to Harvard leaving her in this indeterminate state. So he thought he might try to unravel the Collins relationship a little. Now that he was gone, and she was showing no apparent regret, the topic might not be so sensitive. If there had been secrets to preserve, maybe they no longer needed preserving.

“Were you and Mr. Collins close?”

“Yes, very close.” As she said this, she suddenly realized that it might be misinterpreted. She turned to him with wide eyes, and her characteristic British/French/Dutch accent. “Oh … but not in the way you’re thinking.  Not emotionally close, or anything like that.” Then she looked down, initiating her trademark “down – think about it – back up” sequence. Down: “We worked together quite closely in his lab.” Think about it: “All of the time.” Back up: “I never really left.”

“But you went home in the evening, no?”

“No … I slept there. He had a room there for me.”

The picture was getting harder and harder for Etienne to visualize. So he changed the subject. “Did you work on robotics too … with Mr. Collins? I heard that he was quite famous for his robotics research. Did you work on this with him?”

This caused a clear mental conflict in Evangeline’s mind. She seemed a little confused about how to formulate the answer.

“He was training me. That’s why I was always in his lab … for the training.”

She clearly wasn’t finished with this thought. She sat in silence for a while, then finally said, “It's so unfair. Men are the only people permitted to have any fun. It's so easy for you men. You decide to do something, then do it.”

This struck Etienne as oddly anachronistic – an attitude from a bygone era. "Where did you learn this difference between women and men?"

"From Mr. Collins, I suppose. He decided what to do and when to do it. Then he went out in the world and did it. I had to stay inside and wait for him to come back."

Now Etienne began to suspect that her relationship with Collins had been inappropriately controlling. Perhaps that explained her lack of grief.

As he struggled to find a line of questioning that could delicately explore this situation, she shifted gears, raised her eyebrows, looking straight ahead, permitted herself a half-smile, and drew her own conclusion. “Now I suppose I could do some of the things I've always wanted to.”

Etienne went with it. “Like what?”

“Oh, you can't imagine... I'd, I'd like to do just whatever I'd like, the whole day long!” She laughed, then looked at him. “Yes, and I'd like to sit at a sidewalk café; and look in shop windows; walk in the rain! Have fun, and maybe some excitement. It doesn't seem much to you, does it?”

He smiled at her emergence from her shell. She would be OK now. He didn’t know how long she would need him before taking flight on her own, but he suddenly lost track of his custodial role. He wanted to be there for the first flight – or perhaps all of the flights. “They all seem appealing to me. We could do them together. Would you like that?”

Now the full smile returned. “Yes, very much. That would be very kind of you. But don't you have to work?”

“Work?” He was about to say “It’s Friday,” but then remembered that he promised Morgan he would be back at Harvard in time for the interview with Britta Lindemann. This yanked him back into the world of responsibility. He couldn’t postpone the interview twice. That wouldn’t be fair to Ms. Lindemann. But he also couldn’t just leave Evangeline here to cool her heels all day. She was ready to fly, and this could be an important part of her recovery. She would need help in this new, unknown city. And he had already offered, and she had already accepted. So Evangeline won the conflict of responsibilities, perhaps because she had already won a measure of his affection.

“I’ll be right back. I have to make a phone call … to make sure my calendar is clear.”

With that, he went into the kitchen and closed the door to keep Evangeline out of earshot. “Morgan?”

“Yes, Professor Harris.”

“I’m afraid I’m going to have to postpone Ms. Lindemann one more time.”

“Same problem?”

“Yes, same problem. I really should speak to her directly. Do you have her number?”

“Yes. Shall I call her and patch you in?”

“Yes, please.”

He waited for the telephone mechanics to take their course.

“Ms. Lindemann?”

“Yes.”

“This is Morgan Decker at the Harvard philosophy department. I have Professor Harris on the line for you.” With that, he disconnected himself from the conversation.

“Ms. Lindemann?”

“Yes, Professor Harris?”

“That sounds so formal. Please call me Etienne.”

“OK, Etienne, then please call me Britta.”

He smiled to himself. “Now that we’re fast friends, I must apologize that I have to reschedule the rest of our interview again. A personal matter has come up that I really must attend to.”

“I hope everything is alright!”

“Actually things are getting better. I had to leave for an emergency this morning, but things have improved since then. I just need a little more time to deal with it.”

Britta had no visibility into this “emergency,” nor any polite way to further inquire about it, so she moved to the next step in the protocol. “What time next week would be convenient for you? I have a pretty open schedule.”

“I’m not always in control of my calendar, but I think I’m pretty free as well. Mr. Decker … Morgan … will know for sure, so I’ll have him arrange a time with you again. And I promise, I will make it this time!”

“Thank you for that, Prof … Etienne. I’m really looking forward to continuing our discussion.”

Etienne was too. Evangeline had temporarily eclipsed his experience with Britta, but now it had made a pleasant return. Two attractive women in one day, he thought. Things were looking up.

He returned to Evangeline in the front room and announced, “Schedule all clear. Today will be your day out in the world – doing whatever you want.”

“Thank you,” she said, settling into a knowing smile. “Where shall we start?”

Etienne could see through the small window panes framing his front door that it was still drizzling outside, so the opening event became obvious. “Well, the weather is perfect for your wish to walk in the rain. We’ll use umbrellas, of course.”

He had several small, collapsible ones in the narrow front coat closet, and one large one with the characteristic hooked wooden handle. Large enough for two. That also became the obvious choice.

Then they set out, arm in arm, umbrella between them, down Acorn Street toward West Cedar Street.

If Etienne had had the power to control the weather, he couldn’t have orchestrated a better set of circumstances for Evangeline’s day of freedom. If you are going to enjoy a walk in the rain, you don’t want it to be raining too hard, you don’t want the wind blowing sideways, and you don’t want it to be cold. A gentle drizzle at the end of August checked all of the boxes. The rain earlier this morning had been more substantial, so it had made this favorable transition at just the right moment.

They walked through all of the iconic streets on the south slope of the Hill, as Etienne played tour guide. He did this as a matter of habit with all of his out-of-town visitors, pointing out the irony of historical inversion in the settlement of Beacon Hill. The narrow, cobblestoned lane of Acorn Street, where he lived, was originally the downscale, modest housing for artisans and servants who served the more upscale dwellings on the wider streets of Beacon, Chestnut, and Mt. Vernon. Now, it sat at the top of the heap of prestige as perhaps the most photographed city streetscape in North America.

With each turn to the west on their walkabout, the sky revealed more blue patches invading the overcast. Etienne checked his phone for the weather. The rest of the day would be clear and sunny. So the walk in the rain was now reaching its own natural conclusion. When the drizzle stopped for good, he retracted the umbrella, fastened it, then announced, “And that concludes our walk in the rain.”

“Oh, it was wonderful,” she beamed.

“What’s next on your list?”

Evangeline thought for a moment, then volunteered “Sitting in a sidewalk café?”

“Right this way.” Etienne gestured to the west toward Charles Street, not because that was necessarily the final destination, but because it was the gateway to the Back Bay where they would find plenty of candidates.

His first thought was to take her to one of his favorite restaurants with outdoor seating, but then thought better of it. He would let Evangeline do the choosing, based on what struck her fancy. Either way, the obvious destination was Boylston Street, so they cut through the Public Garden to start their café tour there.

On their way past her prior waiting bench in front of the ducklings, Etienne retrieved the note he had attached to the bench for Mr. Collins, and deposited it in the nearest trash receptacle. Now happy to have closed that too public channel of information, he led Evangeline around the Swan Boat lagoon to the exit at Arlington and Newbury Streets. As a longtime resident of Boston, the Swan Boat lagoon and its ornate bridge were just familiar background. Things that he passed on his way to somewhere else. But they were new to Evangeline, and clearly captured her imagination, so he slowed his pace to let her wander around the water’s edge.

When they started up Newbury Street, Evangeline paused in front of the display window at Tiffany’s. Etienne paused to wait for her reaction. But she just stood there, looking at the window in what appeared to be a mixture of emotions – both delighted and confused. She was clearly trying to process something, unsure of how to respond.

Finally, she asked, “Don’t you just love it?”

“Love what?”

“Tiffany’s. I do. And it’s not that I give a hoot about jewelry … nothing bad could ever happen in a place like this.”

Etienne didn’t give a hoot about jewelry either, but he could easily imagine something bad happening – a robbery, for instance. He really didn’t know how to contribute to this sudden epiphany of hers, so he just silently enjoyed her enjoyment. It was infectious.

Once the thought had passed, they continued on merrily to Berkeley Street, then left to Boylston, where they could begin the tour of sidewalk cafés. It didn’t take long for Evangeline to make her selection, choosing a venue near Copley Square. It turned out to be a place Etienne often frequented.

“Mr. Harris!” the maitre de greeted.  “… and guest,” he added with a pleasant raised eyebrow. “Good to see you again. Table for two?”

“Yes, outside please.”

When the waiter arrived to inquire about the usual “something to drink to start,” Evangeline immediately responded, “Champagne please,” smiling up at the waiter as only she could.

Champagne? Etienne thought, … as if this were habitual for her. This was not something he expected from the ingenue who never left the lab. But then so little of what she did was what he expected. He scanned quickly down the wine list and ordered a glass of the Sonoma Valley Chardonnay for himself.
