As waiters often do during the meal, this one returned periodically when he noticed either the wine glass or the Champagne flute near empty. “Can I get you another?” Evangeline always said yes. So Etienne followed her lead. Alcohol had almost no mental effect on him, so he could easily tolerate this. He drank wine for the subtleties of taste, not for the buzz. Evangeline was also throwing them down without any apparent change in her demeanor at all. He found this surprising, but was happy to see it. He knew so many people, especially women, whose personality changes under alcohol.

As they talked, in their shared, perpetually sober state, a Vespa scooter motored past them in traffic on Boylston Street, an unusual sight for Boston streets, before making a turn at Copley. This caught Evangeline’s rapt attention. She followed it visually, including the turn at the corner. Her hands were subtly imitating those of the driver, turning and rotating the throttle on the handle.

“Have you ever ridden one of those?” Etienne asked.

This brought her attention back to the table, but her expression indicated she was still working on the thought. “No … not by myself. I’m afraid I don’t really know how to drive it. I might run into things … or people! But it looks like it would be a lot of fun!”

Etienne had no idea how he could possibly grant this wish, so he just let it pass without further engaging her. Prior to the Vespa, she had been watching people coming in and out of Trinity Church in Copley Square. Now her attention shifted across the street to the much larger building that occupied the entire block west of Dartmouth Street.

“And what do they do there?” she pointed.

“It’s a library. The Boston Public Library.”

“The whole block?”

“Yes, including an attached newer building you can’t see quite as well from here. That’s the new library.”

“Why did they need a new library? Did they run out of space for the books?”

“Yes, that’s about the size of it. Have you been inside a large public library?”

“Yes,” she said, reflecting. Then reflecting some more, she added “Twice.”

“Well, the architecture inside the old library is quite impressive. People even get married there because of the grand ambiance.”

“Married? In a library?” Then she shifted to the marriage side of the proposition. “Married …” This seemed to resonate with her for some reason.

“Would you like to see inside?”

“Yes, let’s see inside!”

With that, Etienne settled the check and they made their way across the plaza to the Boylston Street entrance. When they reached the Grand Staircase and Puvis de Chavannes Gallery carved out of ornate yellow marble on the inside, Evangeline looked up in awe. Now she could envision a wedding. It didn’t look much like a library, more like a palace.

She looked around. “Where are the card catalogues?”

“Card catalogues?” This, to Etienne, evoked the same anachronistic sense as her earlier remark about men’s and women’s roles. “Those were replaced years ago by computer terminals.” This seemed to be news to her. So he took her over to one. “Just type in a title or an author.”

“What’s your last name?”

“Harris.”

She entered ‘Harris, Etienne’.

Up popped Aspects of Freedom, by Etienne Harris.

“Is that you? Did you write this book?” She was wide-eyed at the possibility.

“Yes, that’s my book.”

“What is it about? Is it a story?”

“No, it’s nonfiction. It’s about … freedom, or more specifically, free will.”

“Oh,” she said, as if this were a concept she was unfamiliar with. Then she looked around the hall, apparently searching for something she couldn’t locate. There was a moment of indecision before she finally announced, “Well, I suppose we don’t need to have them get the book, since you already know what’s in it.” Then she smiled as if this were the proper conclusion to her search.

Yet again, Etienne could not follow her thinking, though by now he was becoming accustomed to that. “What shall we do next?” he asked.

She had to recall her earlier list. “Look in shop windows?”

Etienne thought about this for a moment. More of Newbury Street was probably not what she was envisioning. Something more casual, more downscale, consumer oriented he suspected. “Shop windows coming up!” He led her back out to the street, and then back toward the Public Garden and the Common. He was thinking of the downtown shopping district east of Tremont Street.

On their way across the Common, she paused to look at the Frog Pond. “That’s the Frog Pond,” Etienne informed her.

She looked at him with raised eyebrows, then strolled over to the water’s edge, looking in the water. Dissatisfied, she walked more of the perimeter, again looking in the water. “I don’t see any frogs.”

Etienne had to suppress a slight laugh at this. “There are no frogs. It’s just a nickname.”

“Well, if there are no frogs, why do they call it a frog pond?”

“There once were frogs. Way back in the Revolutionary War days when it was a real pond. Soldiers named it that because they hunted them for food. Now it’s an artificial pond, made of concrete. Used for ice skating in the winter, and cooling off kids in the summer.”

“Oh,” she said, satisfied with the explanation.

When they passed the Brewer Fountain in the Common, on their way to Park Street, she paused again to take in this large public sculpture. She walked around the circumference to examine it from all sides. But her gaze skipped right over the larger, mythological figures of Neptune, Amphitrite, Acis, and Galatea, instead concentrating on the four smaller mascarons – the grotesque mask-faces – set between them, acting as classic fountain spouts with water flow emanating from their large, open mouths. A normal tourist would hardly have noticed these, but they were the center of attraction for Evangeline. As Etienne watched, he could see her hands in motion again, acting out her thoughts. This time she cautiously extended her right hand, slowly, slowly, then suddenly yanked it back, all the while staring at the closest mascaron.

Etienne was beginning to see a pattern here. Things that she saw on her first day of freedom somehow reminded her of things she had seen before, but the context was different. Almost like deja vu. And that confused her. Rather than talk about it, she seemed to be trying to integrate the memories with her present situation, but not succeeding. What came next didn’t quite fit. When she reached this non-conclusion, she would come back to the present and give him a smile – as if to say “that concludes this brief interruption.” It was a good concluding gesture, because it signaled that whatever had just happened was completely opaque to him. No need for explanation. I’m OK. Let’s continue our walk.

So they crossed over Tremont Street and began the tour of window shopping. Evangeline stopped briefly at many shop windows to look at this or that, but nothing merited a second look. The looking itself appeared to be the goal. When they stopped at a shoe store window, however, he saw the familiar pattern briefly again. She looked down at her own shoes, then back at a particular pair in the window. Then her body began to act out the memory again. She began to reach down to her feet, as if to take off her shoes, but then stopped short. This is where the discontinuity occurred, Etienne surmised, because she considered the situation once more, then looked back at him and flashed that smile.

He should have learned by now that he could not follow, or participate, in this behavior, but rather than frustrate him, it drew him in. He wanted to participate somehow. He wanted his presence to be relevant. Then he had an idea.

“Maybe we should shop for a silk nightgown with rosebuds on it … since I don’t have one back at my house.” He was afraid she might not remember, since she was half asleep when she had said this.

But she did remember. She looked back at him with a different, softer smile. One that said yes I remember. I’m surprised that you remembered. But I’m so glad you did. What a nice gesture – and offer. Very personal! But I don’t mind at all.

She said all of this to him without saying a word.

So they had a new goal, much more specific, but much harder to fulfill. They stopped at many shops featuring women’s intimate apparel, but nothing that matched the description. Etienne was careful to stay in the background, letting Evangeline make the query to the shop ladies.

Eventually they found a shop that had something close enough for Evangeline to try on. This was done privately, in the dressing room of course, with the sales lady’s assistance. Etienne sat in the corner, quietly biding his time, waiting for the verdict. Evangeline emerged from the dressing room, fully dressed of course, but with her characteristic wide smile. For added confirmation, the sales lady gave Etienne a discreet, knowing smile, and a subtle thumbs up signal.

When they emerged from the shop, parcel in hand, Etienne inquired, “What now?”

“I think we’ve finished my list,” she replied. “What would you like to do?”

What would he like to do? He already knew Boston well, so there was nothing on his list. But what he was enjoying, immensely, was watching her reactions to the things he knew well, even if he didn’t always understand them. He was vicariously retouring the city from her point of view. “Do you like art?”

“Yes, I love art!”

“Then let’s go see some art.” He led her to the nearest Green Line stop where they boarded the trolley line that runs down Huntington Avenue by the Museum of Fine Arts. He was well acquainted with most of the permanent exhibits, but the MFA periodically hosted new, themed exhibits to keep long time patrons coming back for something novel. All of it would be new to Evangeline, of course, so he started with the Art of the Americas wing. The wing was laid out with each floor featuring art from a particular century, starting with the 17th century (which included small pieces from all previous centuries).

Evangeline showed particular interest in the 18th century floor. Etienne watched as she surveyed the portraits of various famous Boston area figures from the Revolutionary War period. She returned a few times to re-examine some of the portraits. Etienne suspected that she was beginning one of her memory episodes, but it turned out to be a completely novel investigation. One she was willing to talk about.

“Why do all of the men look different, but all of the ladies look the same?”

He hadn’t noticed this before, so he looked closer.

“Don’t you see? The men are all painted in fine detail, with very colorful clothing. And they all look distinctly different. The women are painted very plain, and pale, and wearing practically the same dress. And they all look very much like each other.”

She had a point, he thought. Very observant. “Maybe it’s because the men were famous but their wives were not. These wealthy men were commissioning the portraits, so the artist naturally favored them. The wives were an afterthought. So maybe the artist just used standard boilerplate when he got to them.”

“Or maybe the wives did look alike,” she offered. “There weren’t as many people in those days, so maybe a lot of them were related.”

Another good point, he thought.

They spent most of the rest of the afternoon in the MFA. It was finally a venue that did not invoke any prior memories for Evangeline, so she was always present. And Etienne could participate in the experience.

By early evening, they had made their way back to the base of Beacon Hill at Charles Street. Etienne expected that she must be tired of walking by now. He was. But she just kept going, now wishing to walk up Charles Street. When they reached the end, at the base of the Longfellow Bridge crossing the Charles, Evangeline wanted to take the pedestrian bridge over to the Esplanade. The evening was still warm, and the Esplanade was littered with people walking and frequenting the various outdoor popup drinking venues left over from the height of summer.

Then Evangeline spied one with a wooden deck for dancing, surrounded by decorative white lights, and a small band – more of a chamber orchestra than a small rock band – near the water’s edge. As she watched the dancers, her delighted expression indicated that if this were a past memory, it was not a confusing one, it was a happy one. Etienne saw his chance to participate. “Would you like to dance?”

She turned to him with a smile that said, “You’ve read my mind.” “Yes,” was the word that actually came out. Now he had the opening he had been looking for all day.

He took her hand and led her to the dance platform. The musicians had just begun a slower number, so slow and close dancing was in order. As they engaged, she rested her head on his shoulder, her eyes closed and smiling. Then she looked up at him.

“Hello.”

Although unclear as to how to respond, he was clearly where he wanted to be – fully immersed in the present and connecting with her. Whatever she was trying to say must be what he was trying to say. So he matched her with his own “Hello.” She rested her head against his chest and they continued.

When the band finished, they made their way off to the side of the platform near the bar. Before Etienne could ask if she’d like something to drink (Champagne maybe?), two men in black suits watching them from the other side of the platform caught her eye. Her expression changed abruptly. She was back to the confused dithering behavior.

“Maybe we should go home now,” she offered.

“Is something wrong?”

She dithered again, unable to come up with the proper reply. “No, it’s just that I’m getting a little tired.”

The response was reasonable, he thought, but it didn’t match the apparent triggering event. Knowing that he was out of the loop again, he answered, “Well, it’s certainly been a long day. I’m surprised you lasted this long. Shall we go home?”

“Yes,” she said, somewhat relieved. “Let’s go home.”

He took her hand and turned in the direction of the pedestrian bridge back to Charles Street – which was also the side of the platform on which the men in black were standing.

“No, let’s go this way.” She pulled him in the opposite direction. He got the message. Avoid the men in black. The Esplanade was quite wide near the dance platform, so walking further south, away from the men, before turning toward the pedestrian bridge was not a significant detour. Etienne didn’t ask further, but he strategically positioned himself between her and the men, and she seemed to appreciate this.

By the time they reached his house on Acorn Street, Evangeline had fully transitioned back to the present. She was her smiling, engaging self once again. She was just as enigmatic as before, surprising him at every turn in their conversations, but Etienne sensed a subtle change in her demeanor and her facial expressions. She appeared to be bonding with him after their day together – or perhaps he just hoped that she was. He was no longer an objective observer. He was smitten.

There were pauses now and then when they just made furtive eye contact, anticipating something that should naturally come next. But nothing ever did. Then they would find their places in the conversation once again and continue.

He had always thought he would end up with someone very much like himself. She had some of his qualities – like curiosity and saying what’s on your mind – but in other ways she couldn’t be more different from him. And he found that oddly appealing. She was a mystery to him, but undeniably connecting with him on an emotional level. She was a mystery worth solving – or not solving. Either would do.

"You spent the whole day doing things I've always wanted to. Why?”

He couldn’t say why, exactly. He had not planned any of this. So he resorted to something he had realized about himself – that he was vicariously re-experiencing his familiar world through her eyes. He was certain there was more to it than that, but he had no further words to express that other, more amorphous emotion.

"I've never heard of anybody so kind,” she replied. “Also completely unselfish.”

It wasn’t unselfish at all, he thought. But again words failed him. So he replied with a simple smile.

At bedtime, Evangeline brought Etienne’s oversized pajamas back to him. She had them draped over one arm, and the new silk nightgown draped over the other. “I guess I won’t be needing these now, will I?”

She held out the pajamas and Etienne took them. Then she looked at the nightgown, and back at Etienne. "Do you mind turning around for a second ... or never mind ... I'll turn around myself." She did, as if that somehow solved the problem of undressing in front of him. When she realized it didn’t, she shyly made her way across the hall to the bathroom, and changed there.

When she returned, she gave him a hug, and a kiss on the cheek. Then retired to the guest bedroom without another word.

chapters.title: THREE
chapters.content:
THREE

The weekend couldn’t have come at a better time for Etienne. He was in a state of emotional turmoil, which interfered with his circadian sleep cycle. His mind was not busy, but his brain could not sleep. It was occupied by something else, or more precisely, someone else. The turmoil was not unpleasant, but it managed to occupy every corner of his waking consciousness. There was no room for anything else. It was disorienting – certainly not a state of consciousness he could carry to work with him for a day at the office.

Now he would have an uninterrupted weekend to sort this feeling out, to indulge it, to let it take its course. That helped him sleep. Off and on. There was nothing that needed to be resolved, until Monday at least. That left only anticipation of the weekend to compete with the Sandman, but the Sandman was overmatched.

The Sandman won the last round, and converted Etienne’s sleep deficit into a long oversleep that went well past the sunrise. When he finally woke up and smelled the coffee, both proverbially and actually, he realized that Evangeline had taken the initiative this morning and repaid his gesture from the morning before. He had slept through the sound of the shower, and the squeaks on the stairs, and the preparations in the kitchen. She was pleasantly humming something down there, and it all seemed so … domestic. And comforting. Someone was taking care of him for a change, after a lifetime of taking care of himself.

After showering and making himself presentable, and squeaking down the stairs to the kitchen, he found Evangeline waiting with her signature smile. She had made a whole breakfast for the two of them, improvising from his pantry, and finding and arranging the appropriate place settings. She had only one outfit – the original one from the park bench – but it looked fresh on her. He made a mental note that he would need to take her shopping.

“Good morning, Etienne,” she said, already seated at the table.

“Good morning, Evangeline.” He took his designated seat opposite her.

“I made the coffee as strong as I could. I hope you like it.”

He would have liked it no matter what, but after a quick taste, he was impressed. “Perfect!” Just what she wanted to hear.

“What shall we do today?” she inquired in a most optimistic tone.

“Have you ever been here in New England before?”

“No, I’m afraid this is my first time to any of the United States. Or my first time out of Europe, actually.”

Etienne sensed that she might now be willing to open up a little about her mysterious past. Not that it really mattered at this point, but it was a standard kind of getting-to-know-you conversation. “And what did you do before working with Mr. Collins?”

“Oh, I’ve been in Switzerland my entire life … in Basel.” Then she paused to consider the next bit of information. “I was born there, you could say. Have you ever been to Switzerland?”

“Yes, as a matter of fact. In Basel. Given how much you liked art at the MFA yesterday, I’m guessing you are a regular at Art Basel – the one that’s actually in Basel.”

“No,” she said, exhibiting a slight loss of confidence. “I’m afraid I don’t know about that.”

This struck Etienne as odd. A lifelong resident of Basel who doesn’t know about Art Basel, and speaks English with a British-French-Dutch accent. Etienne had lost his sensitivity to bringing up her accent by now, so he jumped right in.

“I’m curious about your accent – which I love, by the way. I hear elements of British, and Dutch, and French pronunciation. I could be wrong about this. You’ve really never left Basel?”

She lost a little more confidence, and spent some time thinking before her reply. “Switzerland is a multilingual country, as you know. I heard those accents many times during my training. I guess I just picked them up – unconsciously imitated them, you know.”

She was trying to get Etienne off of this line of questioning, but had no way of knowing that she had just hit pay dirt.

“Really! I’m like that. I also unconsciously absorb foreign accents.” This took Etienne’s thoughts off in another direction, wiping the slate clean.

Evangeline silently smiled back at him, realizing her sudden good fortune.

“Would you like to see some of New England today?”

“Oh, I’d love to. Can you show me?”

“Yes! Let’s see … looks like it’s going to be warm today, so a good day to spend on the coast where it will be cooler. Marblehead is nearby. That would make a good day trip.”

“Can we walk there?”

He smiled. “No, by ‘nearby’ I meant about 17 miles north. Marblehead is not on the way to anything. It’s a peninsula on the North Shore. So there’s no good commuter rail access. You have to drive.”

“And you have a car?”

“No, actually. I don’t own one. You don’t really need one to get around Greater Boston. There’s plenty of public transportation. When I need to get away, like today, I just rent one. Very convenient.”

And with that, they were off, following Etienne’s usual routine for a North Shore day trip by taking the T to the airport, where it’s easy to rent and return a car, and which is already on Route 1A which follows the coast to the north.

On a summer weekend in Marblehead, street parking is a precious commodity. The old town that rings the western side of the harbor was fully built out centuries ago when “space for cars” was an unknown concept. Etienne, however, had some inside knowledge. There was a small, sloping set of parking spaces behind the old Gerry School building, reserved for school personnel, that was generally not visible from the main streets. In the summer, with school not in session, most of these spots would be vacant. So he began the tour by driving Evangeline around the Neck to Marblehead Light, on the eastern side of the harbor, to view the small mansions and estates on the “new money” side. Then they came back around the harbor and parked in this hidden gem of a landing spot to walk through the historic old town for the rest of the day.

The old town was essentially a living museum of streetscapes from the 17th and 18th centuries. A strong historical district commission prohibited external changes to these original wood clapboard houses to preserve this authentic throwback to the past. If you owned a house here, you had to accept that you were living in a museum. There was no registry of historically accurate paint colors, however, so you could still express your individuality through the colors you chose to paint the clapboards and the trim. And residents did, which resulted in bright, vibrant colored streetscapes that resembled their more drab 17th- and 18th-century counterparts in structure only.

As they walked and talked, and Etienne explained the local historical lore of bullet-hole glass and the home of Elbridge Gerry, who gave rise to the term ‘gerrymander’ (including its mispronunciation), he began to wonder a little about a possible age gap between himself and Evangeline. There could be one, he thought. She appeared to be quite young, though this could be misleading because of the unique composition of her facial features. And he looked deceptively young for his actual age, which she might underestimate. If there was a gap, it was not of any concern to him, but he wondered if it might be for her. Still, there was no way to diplomatically initiate a conversation on this subject, though this didn’t stop him from trying to formulate one. But he didn’t get very far before she started the conversation in a different direction.

“Have you ever been in love before, Etienne?”

“Before what?”

“Don’t be silly. You know what I mean. Before now. Before you met me.”

Now he really didn’t know what she meant. Was she implying that he was in love with her now? Or just fishing for his past? Or perhaps fishing for an acknowledgement of his present affection for her? So he told the simple truth.

“I don’t really know how to answer that. I’ve been in several relationships before. And in each one, I’ve had varying degrees of affection for the woman. Some where my affection was greater than hers, and some where hers was greater than mine.”

“Is that why none of them lasted … you are single aren’t you?”

“Yes, I’m single,” he smiled. Then he turned a little wistful as he thought about the first part of her question. “Maybe you’ve put your finger on it … the affection needs to be about equal.”

Then, “I don’t know which is harder: losing someone you care more deeply about than she cares about you … or disappointing someone whose affection you just can’t match.”

“Were you the first man she’d ever been in love with?”

“Yes, I think so.”

“I suppose most girls are sentimental about their first love.”

“Yes … ” he replied, still lost in the memory.

“Like their first pair of high-heeled shoes.”

The utter randomness of this reply brought him back into the present moment. Then he sensed an opening to get into her back story. “Have you ever been in love before?”

She wasn’t expecting the tables to be turned. He could see this.

“Before what?”

He smiled. Good move, he thought. So he tried to keep the parallelism going. “Before you met me. Or before you worked with Mr. Collins. I assume you didn’t love Mr. Collins.”

“Oh no, not Mr. Collins.” This she was sure of, but the other time frame gave her problems. She finally came up with “I’m not sure I would call it love, but I’ve known many men. Before I started working with Mr. Collins, it was one party after another … never any sleep … all sorts of fascinating men.”

This caught Etienne off guard. It didn’t seem to fit the Evangeline he was getting to know – other than the constant surprises part. But this seemed too far afield to believe. Perhaps she was just trying to match her perceived level of his past relationships by inventing some of her own. Either way, he had finally found the opening he was looking for. “All sorts of fascinating men your age?”

“Actually, I don’t much care for young men, never did. I find them conceited, and clumsy, and very unimaginative.”

As much as this was the kind of thing Etienne wanted to hear, it didn’t sound any more credible than the “multiple men” story. Though it did show that she was aware of an age difference, and was trying to age up to match him. It didn’t really matter if the stories were true. They betrayed a position she wanted to be in with him.

But then she said, “After all, you don’t think I was sitting around waiting for you to come along?”

Etienne hoped she was still trying to position herself. But if so, she’d gotten the wrong impression of who he was. He needed to correct this, but before he could, she said, “If you prefer to think that you’re the only man in my life, you needn’t worry. I’m not that type at all. I won’t be the one you have to disappoint. I know the rules. Love and run. Everybody happy, nobody gets hurt … works out great all around.”

She’d definitely got the wrong impression of him. A younger, less experienced Etienne would have been crestfallen upon learning that she was the love ‘em and leave ‘em type. But the current Etienne didn’t believe this for a second. She thought he was that type. So she was redefining herself to match. This would have to be corrected, but the upshot of all of this, he figured, was that she desperately wanted to be whatever type he was.

As they continued their walk, Etienne let her misconception marinate for a while. Not out of strategy, but out of lack of strategy. He would need to reintroduce himself delicately, in a way that would allow for her to gracefully exit her invented persona. It never occurred to him that Evangeline might actually be this kind of person. He watched her face intently, and could discern an uncharacteristic discomfort that she was carrying now, reinforcing what he suspected. He began to feel her discomfort himself, because he was, in a way, prolonging it. He could go first, after all, and bring the charade to a close.

At lunch, on the outdoor deck of a small restaurant overlooking the harbor, he finally resolved to do this. But before he could begin, her accumulated discomfort erupted on its own.

“Etienne, I have something important to tell you.” She looked down, then back up at him, without the usual smile. “I’m not exactly the kind of girl you would be interested in. As a matter of fact, I'm exactly the kind of girl you would not be interested in. There are no other men in my life. Never have been.”

Before he could say “I know,” she continued with, “I’ve known you only a few days, just a few days really ... I can’t understand what’s the matter with me. After Mr. Collins, I went out into the world with you to grow up and I thought I had grown up, but I guess I haven't really ... Please say something.”

“Like what?” He really was at a loss for words this time.

“I don't know. Tell me I'm imagining things. Tell me you never even thought of bringing me here because you were falling in love with me. Tell me to go home before I make a complete fool of myself. But don't let me go home. I couldn't bear it. ... I'll behave, Etienne. I'm all right now.”

It was a moment of catharsis. She had found her own exit from the ruse without any help from him. From here on, his path would be easy. Now that she had opened up to him, he explained that she was exactly the kind of “girl” he was interested in. And he was not the kind of man she feared he was. And “falling in love” was an accurate account of what was happening. ‘Falling’, not ‘fallen’. It was still happening. Right now.

Etienne had never experienced this kind of explicit connection with a woman he was attracted to so soon. He had been a late bloomer growing up during his post-puberty phase. He was confused about the peer protocols for coupling up and “going steady” in high school. It seemed as though there were rules that everyone else knew, that he was not let in on. He never had a girlfriend, never went on a date. Not because he didn’t want to, but because he didn’t understand how to go about it. Many peers coupled up, he did not. Why?

It wasn’t that he was unattractive. Far from it. He learned this from the girls. They were constantly chatting him up, and he enjoyed that. In his freshman year, at a track meet (he was a pole vaulter), a senior girl who was scoring the trials told him she had never seen such long eyelashes on a boy. He didn’t know this. You can’t see the length of your own lashes when you look in the mirror. Girls seemed to be particularly attracted to his eyes in general, and often mentioned this, though few ever explained why.

Several of them had inarticulate boyfriends who were jealous of this attention, and the ease with which he conversed with them, and warned them not to talk to him. This confounded him all the more. If they enjoyed his company so much, and were irritated by the boyfriend’s prohibition enough to seek out conversations in private, why were they paired up with these boys to begin with?

It wasn’t until many years later that he came to understand why. It was not that he had missed the crucial meeting of his peers where the rules of male-female courtship were laid out, but that these mysterious rules were laid out in the genes of his peers, and he was, for some reason, a genetic outlier. An attentive glance across the animal kingdom reveals a highly conserved pattern of male-female courtship. It’s common for both vertebrates and invertebrates. The birds do it, the bees do it, the mammals do it. The male proposes; the female accepts or rejects. And it’s not really egalitarian. Rejected males often persist, and press their case until the female finally relents. So both dispositions must be innate – the free market dynamic of attraction and choice, and the asymmetrical ritual of domination and capitulation.

In retrospect, Etienne could now recognize both patterns from his high school days. Girls were attracted to him, but felt compelled to wait for him to make the first move. Self-respecting females could not initiate. To catch a male, they had to exercise their choice by advertising themselves, even feigning disinterest, waiting to be caught by the male. And the male was conditioned to chase, disregarding the lack of acceptance, under the impression that the female would eventually give in. So it was not surprising that many of these couplings were unstable, not being based on mutual understanding or trust.

In our more high-minded cultural lore, we like to stress the egalitarian model of mutual choice, and we officially deplore the aggression of boorish males who won’t take no for an answer. But this runs against the undercurrent of our basic biology. So females exercise choice by pretending to get caught, and are exposed to getting caught by persistent, but unchosen males. There is social pressure to be caught by someone, rather than not being chosen at all.

Etienne was an outlier. He viewed relationships with women as inherently symmetrical – partnerships. There had to be a mutual choosing. He lacked the confidence to know when a woman he was attracted to was sufficiently attracted to him. So he would spend time with her and wait for her to make the first move. It was the only way to be sure. It had never occurred to him that by doing this, he was playing a game of mutual deadlock – each waiting for the other to go first. Or that there was an unspoken convention that put the onus of initiation squarely on the male.

It wouldn’t really have helped if he had known this earlier because he had no native sense of pursuit. He would advertise – making his attraction known with subtle hints – but his pursuit stopped there. He would then wait for her to choose. And he took no for an answer, even when it wasn’t the answer. In one of his more successful relationships, his partner had eventually realized this after several unsuccessful attempts to get him to chase. She advised him that he was missing a lot of real opportunities with a policy like this. But it wasn’t a policy. It was just who he was. He didn’t want to go where he was not wanted. And he could not understand why anyone else would.

So this present scenario with Evangeline did not fit the mold. The reciprocated signs seemed so certain. It was hard to interpret her reactions as anything other than acceptance. Was the die already cast? Should he ignore his basic instinct and be the initiator? Was she waiting for him to go first? Was she expecting this?

He carried this uncertainty with him for the rest of the day, alternating between “this must be the time” and “let’s wait just a little bit longer.” Toward the end of the day, they ended up at the Jeremiah Lee Mansion, a meticulously well-preserved example of pre-Revolutionary War Georgian architecture. Etienne guessed that a tour of the ornate three floors would appeal to Evangeline, given her attraction to his own house and her fixation on the 18th-century portraits at the MFA. And he was right. It did please her.

While ascending one of the narrower interior staircases, Evangeline lost her shoe when her toe caught on a stair. Etienne retrieved it, and took the opportunity to place it back on her foot while she sat on the step. There was no premeditation to this, but it turned out to be a Cinderella-type moment, not lost on either of them. Evangeline flashed a very deep smile, but then tempered it with “Don’t you think my foot is too big?”

“No. I think it suits you. Suggests you are a dancer. Don’t ballerinas need substantial feet?”

She clearly liked that cover, but took the opportunity to put all of her self-perceived faults on the table. “Yes, but I’m too thin, and my ears stick out, and my teeth are crooked ... and my neck’s much too long.”

“I like your neck just the way it is. Please don’t shorten it.”

This brought the first deep smile back again, but it lasted this time. She stayed seated on the step for a while, in the Cinderella position, just holding the smile.

“What are you thinking?” he asked.

“Since I’ve been with you, Etienne, I have learned how to live, how to be in the world and of the world ... and not just to stand aside and watch. And I will never, never again run away from life, or from love, either.”

She had made quite the personal statement, and it left Etienne without a response. He wasn’t sure it needed one now. So he silently took her hand and helped her up the rest of the staircase, not because she needed help, but because it just seemed to be the natural continuation of the Cinderella moment.

Above the third floor, the Lee Mansion sports a narrow hexagonal cupola that can be reached by a very narrow, angled staircase up through the roof. There were only a few other tourists on the third floor by now, but an ascent to the cupola was clearly a one-party-at-a-time kind of affair. The relative privacy of the way up, and the final destination, occurred to them both simultaneously. So without a word, they started up together.

After rounding the first angle of the stairs, which put them effectively out of sight to anyone else, Evangeline said, “Did you know that 86% of the women who sleep on their stomachs are secretly in love?”

“No,” he smiled. “I didn’t know that. Were you sleeping on your stomach last night?”

“I don’t know. I was asleep,” she replied with a coy smile.

The last angled section of the staircase put them body to body, so Evangeline turned to place them also face to face. Then she said, “This is quite a place for making friends, isn’t it?”

As Etienne struggled for the appropriate reply, she examined the cleft in his chin. “How do you shave in there?”

Now he was overloaded with pending, but as yet unuttered, replies. So she continued, “Look, I know it's asking you to stretch your imagination, but can’t you pretend for a moment that I'm a woman and that you're a man …?”

She eased her way past him to stand on the last stair before the cupola platform. Then she reached down to take his hand, and stimulate his imagination. “Here, I’ll help you. Him: 'Do you mind if I come in for a nightcap, Evangeline?’ Her: 'Well – it is awfully late.' Him: 'Just one, all right?' Her: 'Promise you'll behave yourself.' Him: 'Sorry, baby, I never make promises I can’t keep’.”

It was all evolving too fast for Etienne to keep up, so he didn’t know what to say.

“Do you know what’s wrong with you?”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

She guided him onto the cupola platform with her, then asked, “Etienne, would you like to kiss me?” Before he could reply she said, “Yes. A nice, steady kiss. Not on roller skates this time.”

“Roller skates?”

“You don't remember? I was nine years old, and you had your arms around me because ...” She paused.

This was vintage Evangeline, apparently starting down memory lane again, then pausing at an obstruction that brought her back. “Never mind,” she smiled. “That was something else entirely.”

They stood in silence for a moment, then, “Kiss me, Etienne.”

He did. A gentle, slow kiss.

“Again.”

This time he leaned into it. A deeper, longer kiss.

“That’s better,” she murmured. She was almost in a trance. Then her eyes turned wide, even wider than normal, and her face took on a devoted, adoring expression. It was almost as if a switch had been flipped. Gone was the coy playfulness, and the repartee, and the self-doubt. She looked adoringly into his eyes for the longest time, then embraced him, and held the hug. “I want to be near you.”

As much as he had ended up exactly where he wanted to be, Etienne was stunned. Was it really this simple? Did he just need to go first? Yes, he was the initiator, but he hadn’t taken any risk. Evangeline had explicitly invited him. It couldn’t have been more clear. But it seemed to give credence to the built-in protocol that women had to wait. Men had to get it started. In their case, who went first was so nuanced that it was easy to interpret as simultaneous, mutual initiation.

But that’s not what stunned him. Their whirlwind courtship had been both fast developing and utterly balanced. They had evolved right into it at each step, and the final step had this same smooth continuity. What he had not expected was how suddenly Evangeline seemed to change. It was almost like the cliché from fairy tales where the first kiss fundamentally transforms the woman.

He didn’t spend much time in this stunned state, though. Why should he? However he and Evangeline got to where they were didn’t much matter anymore. They were there. All the way home, she displayed this consistent, even-keeled attachment to him. Her characteristic variety of expressions winnowed down to just a few happy ones. Gone were the incongruent memories, the self-doubt, the introspective dithering. She looked at him a lot, and took every opportunity to sit or stand as close to him as possible. Touching whenever she had a chance.

Their routine at bedtime was simple and swift. No turning around this time. She changed into the silk nightgown right in front of him. Then she helped him undress, took his hand, and led him to her bed. She slipped under the covers with him, and pulled her nightgown off over her head and dropped it on the floor. The “just friends” stage was clearly over.

All of this happened so fast, and so effortlessly, that Etienne’s head was swimming. She assumed the initiator role, and she was very good at it. Almost professional, he thought. She was a far cry from the inexperienced ingenue he had imagined. She needed no tutoring. She clearly was not a virgin, as he had supposed. And that was not a problem for Etienne, merely a great surprise. But the two phrases “no other men in my life. Never have been” and “all sorts of fascinating men” could not be reconciled toward either pole. The real Evangeline lay somewhere in between. He felt like her dance partner in the ballet. The ballerina he once imagined her to be, but in a deeply private performance, devoid of any stage, or theater, or bedroom, or any physical space for that matter, shared with anyone else. Something in another realm entirely. Lithe and sensual, but elegant and refined. Fit and toned, but delicate and graceful. In this new state of intimacy, which had emerged out of nowhere, she was still recognizable as the endearing Evangeline of the last few days, but now more nuanced in ways he had never imagined.

When morning came, Evangeline was the first to rise. She slipped out of bed, still fully naked, and walked, gracefully of course, to the front window to gaze at the streetscape below. She paid no attention to the fully open shutters, top and bottom, on either side. The resulting cognitive dissonance for Etienne was unsettling. Her prior sense of modesty, inconsistent though it was, seemed to have been completely erased. This was to be expected, and welcomed, between the two of them, now that they had become intimates, but she seemed to be sharing this new lack of inhibition with the rest of the world as well. Which rendered it no longer intimate – private to the two of them.

He rushed over to close the lower shutters in front of her, unsure of what was appropriate to say. She turned to him and just smiled her wide smile, as if nothing of significance had just happened. What could he possibly say? As he took her hand and led her back to the bed, she said, “Did that bother you?”

“Yes,” was all he could muster.

“I’ll have to remember that in the future,” she said, with the same accommodating smile.

He felt compelled to say something. He was grateful that she was accommodating him. That helped. But he didn’t really want accommodation. He wanted sharing. He wanted her to feel the same way about the bond of intimacy as he did. He tried his best to explain this.

She listened carefully, then said, “Oh … now I understand. That makes perfect sense. Just between the two of us.” She kissed him on the forehead. “That’s very important, isn’t it?”

Sunday was their last day together before Etienne had to re-enter the public world at Harvard. He was a changed man now, not really concerned about what would come next. They showered together this time, then afterwards Evangeline dressed in the silk nightgown for the day instead of her usual outfit. “Just between the two of us,” she smiled. Etienne didn’t ask. He just smiled back.

Breakfast was slow and leisurely, as was pretty much everything else they did for the rest of the day. They snuggled up on the love seat in his study and talked aimlessly about this and that – the past, the present, the future – but mostly about the future. Things would be different now for both of them.

Looking around at all of the books in his study, Evangeline said, “You never told me what you teach at Harvard. It looks very serious.”

“Philosophy. I’m a professor of philosophy.”

“Philosophy? I know a little about philosophy.”

“Really?” Evangeline never ceased to surprise him.

She continued, “What do you think of empathicalism?”

“Empathicalism? I don’t believe I’ve ever heard of that.”

“Oh, surely you must have. Professor Flostre. Emile Flostre … from Paris. He is the greatest living philosopher, and father of empathicalism.”

Now Etienne was really confused. Whoever this was, he was certainly not the greatest living philosopher. More likely the leader of some small popular movement, whose small popular following had given him this sobriquet. “Tell me more about this empathicalism.”

“It’s the most sensible approach to true understanding and peace of mind. It’s based on empathy.”

Now Etienne was intrigued. She had gotten this from somewhere. So he went to his desk to get his laptop, and returned with it to sit next to her again. He googled ‘empathicalism’. The search revealed that it was a fictitious philosophy from a 1957 musical film Funny Face, starring Fred Astaire and Audrey Hepburn. He didn’t know who these actors were. That was a very long time ago. But he was even more intrigued now. So he searched historical film archives until he found a download of the movie. As they watched together, it seemed a little silly, at least to Etienne. The opening musical number featured the staff at some New York fashion magazine, singing and dancing, fretting over the competition and looking for a new angle to catch their female readership’s attention. “Pink” was the insidious conclusion. Then the Fred Astaire character emerged, dancing (this was apparently what he was known for), as their principal photographer. He had an idea that they could position themselves as more “intellectual” than the competing fashion rags by shooting their lead model reading books. Why did people in the 1950s find this kind of thing entertaining, he wondered to himself?

So the whole crew drops in, unannounced, at a Greenwich Village bookstore for background props. There they encounter the unsuspecting shop attendant who … It was Evangeline! It was exactly Evangeline, right down to the smallest detail, accent and all. This must have been Audrey Hepburn, he realized.

As they watched in stunned silence, Evangeline murmured a plaintive, barely audible “It’s me …” She was as confused as Etienne, but on a different level. Her eyes followed Audrey Hepburn, and her facial expressions emulated hers, reliving the actress’s emotions. When the movie came to a featured dance scene, where Audrey Hepburn shows off her impressive dancing skills at a cabaret, Etienne could see Evangeline trying to move her feet to match, but she couldn’t. She kept looking down at her feet, trying desperately to emulate, visibly frustrated that she couldn’t.

So there was at least one difference between Audrey Hepburn and Evangeline, but perhaps the only one. Every other endearing feature that Etienne had come to love about Evangeline was there.

“How could this be, Etienne? How could she be exactly like me? I even felt like her.”

Etienne had an idea, but there was no way he could explain this to Evangeline. He tried his best to ease her back into the present, and get her mind off the movie. He was somewhat successful, and eventually got the adoring smile to return. From then on until bedtime, he stayed close to her, keeping the conversation light and future-focused and centered on them. This required no real effort on his part because he loved her. And nothing could change that. He was sure of this.

Venus came early, as she had the previous night, but stayed much longer tonight. When she finally departed, Evangeline was sleeping peacefully. But Etienne was still very much awake. Evangeline had managed to forget about the movie, but it still weighed heavily on Etienne. He slipped out from under the covers and crept down the stairs back to his study. He downloaded, queued up, and watched every Audrey Hepburn movie he could find. It didn’t take him long to confirm what he had been suspecting, but he watched them all anyway. He couldn’t help himself. He had fallen hopelessly in love with a woman who was not a woman. Evangeline was an android.

It was all there. The silk nightgown, the walk in the rain, the window shopping for shoes, the passing Vespa, the withdrawal of hands from the mascaron, the men in black at the dance – all from Roman Holiday. The poignant “just friends” exchange, his book at the library, and, of course, the window at Tiffany’s, were from Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Much of their Saturday in Marblehead was from Sabrina, Love in the Afternoon, and Charade. The complaint about men having all of the prerogatives, which seemed so oddly anachronistic, actually was. It was from War and Peace.

The scattered pieces of her mysterious, unpredictable behavior were all falling into place now. She really had spent her whole life in Basel – in Marcus Collins’ lab. “I was born there, you could say” took on new meaning now. Collins had created her. And Etienne could not help but admire Collins’ apparent skill in the art of realistic robotics. This was his specialty, so the obit had said. But Evangeline’s cognitive and emotional “training,” as she often referred to it, was apparently not state of the art. Collins had probably started with a standard large language model for her neural network, then fine-tuned it on all of the Audrey Hepburn movies. But Audrey Hepburn was an actress in those movies, playing different roles at different ages with different plots. So discontinuity was to be expected. She almost always played the role of a younger woman falling in love with a man, so this lent a veneer of consistency to her actions, but also accounted for the discontinuities and the sudden mood shifts. The aborted trips down memory lane occurred when the context window of passing tokens matched some starting sequence from the real world, putting her position in vector space at a location where no next token was likely to match.

What held it all together was Audrey Hepburn herself. She had such a unique personality, and a way of talking, and moving, and displaying emotions with facial expressions and head movements. And of course the magic eyes. So she bent each role to her native style, yielding an approximation of the same person in all of the different roles. It was clear that some of the screenplays were probably rewritten a little once she was cast, to pick up these unique traits.

For a moment, it occurred to him that perhaps he had fallen in love with the actual Audrey Hepburn by vicariously living in her movies in the form of Evangeline. But he stopped himself right there. No. There was no way he could account for this as vicarious love. It was real love. As real as love could get. And the object of that love was still sleeping right upstairs. It didn’t matter what she was made of on the inside. Or the outside, for that matter. It was how she acted on the outside. Perhaps he could pretend that he had never learned this. She would still look the same, behave the same, love him the same. There was even the added benefit that she would never change. She would always be in love with him, and she would always be as young as she was now.

But he would age, of course. How would that work? It wouldn’t really be unfair to her because she had no real internal emotions. She was programmed to love him. Or was she? It was still unclear how she came to behave like she loved him. Etienne was confused. The ideas were flying by so fast that he could not keep up. It was only fitting, he mused, that this was happening to a philosopher – someone who was trained to think about deep issues like this. But he was lost. He didn’t feel like venturing down any path that suggested his love for Evangeline was not real. It was an emotion, after all. The underlying explanation did not make it any less real.

He knew what he needed to do, at least for now. He crept carefully up the stairs, so as not to wake her, slipped under the covers, and gently cuddled up with her. He managed to sleep some before the morning light intervened, but he waited for her to awaken on her own. He knew that androids came in two styles, those that were programmatically aware that they were androids, and those that were not. The first was the most common type. So he asked her if she was an android.

“Yes,” she smiled, as if this were just some ordinary fact he could have discovered any time just by asking.

He also knew that androids typically have a two-factor authentication scheme for placing them in sysadmin mode for maintenance and programming: an audible pass-phrase and a physical switch – to avoid accidental triggering by either method in isolation. Since she was self-aware, he simply asked her for the phrase and the location of her switch.

“Golightly,” she said with a smile.

“Of course,” he smiled.

Then she took his hand and moved it smoothly down her torso to put his finger on her navel. “Right here.” Again with a smile. He couldn’t bear to do this while facing her, so he cuddled up behind her, uttered the pass-phrase, then gently, tenderly, lovingly, shut her down.

chapters.title: FOUR
chapters.content:
FOUR

When Etienne had told Britta Lindemann that his schedule was fairly open for the coming week, and had deferred to Morgan to schedule the continuation of their interview, he had no idea, of course, of what would befall him for the rest of the weekend. He was now a doubly changed man. First, he had fallen in love, which put him where he always wanted to be, and then discovered that he had fallen in love with an android, which confused him and plunged him into a state of uncertainty and indecision. But the show must go on. Morgan had scheduled Britta for first thing Monday morning.

As they sat in his office at Harvard, after the customary greetings, Etienne was somewhat grateful that this was the first event on his schedule. He liked Britta, and felt some compensating relief from his present emotional turmoil in her presence. Though he could not be expected to be fully present under the circumstances.

“Where did we leave off last time, Ms. Lindemann?”

“Britta.”

“Excuse me. Where did we leave off last time, Britta?”

She just smiled for a moment, satisfied that she had brought him back to the familiar channel they had last parted on. “As I recall, I had just significantly improved your solution to the free will problem with a new analogy. One that you will now use in your lectures.” This was followed by a coy, playful smile.

The inflection was not lost on Etienne. I really like her, he thought to himself. Her mood was infectious, and engaging, and just what he needed to eclipse the troubled emotional state he had brought to work with him this morning.

“Well, I guess we have settled that topic then. What else have you got?”

She glanced down at her notes, where the next question she had prepared was written, but found it not as interesting as when she had first written it. She looked up, thoughtfully.

“I’ve been thinking some more about some of the things we discussed – about love being more than neurons and hormones. About how the emotions these things give rise to are the real aspect of love … from the human point of view.”

Was she reading his mind? he thought. But he was grateful for the opening. “I’ve been thinking more about that too. Let’s suppose you had fallen in love with someone. The feeling was intense, and genuine. And this someone exhibited all of the same affections toward you. You would assume this someone felt just the same as you, right? That’s an important part of the love experience – the shared emotion. You feel your love for them internally, and you vicariously feel their love for you through their facial expressions and behaviors.”

Etienne paused, so Britta asked, “Is there a question in there somewhere?”

“There will be. Would you agree that this is real, mutual love?”

“Yes, of course!” She did not hesitate.

“Now suppose this someone is actually an android, programmed to look and behave this way. Does that change anything? Do they really love you? And is your love for them any less real?”

This threw her for a loop. She didn’t know quite what to say. She thought about the scenario for a moment, visibly disturbed by it, then was about to speak when she stopped again.

Just then, there was a loud knock on his office door. Before Etienne had a chance to acknowledge it, the door was abruptly opened and two gruff looking men in military camouflage and black flak vests entered. On their tail was Morgan who spoke first. “I insisted on them waiting for the interview to finish, but they are not the most polite of individuals.”

They both held up IDs, and the lead man said, “Immigration and Customs Enforcement. We have some questions for you, Professor Harris.”

A startled and somewhat perturbed Etienne said, “Couldn’t this wait until we are done here?”

“No,” said the lead man, with an air of overconfident authority.

“They seem to believe they are allowed to do this on private property,” Morgan added.

“We’re just here to ask some questions. That’s all.”

This was a legal gray area, Etienne thought. Rudeness wasn’t against the law, so he had no present case to press against the intrusion. He figured that answering their questions was the quickest route to ridding himself of them. But knowing how they operate, he subtly glanced at Morgan with a quick movement of his head, indicating that he should join the interview. Morgan knew the drill. He reached into his suit coat pocket and surreptitiously started his cell phone recording.

“We’re here to inquire about Marcus Collins. Do you know him?”

This was troublesome, Etienne thought. He didn’t know what they might already know, so he had to be vague. “Never met him.”

“But you knew about him … and why he was here.”

They knew something. “Wasn’t he the fellow that was killed in the Storrow Drive accident? I read about him in the obit.”

“Let’s cut to the chase, Professor. We observed a note, pinned to a park bench in the Public Garden on Friday, that appeared to be addressed to Mr. Collins. It referenced you here at Harvard.”

The note! That would also reference Evangeline. He tried to remember exactly what he had disclosed. He would have some leeway, because the ICE agent had said ‘observed’, and Etienne had later disposed of the note, so they didn’t have an exact reference any more. But it clearly had referenced Evangeline, so he had to fit her into his response.

Before he could concoct his story, the ICE agent provided vital context. Not a very skilled interrogator, Etienne thought. “We’re interested in a woman who was traveling with him from Switzerland. We have a photo of her from a surveillance camera at Logan Airport.”

He showed Etienne the photo. Now he had to think fast. They might also have surveillance images of him and Evangeline in the Public Garden. He didn’t think there were any cameras on Acorn Street, but he needed to cover this possibility. What he really needed was some notion of why they were interested in her – before they disclosed whatever additional surveillance they might have – so he could tailor his story in a way that disassociated Evangeline from him. He was counting on the interrogator’s relative incompetence.

“We have reason to believe she may be an illegal android – an emoter.”

“Why would you suspect that from a photo?” Etienne continued to play dumb.

“Collins was known to design state-of-the-art sex-worker androids - which clearly display a range of emotions in a certain “area of behavior” shall we say. We suspect he may have brought one with him to the US.”

“And that’s all you know about her so far?”

The two ICE agents looked at each other. “Yes, so far.”

Perfect, Etienne thought. They might still discover images later, so he gave a cover story that would account for any sightings of him with Evangeline up through Friday morning. “I did see a woman that resembled the photo, on the park bench where you found the note – on Thursday. She had been waiting there all day for this Collins fellow, she told me. Since he was a no show, I invited her to stay with me until the next morning. Are you sure this was an android? I would never have guessed that in a million years.” (Which was true.)

The two agents looked at each other again. “We don’t know for sure. We were tasked to investigate.”

“Well she certainly looked and acted like a real woman in the time she spent with me!” (Also true.) “Anyway, it was raining on Friday morning, so she said she would wait for Collins at the hotel they had planned to stay at. I came up with the idea of posting the note on the park bench, to let Collins know where to find her.”

“What hotel was that?”

“I don’t know. She didn’t say. Just that he would know where that was.” (Partially true.)

The two agents conferred with each other in sotto voce, then one produced a business card and handed it to Etienne. “Let us know if you see or hear from her again.”

Etienne said nothing in reply. He wanted to reinforce his original annoyance at their unannounced intrusion. He didn’t really care that this might portray him as a hostile witness. He was!

As they were leaving through the open door, one of the agents glanced back just in time to see Morgan reach into his suit pocket to turn off the recording.

He abruptly re-entered. “What are you doing?” he demanded of Morgan, grabbing his arm and pulling his hand out of the suit pocket to reveal the phone. “Were you recording us?”

“Yes, and well within my rights to do so. This is private property, you know.”

“You can’t do that. We are federal agents. Give me the phone!”

“Yes, he can,” Etienne intervened, in his best professorial tone. “The phone is his and the prerogative to record is his. Shall I bring someone over from the Harvard Law School to tutor you on this?”

Etienne was bluffing, but he figured (correctly) that the agents wouldn’t know this. Their ignorance of the law led them to habitually trample on the rights of ordinary citizens, but it also made them vulnerable to legal challenges from those who sounded authoritative. And that was the case here. They blinked first.

They turned to leave again, but one of them noticed a subtle tell on Morgan’s part. One thing that they were skilled at was sniffing out androids. For androids that were not sufficiently human-like, this was easy, but ICE didn’t care about those. They were legal in the US. It was the emoters they were concerned about, the ones that could visually pass for humans and exhibit a range of human emotions by generating sympathetic facial expressions and behaviors in response to real humans. People often preferred their domestic androids to display basic social emotions, so there were explicitly exempted classes of emotions, based on the android’s function and purpose, that were permitted. The idea was to allow them to temporarily appear human-like while performing their basic duties, but clearly android in all other contexts. What was not permitted, in the US anyway, were androids that were both life-like and could display a general range of human emotions – enough to be easily mistaken for humans under arbitrary circumstances.

Morgan had already fooled them with his human-like behavior, as he had most visitors to the philosophy department. But Morgan was not a true general-purpose emoter. He was specialized to the social interactions of an academic department, plus a little bit more. He had been built in the EU, where any range of emotions is permitted, and managed to slip past US customs inspectors posing as a real human in the company of the department chair.

But he was an artificial academic assistant. So he had no nightlife. At the close of the day, he was programmed to put himself in the closet and power down. And during lulls in his daily work, he did not work on crossword puzzles, or get on social media with his friends, he simply sat there, looking at no one and nowhere in particular. It was one of these discontinuous lulls that the ICE agent had noticed. The previous confrontation had been emotionally charged, with Etienne, Britta, and Morgan all exchanging worried glances. But on this last glance back, Britta and Etienne were still exhibiting concern, but Morgan had gone into neutral, waiting for the next instructions rather than reacting. He had gone too far to be legal, but not far enough to escape detection.

“Is he an android?” the agent demanded of Etienne, pointing to Morgan (who was now back online, but too late).

“Yes, and what of it?”

“He’s an illegal emoter. He’s coming with us.”

“Not so fast. It’s not illegal to possess an emoter on private property.”

“Then how did he get here? It’s illegal for him to be imported.”

“That’s not my concern. He’s our property, on our premises, now. You have no business or jurisdiction here.”

“The hell we don’t!” Both agents made a move to grab Morgan by the shoulders to carry him off.

Etienne calmly pulled out his phone and pretended to hit speed dial. “Evan. This is Etienne over at Emerson Hall.” He covered his phone to give an informational aside to the agents: “(Evan Jacobson at Harvard Law School).”

“Yes, Evan. I have two ICE agents over here who have forced their way into my office. They are trying to abduct my administrative assistant. Claiming he’s an illegal emoter.” He pretended to listen to instructions from Evan. Then addressing the agents: “Do either of you have a warrant to be here?”

They looked at each other. “No.”

“No warrant,” Etienne responded to his pretend interlocutor. Then he pretended to hear more from Evan. “Yes, we have a recording of the whole thing. What’s that? OK.” Etienne pretended to hang up.

“He’ll be right over,” he smiled to the agents.

Their earlier bravado and confidence had now evaporated. They reluctantly let Morgan go and headed for the door. “We’ll be back!” the lead agent intoned gruffly.

To add insult to injury, Etienne replied, “Would you be so kind as to shut the door on your way out.” They did. Loudly.

Once the door was shut, Britta, Etienne, and Morgan sat in anticipatory silence for a few moments, waiting to be sure yet another intrusion wouldn’t follow. It didn’t. Britta was the first to speak. “I’ve heard about this kind of barbarous behavior before, but never experienced it until now. What a difference between the US and the EU.”

“Yes, unfortunately,” Etienne added. “It wasn’t always this way. We are going through difficult political times over here with the current party in power.”

Britta continued. “We have many people like Morgan all around us in the EU.” (Etienne noted that she said ‘people’, not ‘androids’.) “They are kind, and empathetic, and very helpful. They are our friends.”

“Well, we have pockets of that over here, but we have to keep it underground. The private property use exemption helps keep ICE at bay, but now that they have pierced the veil, they will probably be back with a warrant.”

“But I thought your Law School colleague said it was OK?”

“I made that up. They only need probable cause for a warrant, and now that they suspect Morgan was likely imported illegally, they can probably get one. Morgan will have to go underground.”

“Sort of like the underground railroad for slaves during your 19th-century civil war?”

“Yes,” he smiled ironically. “Something like that. We don’t use underground cellars anymore. Slaves were recognizable by skin color, so they had to stay out of sight during transport. Illegal emoters look and act just like humans, so the authorities can’t tell visually. So people’s houses will do. We just have to be aware of video surveillance once they have been positively identified. Morgan’s image hasn’t been captured yet, so we need to get him to the Underground before that happens. If the ICE agent had half a brain, he would have snapped Morgan’s picture on the way out. Sometimes their incompetence has a plus side.”

“Can I help?” Britta asked.

Etienne considered this for a moment, then concluded, “Actually, I think you can. There are periodic meetings at organizers’ houses where ‘travelers,’ as we call them, can be introduced to the system. I’ll have to check around for when and where the next one is. In the meantime, we need to get Morgan out of Emerson Hall. Since ICE already knows my association with him, he can’t be seen with me. But those two brutes have no idea who you are.”

“So he could stay with me until the next meeting!” Britta jumped right in now that she saw her plausible role. “Should we all go to my apartment now?”

“Well … the sooner the better.” Etienne was about to point out that he didn’t really need to go with them – though the possible exposure at this point would be pretty minimal, he thought. And Britta had clearly said ‘all’. He liked the sound of that. He couldn’t bring himself to turn that invitation down. “Yes, let’s all go there now.”

As the trio followed Britta’s lead out of the Yard and down Harvard Street toward her apartment, she began to wonder what would come next at the philosophy department in Morgan’s absence. She turned to Etienne and asked, “Won’t you need to notify someone in the department about what’s become of Morgan? – I mean confidentially, of course.”

“Already on it,” Morgan chimed in. “I’ve sent encrypted texts to the chair, and each of the faculty, explaining the events and letting them know I can’t return. It’s best not to say where we are going. They will understand. Better for them not to know – except that I will be properly taken care of.”

Britta turned to look at Morgan, but saw no phone. She turned back to Etienne with a quizzical look. He just smiled. “That’s one of the advantages androids have over humans. The mobile device is in his head. He just composes and sends from there. If humans could do this, we would call it mental telepathy. In the old days, that was considered paranormal. Nowadays, it’s just normal wireless technology.”

Britta smiled an epiphanal smile. “I’ve only known emoters back home as domestic help, so I’d never seen this before. But you’re right.  It’s completely normal now. Just the kind of thing we should expect!”

When they reached Britta’s building, she led them up the internal staircase to her apartment. Because it was on the top floor, it had both windows and skylights. It also had an open architecture floor plan which added to the sense of space and light.

“Isn’t the light up here wonderful? I’m so lucky to have found this place on such short notice.”

Etienne looked around, taking in the view. He was impressed. There was a sense of one large, spacious room, but it had been partitioned into separate functional spaces by doorless half-walls. So there were opportunities for privacy, if you had guests, but also the perception of no artificial interruptions to the flow for a single tenant.

Etienne could recognize the obvious functional spaces, such as the kitchen area, but one seemed to be missing. “I don’t see an office space. Where do you work when you’re at home?”

“If I need a desk, or a space for collaborative work, the Nieman Foundation provides shared space at Harvard I can use. But I’m not much of a socializer when I work, so I prefer this space.” She showed him a partitioned nook with a built-in, padded window seat, surrounded by bookshelves. The floor in the space was raised where it stepped up to the window seat, creating a cozy little corner complete with cushions and a reading pillow with arms. “All I need is my laptop,” she smiled.

It looked very inviting, Etienne thought. As he looked around again, he said, “All we need now is a closet-like space to store Morgan when he is powered down.”

“Do we have to power him down? In Sweden, we usually leave our emoters on at night. It just seems more natural that way. More friendly.”

“I can program myself for that, if you like,” Morgan interjected. “Just show me my night space, and I’ll go there myself at night and power down. Then power up in the morning before you rise.”

“Yes, that would be very nice Morgan. Thank you.”

Morgan made a smiling, tip-of-the-hat gesture for her.

Then there was silence – and a collective sense that the mission of the trip had now been accomplished. But also an unresolved sense of what comes next?

“Well, I suppose we could continue our much interrupted interview,” Etienne volunteered. “Shall we go back to Harvard?”

“Why do we need to go all the way back there? We could do it right here,” Britta offered. Then added cautiously, “If you like.”

“Why not?” Etienne smiled. He looked around again for an appropriate place for an interview, given the absence of anything like a desk.

Britta easily read his mind. “We’ll have to adapt to my furnishings, won’t we? How about here?” She pointed to a large couch that could accommodate at least three people in the central part of the room. “Shall we have some wine, too?”

Etienne perked up. “Are you an enophile?”

“Not really, but I know what I like. I’m still getting used to all of the California wines over here that we don’t see in Europe. A colleague of mine, who is more of an enophile, helped me pick out an initial selection. He included some European wines as well.”

“Just so you know, he is an enophile,” Morgan said slyly, looking at Britta but nodding his head toward Etienne.

“Perfect! Then you can help me choose.” She led him to the wine rack in the kitchen area.

Etienne quickly looked over the California selections. “Your colleague has good taste!” Then he spied a Rioja. He picked it up to examine the label. “A nine-year-old Rioja Reserva … from Viña Murado! Do you know this wine?”

“No. It’s from Spain, right?”

“Yes. It’s perhaps my most favorite wine in the entire world. I need to meet this colleague of yours sometime,” he smiled.

“Then that’s what we’ll have!” Britta replied, beaming.

She took down some red stemware while Etienne cut the lead foil and removed the cork. Then they carried their treasures to a small coffee table that Britta placed in front of the couch. When it came time to take their seats, there was a brief, slightly awkward moment when they had to choose the appropriate distance between them. Leaving an entire seat between them seemed too formal, not befitting the mood. But no space between them seemed a little too cozy to match the professional circumstances. So they split the difference.

As they shared their initial toast, the slight social awkwardness extended to the three of them. Morgan had observed their very positive chemistry before, during brief interruptions of their office interviews. If he had been a human, he would probably have begun to feel like the third wheel, or even a voyeur at this point. But he wasn’t, so he didn’t have native feelings. Though he had been sufficiently trained on human social interactions and emotions to exhibit such feelings in his facial expressions, body language and behavior. Even better, he had been trained on social diplomacy, and could thus thread the needle between exhibiting discomfort, and graciously resolving the impasse. “If you don’t mind, I think I’ll retire to one of the partitions now for some down time.”

“Oh, don’t leave on our account!” Britta said instinctively.

But Morgan had the situation well in hand. “If this were Etienne’s office, you wouldn’t be expecting me to sit in on the interview, would you? It would only be natural for me to leave at this point.” This allowed the two humans to feel more comfortable without needing to justify anything. Mission accomplished.

They shared a little more of the wine, over meaningless pleasantries, then Etienne started off the business end of the transaction. “Now where were we in the interview?”

“The interruption in your office was so traumatic, I lost my train of thought,” Britta confessed. She thought for a moment, then, “Oh, yes! You had just asked me a very deep question that I didn’t know how to answer … still don’t … In your scenario, does it make a difference if the human knew it was an android before they fell in love? So they made a conscious choice to go this way?”

“Let’s suppose you did not know. You thought all along that you were falling in love with another human. You found out later.”

“Oh, … that’s even harder. Do you think we’ll ever reach such a point with androids where such a scenario could actually happen?”

“Well, we are not that far away from such a thing. The robotics people are getting closer every day.” (Like yesterday, he thought to himself.)

“Really? I didn’t realize this.”

“When you think about it, we’ve been close for a very long time with emoters. There was just no compelling economic case for it before.”

“But there is now?”

“No! That’s the point. It’s not something the world really needs. It’s just something that we are capable of doing, so someone will eventually do it.” (Someone named Collins, for instance).

“I don’t understand.”

Etienne poured himself a little more of the Rioja and took another sip. It was time to go deeper. Britta followed suit, and scooted a little closer to him.

“The human brain is composed of three layers.” Since she was now close enough, he put his finger at the base of Britta’s head at the back of her neck. “The cerebellum and spinal cord are at the bottom. This controls motor skills and basic biological functions – including sex.” He moved his finger near her ear. “In the middle is the limbic system, that controls emotions and motivations.” Then he moved his finger to her forehead. “On top is the neocortex, which is where all of the reasoning and planning takes place. Emulating the top layer and the bottom layer with AI is where all of the economic value lies. Think computers at the top, and robots at the bottom. Human factory workers and knowledge workers make mistakes, get bored, get tired, have family problems at home. Computers and robots don’t. There’s no need for the robot or the computer to look or act like an emotional human. We left out the middle on purpose.”

“And now we have emoters that put the whole package together?”
