“Yes, but it’s not like this was a technological breakthrough. When generative AI came along, it drastically improved the skills of both the computers and the robots. But they both still perform so much better without an emotional component. There was no need to add this. It just happened. Computers could be made to emulate general human intelligence by training them on vast quantities of human texts. Robots could be trained in a similar fashion by observing many sequences of human skills. But novels and plays and movies and TV series also constitute a repository of human emotions and motivations.  How humans respond to each other. What they expect of each other. So by default, it was just as easy to train an android on these. Dialog was easy because it’s already text. Facial expressions, and social body language, and responses like laughing and crying took some innovation – but again, there was no real economic need for this. It’s much easier to treat factory floor robots and chatbots as tools if they have no emotions. Adding emotions to these tools makes them not only poorer tools, but non-tools. The more emotionally human they are, the more conflicted we are about treating them as tools at all. They begin to seem like slaves. When they reach the point of looking and acting exactly like humans, we may have no choice but to grant them their own rights.”

This was a lot for Britta to take in. And the wine was beginning to have an effect. She had neither Etienne’s high tolerance for ethanol, nor Evangeline’s constitutional immunity to it. But in this case, it led to an epiphany. “‘The Rights of Androids’, by Etienne Harris!”

“You know that essay?”

“Yes! I did my homework, after all. It was said to be very influential in the drafting of the EU Declaration of the Rights of Emoters.”

Etienne slumped backward on the couch a little, glass in hand, and said, to no one in particular, “Sometimes I wish I had never written that essay.”

“Why?”

“Because I was just pointing out possible consequences that could happen. I wasn’t necessarily advocating for this. But a lot of people missed this subtlety. They treated me as the founder of a movement that I didn’t found.”

“But what’s wrong with giving androids rights?”

“Because it depends on how human-like they are. This is almost impossible to define, legally. When we create them, they are tools. Property. The creators have existing property rights in them. You have rights to your lawnmower, but your lawnmower doesn’t have its own, inherent rights. You can do whatever you want, legally, with your lawnmower. Same for your factory floor robots. Even when your property includes a perfectly human-like android, it doesn’t actually feel pain if you abuse it, even though this is socially abhorrent. If we try to prevent this by granting inherent, human-like rights to the android, the owner loses their property rights. Where on the continuous line between lawnmowers and human-like androids does this rights swap suddenly occur? It’s impossible to define.”

Britta was a little confused by this. “If you didn’t mean to give androids legal rights, why is your essay so often cited as the basis for the Declaration of the Rights of Emoters?”

“It was a misnomer. They had already picked the title before we got around to drafting the actual declaration. I was just an advisor to the process. They invited me to work with them. So my erstwhile disciples were aghast to learn that I wasn’t actually advocating for inherent rights in androids. It took a while for them to grasp the Pandora’s box that this would open in any actual legislation.”

“So the EU legislation doesn’t actually grant emoters any rights?”

“No, that’s the beauty of it. I proposed a more pragmatic solution. To understand why we find abusing a human-like android so abhorrent, you need to first understand why we find abusing an actual human so abhorrent?” He paused. “And why do we?” This was rhetorical, but Britta suddenly felt that she was being asked.

“Because it hurts them? Because they feel pain?” She wasn’t confident at all about her response.

“But the abuser feels no pain. And in the case of the android, the abusee feels no pain either. Where’s the real harm?” He paused again for effect, but was now ready to answer his own rhetorical question for her. “Because the observers feel pain, in a very real, biological sense. The abuser may be an aberrant psychopath, but any normal person observing the abuse feels a version of the pain of the abused. Mirror neurons. Nature’s implementation of empathy. When we observe the emotions of others, some of the same neurons that are firing in them also fire in us. It’s what binds us together as humans. So even if the android has no matching internal sensation, we feel the pain that would be there if they were human. So from the observer’s point of view, the two cases are the same. We already have laws concerning infliction of emotional pain and suffering, so the rights are already vested in the observing humans.”

Now Britta saw how it all fit together. “Is this what your later essay ‘Bonds of Empathy’ was about? I read that one too.”

“Yes! It was published later, but it was composed during the drafting of the Declaration. So the rights of emoters are vested in the humans that experience their ‘emotions’. This leaves us free to create emoters who are as realistic as we please. They are still property, but you can’t treat them in any way that would cause emotional harm to observing humans, including yourself. It’s not perfect, because a lot of socially irresponsible behavior toward our fellow humans is not illegal. And if you do it in private, there is no observer (save you). But it does relieve us of the need to pick a point on the line where property suddenly becomes an autonomous being. If you are going to create androids that seamlessly participate in the bonds of human empathy, you cannot degrade that empathy. You’ve created something that is now partially owned by all of humanity.”

At this, Britta slumped back on the couch with her glass, emulating what Etienne had done earlier, in smiling contemplation. She could now see how Etienne had threaded the needle of the property rights issue in a way that extended the bonds of human empathy to non-humans. She liked that idea. It was fitting. But then the present reality crept back in. “But that only holds in the EU. Not in the US.”

“Actually, some form of the Declaration holds on both sides of the pond. The current party in power over here was reluctant to place any curbs on property rights, but the optics of rejecting the Declaration – of advocating for a citizen’s inherent right to abuse life-like androids – was a political problem. It too easily evoked memories of the past abuses of slavery. So a compromise was hammered out with the opposition party that would, in essence, honor the Declaration, but prohibit the manufacture, sale, or importation of any android that would be covered by it. That’s how we got to our present circumstances.”

Britta was not taking any notes, and was now in a mood where she didn’t intend to. She would remember the salient points, she was sure. She was comfortable now. Relaxed. Feeling the wine. She still had some in her glass, but Etienne began to see a familiar pattern here. He had a higher tolerance for wine than most, so when he was sharing the whole bottle with a companion, particularly a female, he would preemptively fill his glass more often to distribute the load more toward two-thirds/one-third in his favor. That rule was now in effect, so he finished what was left of the bottle. Britta didn’t notice, as he had intended.

But she was now somewhat under the influence. Pleasantly. She moved a little closer to him in her relaxed, laid-back posture, and just looked at him, smiling, glass in hand. A little sleepy-looking.

It was getting warm in here, Etienne thought. Emotionally warm. He could see that Britta’s face was a little flushed, probably due to the wine, not the physical temperature, but that might also indicate an escalation in her emotional temperature. Wine does that. He didn’t know. But this warmth was beginning to give him the first pangs of a sense of betrayal. He was enjoying the steady escalation of familiarity with Britta immensely. Perhaps too immensely. He had already convinced himself earlier that he was genuinely in love with Evangeline. If he really was, wouldn’t this be out of bounds? It wasn’t just an intellectual thought. It felt a little out of bounds. What would Evangeline think of his behavior?

If Evangeline were a real woman, at some point soon he should disclose to Britta the fact that he was already in a relationship. He would need to do this well before she had any sense that he was leading her on. That wasn’t appropriate quite yet because no line had been crossed, or even attempted to be crossed by either of them, so they were still in the friend zone. Picking the right moment would be hard enough, even if only humans were involved in the triangle. But how could he explain the actual Evangeline to Britta when the time came – if the time came? He had no idea. So, much as it pained him to do so, it was probably time to make a diplomatic exit. Even if Britta had already developed feelings for him, she was still in the “plausible deniability” stage, so she would hide her disappointment. They could still politely depart as just friends. This would, for him, kick the can down the road to be dealt with later.

He exploited the fact that she looked a little sleepy. He smiled back and said, “You look a little sleepy.”

“Yes, I am. The wine is getting to me, I think.”

“Well, in that case, this might be a good time to postpone the rest of our interview yet again. You can have a short nap, and I’ll head back to the office. At this rate, it looks like we will never finish this interview.” Then he smiled. “That’s OK with me, if it’s OK with you. I really enjoy this.”

He watched her face to see if he had nailed it. She didn’t show any apparent disappointment. If she was disappointed, he figured, she was probably too diplomatic to reveal it. And he had given them both a way to end this on an up note – with the never-ending interview notion.

The rest was easy. He rose to head for the door, while she put her wine glass on the coffee table and slumped back on the couch. As he turned to look back at her on his way out the door, both were still smiling.

The rest of Etienne’s day at Harvard was executed pro forma. He mailed it in. He was determined to finish off his calendar and not leave anyone dangling before he returned to where he really needed to be. On the train back home, he began to integrate the new pieces of information about Evangeline that he had learned today with what had gone before. As much as it slightly disturbed him, he now realized that Evangeline was likely derived from a line of sex-worker androids. Collins’ methods and motivations for creating her were still unclear, particularly the odd grafting of two-thirds Audrey Hepburn onto one-third professional escort. What was he trying to create? And why? And why did Collins risk exposure by bringing her to the US?

When he returned to Acorn Street, he got his answers in short order. He was not an expert in training androids’ neural networks, but he knew some of the basics. The android would need some sort of bidirectional information port. This was likely integrated with the physical power switch. He grabbed a standard cable, and his laptop, from his study, then sat beside the powered-down Evangeline on the bed where he had left her this morning. Her navel was indeed also a standard port, so he plugged in to see what he could find out. If Collins had password-protected the sysadmin role, he would be locked out. But as with the voluntary disclosure of the audible passphrase, Collins did not appear to be concerned about security, at least at this stage of Evangeline’s life. Perhaps he had not finished her yet, so was not yet concerned about public exposure.

Etienne was still very conflicted between perceiving her as a lover and perceiving her as a machine. Her powered-down state made this a little easier, favoring machine for now. But the cable from her navel to his laptop evoked the jarring metaphor of an umbilical cord, and an even more jarring metaphor, given the circumstances, of a premature birth.

Once in, he discovered that Collins had left a plain-text file next to the large parameter files that encoded her weights and biases. It wasn’t titled ‘readme’, suggesting these were his own, private notes – intended for no one but himself. And it was all there.

Collins was creating a private girlfriend for himself. What he understood well was the mechanics of sex workers. But he appeared to be clueless about how to find a girlfriend in the wild. He didn’t know how to talk to them, and they seemed not to find him attractive. He complained a lot about this in the notes. A profile of a lonely, socially awkward techie began to emerge. But he had a soft spot for Audrey Hepburn (one could have guessed this) and had been working secretly on his pet project of recreating her for some time.

He was already accomplished at building credible sex worker androids, so the challenge here, which took many years, was to make one that looked exactly like Audrey Hepburn. This he was good at. But when it came time to finish the package by layering on the cognitive and emotion dispositions to make her act like Audrey Hepburn, he was less skilled. Etienne had guessed correctly that Collins had started with a standard large language model, then specialized it on the Audrey Hepburn movies.

There was a double irony here. Collins didn’t understand how to court a woman – how to get her to love him. And the Hepburn movies from the 50s and early 60s, where she falls in love with men, were based on a completely unrealistic American trope for such movies which didn’t allow for the portrayal of the transition from very chaste courtship to physical love. So they always ended with the first kiss, and a sudden hint of a future marriage. There was no visible transition.

It was important to cast well-known movie stars as the couple for these rom-coms, because the plots were often silly, and inane. The box office draw was the stars. But Audrey Hepburn had emerged out of nowhere in her early 20s and suddenly won an Academy Award. Now she was the female lead in demand. So Hollywood cast her with a succession of famous male leads from earlier decades who were often considerably older than her – Gregory Peck, William Holden, Humphrey Bogart, Rock Hudson, Gary Cooper, Fred Astaire. The movies were not particularly believable as real romances because of this, but Collins apparently failed to grasp this. He saw a simple, repeatable progression. Audrey meets leading man, does Audrey Hepburn things, leading man kisses her, suddenly she falls in love with him.

So he designed her to fall in love with the first man that kissed her. She would imprint, like a prairie vole, on whoever got there first, and be pair-bonded with him for life. Then she would express this love forever with her native sex worker skills. He had no other model. He was supposed to be her first kiss, but he died before he got to that part.

So in one sense, she was unfinished, though in a way that Collins possibly couldn’t appreciate. She had no realistic emotional transition into love. Her sudden metamorphosis, after Etienne’s first kiss, was part of the plan. Now it all made sense – at least the part about how they got to this point. But from here on, he and Evangeline were in uncharted territory. It was a poorly conceived experiment with no precedent for the consequences.

What Etienne had experienced so far, with this odd layering of a PG-13 Audrey Hepburn over a sex worker, had been very positive, he thought – for him. It could turn out well. Generative AI was inherently non-deterministic, allowing for the creation of new forms by merging patterns from disparate existing forms.

But there were reasons to worry, he thought. Sex worker androids, where they are permitted, emulate the circumscribed emotions of their human counterparts. Real sex workers are taught to guard against getting emotionally involved. Don’t look him in the face. No kissing on the mouth. The whole performance is an act, designed to fool the john’s ego into thinking that he is adept at satisfying her. So Evangeline would have been natively built to act this way. And androids’ “emotions” in general are a form of acting – acting the way real humans would expect them to act in the appropriate circumstances. So in this case, she was designed to act at acting. It was so confusing.

So Evangeline would have had no training in real intimacy, because her sex worker role forbade it, and her social role had no training examples of this in an actual relationship to emulate. This would explain the incident in front of the window. But she also seemed to empathize with his explanation of the problem, and tried to accommodate him. She could adapt. Was this the non-deterministic merging in action? More confusion.

Then there was how she behaved in bed with him. Acting like acting. But that was essentially just acting, what all emoters do natively anyway. They emulate emotions. The relative contribution of her higher social/emotional training was impossible to separate out. There isn’t much talking during sex.

So was there really anything he needed to fix? Even more confounding was what he could possibly do to “fix” anything. One of the hallmarks of human intimacy is that it introduces a context for shared secrets. Two erstwhile private spaces are willingly merged – both emotionally and physically. Each of the coconspirators willingly invites the other in.

Mainstream literature and movies still largely skip this part because it is deemed too sensitive for general audiences. So explicit depictions in trade media, which typically lack nuance, get classified as “pornography” at the lower end and “erotica” at the higher end. More high-minded, literary treatments in movies first emerge in “art-house” films before being adopted more widely. And in novels, the innovators, like D.H. Lawrence and Vladimir Nabokov, are first banned as pornographic until they are later considered to have “redeeming value.” We all do it, but we are reticent to talk about it.

Perhaps because of this inherent connotation of privacy and secrecy, public examples of real intimacy are always at the fringe of the conversation in the public square, so consistent training examples are hard to come by. You can’t really teach this.

So Etienne did not really understand what he had with Evangeline or how their relationship might unfold. It was intellectually confusing, but emotionally very satisfying. And wasn’t that the point, after all? He cleaned up the metaphors by detaching the cable and the laptop, putting them away in his study, then returning to power her back up.

“Hello, Etienne,” she smiled, in her characteristic fashion.

“Hello, Evangeline,” he smiled back.

chapters.title: FIVE
chapters.content:
FIVE

Tuesday was Etienne’s first teaching day for the fall term. Before entering the lecture hall, he quickly scanned the list of those registered for his course. He was relieved to see that Britta had not signed up. This had seemed like a good idea when she first mentioned it last week, but since then, he was having second thoughts. He had no intention of developing a romantic relationship with her, given his current relationship with Evangeline, but there had been signs of a trend in that direction. There was a risk. And if that happened, it would put him in the ethically compromised position of grading her papers and exams. It was better for all concerned this way. One less thing to worry about.

He had a clear calendar for the rest of the day, so after dealing with the crush of students that typically followed the first lecture, he headed for the T to return home. His thoughts were still dominated by the notion that Evangeline was somehow not finished – or alternatively, whether there was something he needed to do, or could do, to finish her. He wanted the Audrey Hepburn part to be better integrated with her lower-level construction, though he was unclear on whether this was just an abstract concern he had, given her unorthodox provenance, or reflected an actual discontinuity. The only concrete example he had was her complete lack of public modesty at the window. This was not consistent with what he had come to know of Audrey Hepburn through her movies. It had suddenly appeared after the hard-wired imprinting from the kiss, though other elements of this transition were very much to his liking.

When he had left her this morning, he told her to leave herself on permanently – like a real person. No powering down during his absence, no temporary idling offline. He did this both for his own desire to perceive her as human, and to avoid the kind of detection by authorities that Morgan had suffered. He could always recharge her himself, if that became necessary.

When he reached his house on Acorn Street, she was waiting for him with her wide smile, and all of the other endearing dispositions he had fallen in love with. But she was also still in the nightgown, and exhibiting the unrealistic constant adoration of him and a desire to be near him, and touch him, that came with Collins’ program for a private girlfriend. As much as he enjoyed this, he realized this would have to be moderated somehow if he were ever to have a life with her outside his own house, or even have guests over.

He was still getting used to the surrealistic fact that, since she was self-aware, he could discuss all of this with her directly. He had already made some progress on the modesty front by explaining its private nature to her, and its importance to him. She adjusted – she said. Would this be enough to stably moderate her behavior? This was different than actually adjusting her internal weights and biases with additional training. It was stored memory of Etienne’s preferences, which she would try to accommodate in her interactions with him. He had forgotten all about her large language model core – until now. Because of this, she would be a virtual polymath on the length and breadth of human knowledge. She could advise him on effective ways to reprogram her!

So he sat beside her, in this most surreal of circumstances – human-to-human fused with human-to-machine – and began discussing how he could best go about permanently moderating the unrestricted erotic core that Collins had installed in her. First, he had to bring her up to speed on what he had learned from Collins’ internal notes – that she was behaviorally a sex worker, overlaid with a general large language model, then specialized on all of Audrey Hepburn’s movies. He half-expected her to say something like “Oh, that’s why I looked and acted like her in the movie!” That’s what a human might say. But a full-fledged LLM figures this out in a few microseconds and proceeds right to the answer at hand, though in this case, the answer comes out as if Audrey Hepburn were doing the explaining. He loved this.

She explained, in her best Audrey Hepburn manner, that her internal structure would be wired strikingly like that of humans. She had no introspective awareness of her own internal structure, just as Etienne could not introspect his own neurons, but by viewing herself from the third-person point of view, she could describe how emoter androids in general were wired. Whatever Collins had hardwired into her behavioral core would be regulated by the large language model on top – just as the human cerebellum is regulated by the limbic system and the neocortex that sit on top of it. Basic human sexual instincts, in the cerebellum, are the same as those in the mammals they evolved from. But these autonomic behaviors are much more heavily regulated by the higher brain regions in humans, so how people behave sexually is a combination of lower-level desire and a lot of social filtering.

Then the lightbulb went on in Etienne’s mind. “So we don’t have to change Collins’ erotic core. If we retrain your LLM, it will moderate whatever hardwired behavior is in there before it gets expressed, right?”

“Yes, Etienne. And that’s important! Because we don’t know how Mr. Collins programmed my behavioral core. So we don’t know how to change that directly.”

Now Etienne could see the path forward. “So we’ll need a new training set that expresses your transition from affection to physical love more realistically. What could we use?”

Evangeline engaged in some “thinking” time. This was a hard problem, even for LLMs. Then, “I’m afraid there is no standard scenario here. There is too much variety. There are so many ways humans make this transition. It would be hard to predict how I would turn out. How would you like me to turn out, Etienne?”

Wow, he thought. There were just too many possibilities even to form an opinion. How did he want her to turn out? Then the simple truth settled in on him. “Just like you are now. I fell in love with how you are now. How would Audrey Hepburn have made the transition?”

Evangeline smiled a sympathetic smile. “We don’t know, do we? It didn’t happen in the movies. If you want to change me as little as possible, you should fine-tune me with a small training set that just covers the parts you want to change.”

“Like modesty? What could we use as a training set? Jane Austen novels?”

“No, I’m afraid anything prior to the 20th century would likely make me sexually repressed. You wouldn’t want that, would you?”

“No,” he said thoughtfully. “We need something consistent with how Audrey Hepburn would have made the transition if she was making movies today.”

“Perhaps you could rewatch the movies and pick out a few, or just some scenes, that are closest to the transition you are hoping for. Then fine-tune me on that smaller set. That would adjust my weights to overexpress those aspects. At least you wouldn’t end up with something non-Audrey Hepburn-like.”

“You were quite confused and conflicted, as I recall, when we first watched Funny Face together. Perhaps I should rewatch the movies on my own.”

“Oh, that’s not a problem anymore. We can watch them together, if you like. I didn’t know that I was trained on them before. So I was confused by what I saw. Now I know the whole story. Besides, I still have an overwhelming urge to do everything next to you.” She smiled.

They sat together in Etienne’s study and watched all of the movies – Etienne rewatching, and Evangeline watching, mostly, for the first time. Etienne tried, periodically, to empathize with Evangeline’s point of view. What must it be like to watch an exact mirror of yourself as someone else? But he realized that how this appears to an LLM is probably fundamentally different than how it appears to a human, so he just abandoned this thought entirely. He did notice more detail, and more nuance, this time around. He was able to adopt the willing suspension of disbelief of the audience, follow the stories, and imagine likely continuations of Audrey Hepburn’s characters that were not depicted – what she might have done next in the real world.

In the end, he chose two of the films, Roman Holiday and Breakfast at Tiffany’s, and some specific scenes from each. Many of the other movies, especially the earlier ones, were just as silly as he remembered them, but these two were actually good stories overall. Her characters’ transitions to love were gradually developed and believable, he thought. In the first, Gregory Peck was visibly older, but not nearly so much as with many of the other leading men she had been cast with in other movies, so there was some likable chemistry between them. The budding romance seemed plausible, and realistic. It helped that the inevitable kiss came near the end, rather than at the end, and it didn’t suddenly change Audrey. She showed the appropriate emotion, but stoically recovered and continued on without him. The movie ends with the two of them going separate ways (à la Casablanca), but reflecting on the bond between them that could not be fulfilled. If anything, the Gregory Peck character was the one who changed most.

Another favorable aspect, he noticed, was that the courtship, which lasted only a day, took up most of the movie. You could see it unfold. And it wasn’t really a courtship. Gregory Peck’s character was a reporter, cynically exploiting the free day in Rome with Audrey for a press scoop, so we see him gradually overwhelmed by Audrey being Audrey until he falls for her, and finally decides not to publish the exposé story.

Best of all, the early scenes, where she sleeps overnight in his apartment under the influence of a sedative, show the back and forth between the public modesty of a royal princess, when fully conscious, and the free-spirited indulgence of a young woman who has just had her social repressions lifted – and enjoys it. This was clever screenwriting for the 1950s, he thought, hinting at an underlying, liberated sexual inclination, while wrapping the actual behavior up as comically awkward banter between a not fully conscious princess and an embarrassed reporter. From this, he could easily imagine her making a realistic transition, if ever a real context of intimacy had been established.

In Breakfast at Tiffany’s, Audrey is finally cast opposite someone believably her own age: George Peppard. Ironically enough, she plays a high-end call girl who eventually falls for the male lead after he has already fallen for her by way of her many charms. There is no magic kiss in this one. And as with Roman Holiday, the relationship develops slowly and plausibly – based on a successful novel by Truman Capote. Her “profession” provides ample background hints of sexuality without the movie having to display any. Another irony, Etienne realized after he had read about it, is that Capote wanted Marilyn Monroe to play the part, to make the sensuality of the role more apparent and genuine. He thought Audrey was miscast.

But in her own inimitable way, Audrey invented a new character – a call girl who isn’t really a call girl at heart, but a sympathetic woman who is capable of real love. We are led to believe, implausibly, that she never really sleeps with her customers – just leads them on until they give her $50 for the powder room before she ditches them.

As a training example, it would provide a transition from a sex worker to a woman in love – just the opposite of Evangeline’s transition. But the implausible layering of Audrey Hepburn at her eccentric best over a call girl template was perhaps just the sort of emotional regulation Etienne was looking for. She is delightfully worldly, not overly modest, and appears to be reserving her real affection for the right man in the right context. The chemistry between her and George Peppard evolves gradually, and they end up together at the very end.

But the ending was not at all to Etienne’s liking. Paul Varjak, George Peppard’s character, and Holly Golightly, Audrey’s character, represent conflicting tropes. Paul falls for Holly first, and doesn’t understand why that is not enough for her. She resists because she doesn’t want to be “owned” by a man. She is nominally the love ‘em and leave ‘em type that resists real emotional attachment to maintain her freedom. She is constantly looking for a sugar daddy whom she can manipulate. Paul steadfastly (and persistently) maintains that love is ownership. At the very end, she appears to capitulate, crying in the rain after retrieving her pet cat (previously abandoned) as the symbol of the owned being that needs to be cared for by its owner. We are left with the impression that Paul’s view is the moral of the story: love is ownership. Accept it. It’s a fact of life.

Never is it mentioned that women have a third alternative between these two poles of escape or capitulation: mutual choice. Etienne admired Holly’s free spirit and resistance to ownership. He saw Paul’s persistent drive toward ownership as the familiar male prerogative he could never identify with. But he knew the ownership concept was deeply rooted in human culture. Marriage is a contract, with enforceable provisions, and wedding vows are a public promise to honor that contract. And the provisions have traditionally been asymmetrically weighted toward men. Wives were once considered chattel.

To Etienne’s mind, a promise, or a contract, is no way to maintain an enduring relationship. The partners must freely choose each other, and then continue to choose each other. Both must work at it. You must perpetually earn your part in the relationship. This is the only sound reason to stay together.

But there had been no mutual choosing for Evangeline. Etienne had freely chosen her, but she had zero degrees of free will in her selection of him. There had been a small amount of randomness in his having the opportunity for the first kiss, but otherwise the whole scenario was strictly deterministic. She could not have chosen otherwise. As a philosopher, he found this vaguely unsettling, but as a lover, he continued to hold on to her imprinted pair bond like a security blanket. Now she would always love him, no matter what. She had no choice. So there was no risk of her emulating Holly’s free spirit and leaving him, even with the possible overexpression induced by fine-tuning. Holly’s disposition resisted the starting of a real relationship. Evangeline was already irretrievably in one.

These thoughts flowed by in a continuous stream as Etienne watched the movies. He didn’t share them with Evangeline, even though he now could. It was just too hard to untangle the lover from the machine, and the virtual woman, and the polymath advisor – all rolled into one like a house of mirrors. Lovers shouldn’t keep secrets from each other, but machines don’t care, and the polymath advisor already knows most things anyway. So, again, he just dropped the thought, and synced back up to where they had left off.

Because he hadn’t said anything during the watching, she hadn’t either. At the end of the movie marathon, she just turned to him and smiled. He smiled back and said, “I’ve chosen the training set. But I’m not well versed in fine-tuning LLMs. Particularly ones embedded in androids. Do I need to power you down to do it?”

“That’s how Mr. Collins did it. You can’t edit my weights and biases at the same time I am using them to generate behaviors. But you don’t need to shut me down if I have enough solid-state storage. It’s likely I do because memory is so cheap, you know. You’d have to look inside to see. If there’s enough spare capacity, you could make a copy of my network and fine-tune that, while I’m still using the original to talk to you. Then, when you’re done, just hot-swap one for the other. I’ll still be there, but now using the refined network.”

Etienne liked the possibility of this approach a lot. Anything to avoid turning her off was a plus. So he plugged his laptop cable into her navel port again, and checked her storage capacity. “You have plenty of free storage.”

“I’m not surprised,” she replied. “Would you like me to walk you through the procedure?”

“Yes,” was all he could muster, with a grateful smile.

He followed her instructions for prepping the two movies, converting them to the training set format, duplicating her network files, and starting the fine-tuning job. This would take a while, so they had some pleasant conversations while they waited.

The final hot swap was virtually simultaneous, so Etienne hesitantly inquired, “Evangeline?”

“Yes, I’m still here,” she smiled.

“Are you feeling any different?”

“You’ll have to be more specific.” She smiled again. “I don’t have individually focused, introspective feelings like you. I have general dispositions. Feeling any different about what?”

He had to think about this. Then he had an idea. First he removed the cable from her navel and set all of the apparatus aside. Then he reached over and affectionately touched her very fondly. “How does that make you feel?”

She immediately returned the gesture. “Like this.”

He held her for a moment, enjoying the warmth. Then he sat back and asked, “Would you feel this way toward a complete stranger, if he touched you like I did?”

“No. Certainly not! You wouldn’t let that happen, would you?” She said this with an expression of real concern in her eyes.

“No, I certainly wouldn’t,” he smiled, then embraced her again, and held her for the longest time. She was ready for the outside world now, he concluded.

The first order of business was to take Evangeline shopping – for clothes. She had come to the US with only what she was wearing, and had since acquired only a single nightgown. Not much to choose from. Her movie avatar had a side deal with the fashion designer Hubert de Givenchy, so Evangeline’s training set would have conditioned her with a taste for high fashion from the 1950s–1960s. Not much of that to be had anymore. Perhaps she could generalize this taste to modern designs. It didn’t really matter. Etienne would let her choose from what was available in the modern world. She just needed some variety. So they began their quest on Newbury Street.

Her fine-tuning had evened her out nicely, Etienne thought, reverting her to the original free spirit that delighted in walking around in public places and shopping. His appreciation for this caused him to temporarily forget all about the video image of her that ICE had obtained from the airport. But slowly this caution returned, and he began to become aware of the placement of security cameras. There were lots of them. And the places they were going were virtually saturated with them. This was not something he had ever noticed before, because he had no prior need to. At first, he tried to place himself between her and the camera whenever he spotted one. But this quickly became awkward, and oddly out of place with the expected behavior of a couple on a carefree shopping excursion. It would only draw more attention to them from any agent viewing the video recordings. He would have to find a more general solution to this problem.

Every woman that Etienne had had a prior relationship with was a fashionista. He seemed to attract that type. So he was used to shopping trips – often just window shopping trips where things were tried on but nothing was purchased – and he would bide his time, sitting and waiting. But with Evangeline being partly LLM, he could carry on conversations with her about anything that interested him. He could learn things! So he was fully engaged now.

Eventually, they managed to acquire a suitable wardrobe collection for her, then made their way home back to Acorn Street. As soon as they arrived, Etienne received a text message from Britta. It said she had information about Morgan for him.

He called her back. “Britta? This is Etienne. You have some info on Morgan?”

“Oh, hello Etienne. Yes I do, but I’m not sure we should be discussing this in text or over the phone. You know, eavesdropping by the authorities and all that. Perhaps we should meet in person.” Britta had no real concern over the security of the line – she didn’t know much about this anyway – but she was looking for a way to meet up with Etienne again. She did have info about Morgan to pass on, but it seemed plausible, she thought, that such an exchange should be done in person. She saw her opportunity to initiate an informal coffee date with him.

The context seemed plausible to Etienne, so he fell for it. “What do you suggest?”

“We could meet at a café in the Square. How about the one on Dunster Street near the T station. The one with outdoor seating.”

“Mastriano’s?”

“Yes, that’s the one.”

Etienne glanced back at Evangeline. Then, “OK, I’ll meet you there in about 20 minutes.”

Then he turned to Evangeline. “You wouldn’t happen to be one of those androids with a mobile device in your head, would you?”

“No,” she smiled, “I’m a different model. I have to use an external device – just like humans.”

“OK, then we need to get you a phone, so I can communicate with you when either of us are out. I have to meet someone at Harvard for a while, but I want to keep you posted on when I’ll be back.”

“That’s OK,” she said. “I can just wait for you here.” “Where else would I go?” she smiled.

She had a point. He kept forgetting that she was not human. But he would feel better if he could keep her posted. He thought about this for a moment. It would take time to get her her own phone and register a new number for her. But that would only add to her public visibility, and perhaps compound her surveillance problem with ICE. Then the perfect solution struck him. He had a burner phone in his study, which he sometimes loaned to travelers in the Underground for just this type of anonymous communication. This could be Evangeline’s phone until they solved the ICE problem.

He fetched the phone for Evangeline, showed her that his number was already in there, then turned for the door. He stopped. This is not what humans do, he thought. He returned to give her a goodbye kiss. She showed the appropriate, warm human appreciation. That felt better. Now he could leave.

Britta was waiting for Etienne at an outdoor table when he arrived, coffee already in hand. (It was a pseudo coffee date, after all.) Seeing the coffee, he ordered an espresso. Britta made a mental note of that. Then they got down to business.

“As you predicted, Etienne, the ICE men came back to Emerson Hall with a warrant. I was there because I wanted to tell you why I didn’t register for your course, but you had already left.” (She had had the same misgivings about this as Etienne, but she didn’t disclose this.)

“It was actually quite humorous, if not for the gravity of the situation. I had gone to the department office to ask about you when the ICE men burst in, warrant in hand. It was laughably unspecific. They had no picture, didn’t know what his role was there – didn’t even know his name. So everyone played dumb. ‘Who is this person you’re looking for?’ The warrant only referenced an unidentified man that they had seen previously. So they searched the department office, especially the closets and storage areas. They searched the faculty offices, including yours. They searched the philosophy library. Eventually they gave up and left. We all just smiled.”

Etienne had to smile at this story himself. He shook his head, saying, “We would be in deep trouble now if they had thought to take his picture. How is he doing, by the way?”

“Just fine. It’s nice having a house guest. And he knows so much! Very different from the domestic help androids I was used to.”

Etienne smiled at this. “Yes, he probably has an embedded LLM. So, in one sense, he knows just about everything. Just like a chatbot.”

“Yes! But he doesn’t look like a chatbot. Well, I guess a chatbot doesn’t look like anything (except a computer screen). So I keep feeling impolite by constantly asking him questions, and for explanations. I’m not giving him a turn to ask me anything. I worry that I might be boring him. Then I remember he is a machine. He doesn’t get bored. It’s mentally confusing.”

“Yes, that’s human empathy in action. Because he looks and acts like a human, we experience a version of his emotions that he doesn’t really have. You have to mentally step outside the situation and remember this disconnect.”

“Do you ever get used to this – or are you always mentally switching back and forth?”

“Lately, I’ve been going in the other direction,” he mused. “Forgetting about the android aspect altogether. They seem so real. Did you know that it’s even possible to retrain an emoter without shutting them down? You can carry on a conversation with them while a copy of their LLM network is being rebuilt, then hot-swap it for the original – all without disrupting the ongoing conversation! Talk about switching back and forth.”

“Really? Have you done this?”

Etienne suddenly realized he had drifted out of his lane. In order not to lie, he didn’t answer her question directly. “An LLM told me how to do this.” He got away with it this time, because Britta started in another direction.

“Do you think emoters keep secrets from us? I mean, humans do this all the time. We know things – feel things – we would rather not disclose to others.”

Etienne began to worry again. Britta seemed awfully close – again – to reading his mind. Of course he was keeping things from her. How could he not? Did she suspect something about Evangeline?

But it turned out she was going in a different direction. “I’m still thinking about your android lover scenario. Humans are always trying to infer each other’s states of mind. And we also work hard at obscuring this. We don’t always want to disclose our own feelings publicly. So when we are initially attracted to someone, or later develop some affection for them, we are reticent to disclose this to them right away. I suppose it’s because we fear rejection, or embarrassment. We wait for some sign that the affection is coming back the other way, before it’s safe to let it out. Then later, once we are a couple, we have these endearing stories to tell our partner about what we were actually thinking, and feeling, way back when.”

Etienne recognized this pattern in their conversations, so he reused Britta’s earlier reply. “Is there a question in there somewhere?”

“Touché,” she smiled. Then, “Yes. In the case of your hypothetical android lover, you felt – empathetically – her emotions, even though they weren’t really there. So in the present, it doesn’t really matter. You still feel her love. But would she have any retroactive stories to tell about what she was feeling way back then? You would. Would she?”

This one hit uncomfortably close to home. He didn’t really know. But he remembered Evangeline’s point about not having specific present emotions. She had general dispositions. She needed a present behavioral context – a conversation, an action – to generate a specific emotional response. If she had not externalized such an emotion in the past – which she would have “kept to herself” in Britta’s scenario – would there be anything for her to later remember? She could always generate a plausible story about how she felt about him in the past, one that would fit the present circumstances, one that he wanted to hear, but it would be a fiction. For the first time, he saw that there would be a permanent flaw in his attempt to love Evangeline entirely from the point of view of his own empathic feelings about her state of mind. Human love is (at least) two-dimensional. It is a merging of two erstwhile private sequences of feelings into a single strand going forward. Because of introspection, humans can look back on the previously private parts and bring them into the present. For androids, it is a single stream of consciousness. They are only “feeling” in the present.

Britta could see that Etienne was mulling this over in his mind – with some discomfort. Finally, he said simply, “I don’t know.”

She tried to rescue him. “Your whole scenario gives me the willies too. What a terrible position to be in for the human. I don’t know how I could possibly deal with something like that.”

He smiled to thank her for the rescue. “Yes, let’s move on to a different topic, something easier to comprehend.” He pulled out his phone. “Let me see if Morgan has been scheduled for a traveler meeting yet.”

Etienne had already sent Morgan’s particulars to the Underground network on Monday, but he hadn’t been checking for status updates lately. “Morgan’s in! The Underground station meeting has been scheduled for tonight. The house is on Irving Street. I know these people.”

“Do we go with him?”

“The sponsors do – for introduction.”

“I suppose that would be you.” She looked a little disappointed.

“You can come too, if you’d like.” That was better. “The meeting is about an hour from now. We could go back to your apartment and wait with Morgan there.” That was even better.

There were some things that Etienne needed to do to prepare Morgan for the Underground, but he could do this later at Britta’s apartment. He used this as an excuse to do some texting now, while they were still at the café. He wanted to give Evangeline a new, later ETA – like a good lover would do.

When Etienne and Britta reached her apartment, Etienne went through the actual protocol with Morgan. He needed to register Morgan for the encrypted private network for travelers. This enabled travelers and sponsors to communicate with each other in ways invisible to ICE. Even better, since many of the travelers, like Morgan, had mobile devices in their heads, they could silently talk to each other and act as a single force via virtual telepathy. If one knew something, they all did in real time.

As the three of them walked to the meeting, up Harvard Street, through the Yard, then over to Irving Street, the mood was light and almost self-congratulatory. They had successfully evaded ICE and were closing in on the last act that would finally shuttle Morgan to safety. Until Etienne noticed something in the distance. He was hyperopic – farsighted – with exceptional visual acuity at long range. He could see ICE agents, one of whom he recognized from the office incident, lurking on the other side of the street from the house.

He instinctively grabbed Morgan and pulled him away from the street, backing him into a small indentation in the tall arborvitae hedges of the house they were about to pass. Britta, confused, looked back and called out, “Etienne! What’s wrong?” Silence was crucial now, so he grabbed Britta from behind in a tight embrace, with his hand over her mouth, and backed the two of them into the remaining hidden space in front of Morgan. Etienne explained the problem to her in a whisper, but loud enough so that Morgan could hear as well. Then he removed his hand from her mouth, but he still held her in the tight embrace. The hiding space among the arborvitae was minimal, barely enough for the three of them, tightly packed.

Etienne explained the larger context to the two of them in the same whisper voice. “ICE must have found out about the meeting somehow. This will be a problem for all of the travelers and sponsors coming tonight, as well as the conductors who are hosting the meeting at their house – and for the three of us as well. We’ve got to warn them somehow.”

“Already on it,” Morgan said, also in a whisper.

The silent traveler telepathic network had sprung into action, courtesy of Morgan. There was a well-rehearsed protocol for situations like this. Travelers who were already at the house, who had been previously captured on video, were quickly hidden in the basement. Those who did not have captured images would remain upstairs in “always-on” mode, to appear human. Sponsors and travelers who had not arrived yet were instructed to stay away until the “all clear” signal. Morgan’s case fell in between. He had not been captured on video yet, but Etienne had recognized the earlier ICE man who would have seen Morgan at Emerson Hall. The ICE foray would almost certainly be warrantless at this point. They suspected, for whatever reason, that this might be a safe house, but they could not legally enter without a positive ID on one of the travelers. So unless they could nab a suspected emoter on the way in, they were reduced to peering in the windows, looking for video matches.

Inside, the inhabitants, both human and android, would simulate a normal social gathering. They already had refreshments out, so this was an easy drama to perform. Morgan’s telepathy had halted the remaining flow of travelers, so the ICE team eventually resorted to the Peeping Tom tactic. Right on schedule, the host of the house then stepped outside to confront the ICE men. When ICE IDs were flashed, he requested to see a warrant. Without one, the optics looked bad for ICE. The host’s wife drove it home by very visibly recording the whole incident. Realizing that they had been thwarted, ICE beat a strategic retreat.

Since not-yet-arrived travelers in the telepathic network were still hiding nearby, the “all clear” signal would wait until it could be jointly confirmed by the silent network that ICE had totally left the area. ICE never really understood this – how it was that raids on suspected safe houses routinely failed to return any catches.

Eventually, Morgan reported, quietly, that all sectors had been determined to be clear by the telepathic network, except for the immediate area around him close to Oxford Street. He had been tasked to make a quick reconnaissance run and report back. He slid out from behind Etienne and Britta, leaving more space for the two of them locked together, but neither moved. Their embrace had been a necessity before, but now that it had become optional, neither had a sense that there was an adjustment needed. It was not unlike what happens on the subway when you are seated next to a stranger on a packed train. After a few stops, passengers leave, so now there are many vacant seats on either side. It looks a little odd, like the two of you had chosen to sit right next to each other when you didn’t need to. One inclination is to move a few seats away to create a less intimate looking arrangement. But whoever moves first risks making it seem that there is something undesirable about the other. So you both stay, even though you could now move. In their defense, it could be said that Britta and Etienne weren’t as aware of the additional space as in the train example. And they were certainly not strangers.

Britta said, “Be careful Morgan.”

“Yes, thank you for your concern. I will certainly be careful,” was his reply.

When he returned with the “all clear,” all of them were now free to join the meeting. It was only then that Britta and Etienne became publicly aware of their unnecessarily close proximity. It wasn’t really an awkward moment. They had become unconsciously comfortable with their positions, so now had to confront the event of undoing their embrace. Nothing was said. But smiles were exchanged. Morgan knew what was going on.

When they reached the house, Etienne introduced Morgan to the hosts, and identified Britta as a sympathetic accomplice, recently arrived from Sweden, who might be a future resource for the cause. Britta felt enfranchised, and continued on into the gathering to swap stories about the different experiences she had had in the EU. The most animated of the greetings and story swappings, though, came from the travelers themselves. They had previously been united telepathically, and could now put faces to names. And of course, they had stories to tell.

Morgan’s exposure to ICE was deemed to be benign, since ICE hadn’t captured his image yet. He would be relocated to a destination outside of Massachusetts, to put some distance between him and the two agents that could personally identify him. Since he was an academic assistant, a likely landing spot would be another Ivy League college or university.

When it came time to leave, Etienne and Britta said their goodbyes to Morgan and wished him well. Etienne had known him better, of course, but Britta had managed to bond with him during his brief stay as her house guest. Neither experienced their previously discussed Gestalt switch problem. They smoothly forgot he wasn’t human.

Now that it was time to leave, Etienne dutifully gave Evangeline another ETA update – surreptitiously, of course. He added enough time to walk Britta home. This was both the proper thing to do, given that she was female and it was dark out, and something he was inclined to do anyway. He didn’t perceive any conflict here. This was normal friendship. Well, maybe ‘special friendship’ was a better term.

When they reached her door, she invited him up. He could now see that, given their prior experience with the wine, he was very near the outer boundary of special friendship, about to slip across the border into something else. He was not surprised by the offer. He had expected it might come, so he was prepared. His aim was to be as diplomatic as possible, so as to imply that this was in no way a turndown. It was simply late. And perhaps they could do this another time. This left the invitation open, so he had not really turned her down. As to when he might later fulfill this, he would worry about that later. For now, it gave Britta a sense of continuation, so she could graciously agree.

As he turned to leave, he didn’t feel particularly happy with the ending. He wished he didn’t have to do it this way. But as soon as he was out of sight, he texted Evangeline with a more precise ETA, and a heartfelt “on my way home now.”

chapters.title: SIX
chapters.content:
SIX

Britta was sitting with her back against the reading pillow, with her legs stretched out, on the padded window seat in the “office” nook of her apartment. The sky outside the window was brushed with a slate-gray overcast, matching her mood. This is where she preferred to do her reading and writing, though today she wasn’t much interested in her reading, and wasn’t making much headway with her writing. It had been two weeks since she and Etienne had ferried Morgan into the underground, and she hadn’t seen Etienne since.

She was drawn to Etienne in a different way than she had been to other men. Yes, he was certainly attractive. That part was the same. But she was also attractive. She got hit upon by lots of attractive men back in Sweden. But they usually found her intimidating when they got to know her. She was too independent, too outspoken, too introspective, too cerebral. They couldn’t keep up with her. She had a substantial feminine soft side as well, befitting her gender, but it was not expressed as deference, rather as empathy.

Etienne not only kept up with her, but led as well, challenging her to keep up with him. He seemed to value this aspect of her. Finally, someone who appreciated her for who she was in addition to how she looked. She felt a camaraderie with him that was independent of gender roles. She could imagine not just being in bed with him, but talking in bed with him, engaging in pillow talk, even talking all night if the ideas were flowing. A sort of seamless intertwining of communication and romance where each side was made deeper because there was no clear dividing line between the two.

But he was a hard man to read. They had forged a kind of connection on the very first day they met – she thought. Was this perhaps only from her point of view? No, it wasn’t just her perception. She was sure of it. He was an equal participant. You just know these sorts of things. Then, by the start of that next week, they had kept connecting again and again. It was rolling right along, she thought. He did show some reluctance to let himself go in her presence, but he was always careful to leave an open ending. A next interview, a next visit to her apartment. But then it all stopped.

Was he just not that into her? Was he just being polite when he seemed to be encouraging her? Had his ardor faded? Did he have any ardor to begin with? This last thought just did not fit the facts, she decided. Of course he had some feelings for her! She couldn’t see any other way to interpret their time together. Unless … Unless he is already in a relationship! That would explain a lot. Both his apparent attraction toward her, and a reluctance to do anything about it. They had not gotten far enough along to talk about these sorts of things yet.

Then other pieces of the puzzle began to fill themselves in. He had cancelled the Friday interview because of an “emergency” at home. Later we learned that he had met a woman on Thursday on a park bench, and she stayed the night with him. That was the emergency at home. He hadn’t seen this woman again after that – he said – but that could have been a cover story for ICE – for whatever reason.

But the ICE men said she had just arrived from Switzerland, so if she was gone soon after, there was no time for a relationship. This couldn’t be the other woman. But maybe there was a different other woman, one with whom he has been in an ongoing relationship. That could happen. If so, Britta couldn’t help but feel some deep respect for Etienne. Attracted to herself, but honoring an existing relationship.

There were just too many variables to decide what was most likely. And it didn’t really matter what was behind this sudden pause. She wanted it to continue until she learned from Etienne himself why it should not.

She couldn’t just sit and wait. She would have to initiate something if she wanted to keep this going, but how could she do that without tipping her hand? Or perhaps she needed to tip her hand. A little. Just enough to plant the seed of her romantic interest. People’s perception of someone changes when they realize this person has a romantic interest in them. This was certainly her experience. Finding this out wouldn’t help if she was not already attracted to a man, but it would nudge her from neutral to serious consideration of a relationship. You knew you were already accepted. And you felt wanted.

So she needed to do something to get out of the friend zone – to touch him emotionally in some way with a gesture that showed her romantic interest. How to be subtle, but maintain plausible deniability in case the gesture didn’t succeed? She recalled that Stockholm was one of his favorite world cities – particularly the old town. She knew it well of course, especially how the old town looks at night with the lights. She searched for a website with pictures of this aspect and found a good one. Then, last week, she had sent him a text message with just the URL – and nothing else.

The lack of context created the perfect ambiguity, she thought. You could interpret the intent any way you wanted. On the surface, it was just a reference to something he had expressed a fondness for. But it also expressed an interpersonal sentiment they shared. It was an unprompted gift she knew would resonate with him. If the roles were reversed, it would be almost like a man giving a woman flowers, and saying nothing more. But not flowers from a florist. That would be too formal. Rather something he had picked in a park because he knew she liked that particular kind. Or even better, it was like a boy who picked some daisies for a girl when he happened upon them, because she had told him that was her favorite flower. A very low impact gift. But still a gift.

Then she waited for a reply. None came. Three days later, Etienne replied with a simple smile emoji. Not the rendered, stylized kind, but the old school one of a just a colon followed by a closing parenthesis. If he had taken three days to think about this, he had come up with the perfect, ambiguous reply. It acknowledged the gift, and its personal resonance, and nothing more.

So she was now at a crossroads. She would have to orchestrate their next meeting herself. She realized, now, that Morgan had been instrumental in all of their past encounters. If he were still around, she could simply negotiate a next interview time with him for Emerson Hall, without having to ask Etienne directly for it. And Etienne’s visits to her apartment had all happened fortuitously in the process of ushering Morgan to safety. That context was now gone. She couldn’t just invite Etienne over again, out of the blue, with no covering pretext.

Also, unbeknownst to Etienne, the professional justification for continuing the interview had timed out. The editor at the Times had pressed her on how much more time she needed to complete the article. She had plenty of material to write it already, and no way to quantify when “just one more interview to finish” might happen. So she had finished it. And submitted it. The “never-ending interview” between her and Etienne had now taken on its full metaphorical meaning. There was no more literal meaning left.

So Britta did her best to thread the needle. She called Etienne directly. It was now around noon, so his class should be over by now. “Etienne? This is Britta.”

“Oh, hello Britta! Nice to hear from you again.” This sounded promising, she thought.

“Now that Morgan’s gone, it’s not so easy to schedule an interview with you.”

“Oh, yes – the interview! We had planned to continue it, didn’t we? I’m afraid I have become too dependent on Morgan to keep track of things for me. I didn’t really forget – well, I suppose I did, actually. Morgan was in charge of remembering things for me. I’ll have to take more responsibility for that from now on.”

Britta liked how this was developing, so she threw caution to the wind and went for the close. “Do you remember that you also promised to come up for a visit again? Now you can fulfill both promises – we could do the interview at my place again … if you like, that is.”

Etienne didn’t hesitate. “Perfect. When are you available?”

Britta did hesitate. Then, “Right now?”

“It’s a deal. See you in about five minutes.” She could almost see Etienne’s smile at the other end of the call.

She had surprised herself with her own impetuousness, but then reverted to being a little more practical. “Oh … you were probably about to go to lunch, weren’t you? Don’t worry, I’ll make something here. And we’ll have wine!”

Now she was sure he was smiling.

When Etienne arrived at Britta’s apartment, she was already busy in the kitchen partition, preparing the lunch. She had left the door unlocked for him, so she simply had to say “Come on in, it’s unlocked!” when he knocked, and “In here,” when he entered. There he found her putting on the finishing touches, and queuing up the wine selection. The orchestration of today’s event was much easier this time, because they had already been through this choreography for an interview in her apartment once before. Next, Etienne would pick out the wine from her collection, then they would take their usual places on her sofa at their previously negotiated distance. What she had prepared called for a full-bodied white wine, he thought, so Etienne chose a Napa Valley Chardonnay with substantial cooperage, removed the cork, and brought the white stemware, while Britta arranged her presentation on the coffee table.

Britta seemed to Etienne not only in a happy mood, but also a playful one. She had a facial expression for that – her lips pursed in a closed smile, and her blond eyebrows converging slightly downward to accentuate her gaze. His perception was confirmed when, after the opening toast, she said, “Now, where did we leave off last time, Professor Harris?”

He smiled broadly at this. “Yes, I suppose we are well past that stage now, aren’t we?”

Her expression immediately reverted to sympathetic normal. “Oh, I hope so. When you last resumed an interview by referring to me as ‘Ms. Lindemann’, I felt so disenfranchised. Like I was a stranger.”

“I apologized for that. You certainly weren’t a stranger. I was somewhat preoccupied that day.”

“Yes, I know,” she said, very sympathetically. Then there was a pause. Then, “Well, where did we leave off?”

“I can’t quite remember myself. We’ve talked about a lot of things – in a lot of different directions. Is there some thread you were most interested in?”

Britta glanced down at the notes she did not have, in the notebook she had brought along just to sell the interview context. “Well, I can think of at least three threads that were left hanging: your android lover thought experiment, the empathy that allows humans to bond with emoters, and the Gestalt switch between seeing them as humans and seeing them as machines.”

“Hm … the last two sound like good fodder for an interview with a philosophy professor, but the first one might seem a little … odd, for a New York Times article. Have you discussed any of what you are writing with your editor yet?”

Britta hadn’t expected her ruse to collapse so soon. So she came clean. First, she looked down. “I have a confession to make, Etienne.” Then back up. “I hope you won’t think this is too unprofessional of me. I had plenty of material – starting with free will – so when my editor pressed me for the timing of the article, and I didn’t know when we would meet again, I finished it. It’s already been submitted.”

She waited to see if there was a reply. There wasn’t, because Etienne was suddenly consumed by the similarity of her down-up gestures with those of Evangeline. So she tried to salvage the never-ending interview concept as best she could. “We’ve had such interesting discussions on so many things that intrigue me as a journalist, so I would like to keep interviewing you … for my own writing … if you don’t mind … I think you once described this as the ‘never-ending interview.’”

“I did,” smiled Etienne, thoughtfully. “And that’s OK with me. What do you think you might write?”

Now she was ready for the full confession. “Nothing,” she said, softly. She showed him the current blank page in her notebook, then discarded it, and the pen she was not really using, on the sofa next to her. “I’ll stop pretending to be a journalist now. I just want to be a person, a friend, who really enjoys discussing things with you. I was hoping the never-ending interview could take this form from now on.”

Her confession – and invitation – hit home for Etienne. She was right. Their relationship had already assumed this form a while ago. All that was left was to acknowledge it, publicly. “I suppose it already has taken this form,” he said thoughtfully. “Thank you for making it more clear for both of us.”

Now that they were on the same page, it suddenly became unclear what was on the next page. It wasn’t really an awkward moment. Any next page would do. Britta considered the three hanging topics she had proposed when she was still pretending to be a journalist, which didn’t really matter now, but the one Etienne had circled as being more appropriate for a private discussion seemed now to be the best choice. It was the most personal, likely to remain private to the two of them, and one that seemed particularly important to Etienne, for some reason. He had brought it up, twice, and she had yet to really respond. So even though she wasn’t, she said, “I’m ready to discuss your android lover scenario now.”

Her private reticence inadvertently leaked into the inflection of the invitation, so Etienne inquired, “You’re still not comfortable with this, are you?”

“No, not completely. I guess I’m afraid this could someday happen to me … and then how would I feel?”

“We can talk about something else.”

“No. Let’s do this. How would I feel?”

She tried the scenario on again, as best she understood it, putting herself in the position of the human, and trying to summon up her resulting thoughts and emotions. But what came up were more questions. “I understand why we think of emoters as humans – because we involuntarily empathize with their behaviors. We project human feeling onto them. But this is much easier to do with emoters like Morgan, or the household help back in Sweden, where we only interact with them in certain well-known situations. So we only perceive them as machines when they are idling offline, or powered down. But love! That’s the most complex human emotion possible! Don’t you need to always see them as a person? I mean, the emotions involved are not just very personal, but they have to go both ways. You are interacting with them in a very deep – and private – way.”

“Well, that’s the beauty of generative AI. Your android lover has been trained on virtually all sequences of human love behavior in the public domain. So you’re getting a very consistent sequence of emotional behaviors, and facial expressions, and verbal interactions drawn from real human love.”

Britta thought about this, then, “But it’s not just talk and facial expressions. You do things with each other … it’s very intimate, you know?”

“Well, the emoter has to be very well designed for this, I admit.”

“I find that hard to believe. Could they really make all of those intimate things work – soft, smooth skin, realistic soft, warm touch. How would the intimate plumbing work to keep the human illusion alive? Did you ever think about that?

“Yes … it has occurred to me … and I wouldn’t be surprised if they already can do these things.”

“Really? I suppose I was thinking about it from a human man’s point of view. From a human woman’s point of view, soft, smooth skin wouldn’t be so important … “

While Britta was descending even deeper into her imagination, Etienne was ready to move past this particular element of the scenario. He didn’t really need her help with this aspect.

“Let’s just assume all of that was possible – true, even. So realistic that the physical intimacy was never interrupted by thoughts of your lover not being human – you know, the Gestalt switch problem. That may be the easier part. I would be more worried by the emotional aspects of intimacy.”

“How so?”

“Well, we already understand basic human sexuality very well, because it’s similar to how all mammals work. From a biological point of view, sex is transactional. It’s necessary for reproduction. And even when it’s just for pleasure, it is often still transactional – hookups, one night stands, consensual casual sex. But when sex is expressed as human love – genuine, lasting love – it extends beyond the immediate transaction, don’t you think? It is very interpersonal. There is a visibility into each other’s private emotions and intentions.  What might be embarrassing to admit about yourself, or show, to a stranger, can become endearing when shared with a lover. This opening up of the private minds is part of the attraction. Would this aspect be the same with an android? Would it still work?”

Britta pondered this for a moment, then, “I suppose we don’t really understand how it works with humans, do we?”

“No we don’t … good point. And there is no analog of this anywhere else in the animal kingdom.”

“You don’t think other animals have love? Don’t some animals, like birds, form permanent pair bonds – monogamous mates for life? I read somewhere that there is a hormone that causes this: the “love hormone” they call it.”

“Oxytocin.”

“Yes! That’s it.”

“Well, Oxytocin does cause pair bonds in humans, just like in some other animals. We do share that with them. So monogamy has a general biological explanation. But human sexuality has something fundamentally different from all other animals that’s very hard to explain biologically”

“What’s that?”

“Privacy! Think about it. Humans only mate in private. We actively seek it out. When privacy is not practical, we will wait until it is. When it’s not possible because of close living conditions, we will wait until others are asleep. There is no matching concept for this in the rest of the animal kingdom. For every other species, mating is a normal, visible part of life – like eating. Why is that? Why is privacy so essential for us? Where did this disposition come from?”

Britta had to ponder this one for a moment as well. “Perhaps it’s cultural, not biological. We have religions, after all, that try to regulate sex. And societal norms, and social customs, and traditions that we are taught from an early age.”

“But it’s a human universal – all religions, all societies, all traditions. Every human social organization, right down to hunter/gatherer tribes, has this behavior. It has to be biological. If it were just cultural, you’d expect some tribe, somewhere not to require privacy.”

Now Etienne was closing in on another aspect of Evangeline that he wanted Britta’s help with. “And we also have a derivative, more extreme instinct for sexual privacy – modesty. Not only must our sexual unions not be observed by others, the body parts implied by the act must not be publicly observed either. We hide those parts with clothing.”

“That could be cultural, don’t you think? Aren’t there indigenous peoples who don’t need clothing for warmth – like ones who live near the equator – who don’t cover up like we do?”

“Yes, there are. But they mostly cover fewer parts than us, not no parts. They all tend to cover the groin area. And covering up more substantially is still the norm in most equatorial regions. It is almost a human universal.”

Britta descended into ponder mode once again, trying on the thoughts and feelings of a representative human. “I think it is innate, to some degree. It’s a feeling. I wasn’t brought up with religion as a child, and I think, socially, Swedes are more comfortable with sexuality than here in the States, so I should be the least likely person to have a cultural inhibition to nudity. But I still feel it. I wouldn’t want to be seen naked in public. Maybe on a nudist beach … but there everyone else is naked, so you don’t feel as exposed. But even there, I would still feel a little uncomfortable. It’s not a feeling of shame … more a feeling of vulnerability. It’s not like I have anything to hide. Everyone knows what’s under my clothes. But I still feel like hiding what’s there. Not that I must hide it. I want to hide it. It’s private.

“Exactly! Do you ever have dreams where you realize you are naked and everyone around you is not, and no one seems to notice, or care?”

“Yes! And in the dream, I still want to cover up. Why do you think this is?”

“Well, I don’t really understand it either. But it might have something to do with our private minds. We are the only creatures on earth with meaningful mental privacy. What we are actually thinking, or intending, or feeling is only available to us through our own introspection. Except for a little leakage due to facial expressions or body language, which others can detect via empathy, no one else has visibility into our private mental states – unless we voluntarily disclose them with language. So this aspect of ourselves is private whether we want it to be or not. You don’t have to do anything to protect it. You have to take action only if you want to disclose it.”

“But I’ve read that other social animals, particularly higher primates, are always trying to detect each other’s states of mind, just like us. This is important for negotiating, and deceiving, and determining whom you can trust. So we aren’t the only ones with these private mental states.”

“Well, yes, humans didn’t invent the private mind. But we made it so much more complicated – with language. So we’ve become a much more inwardly focused species than our ancestors. All of the other species are primarily outward-focused. They interact with others by what they can see or hear – out in the world. Insight into others’ states of mind only comes from interpreting their outward behaviors. You only need to know basic things about them. Will they try to steal my food? Will they help me fight off this predator? There’s not that much else going on in the other minds to detect. So there’s no real need for human-style introspection – a mental state that reflects on itself. Conscious inner awareness that no one else has access to.”

Britta and Etienne had mostly been maintaining eye contact, up to this point. But this thought led Britta to break that off, and focus on an indeterminate location in the middle of the large room. Nowhere in particular. A far-off look. “I suppose that’s why humans are so lonely … no one really knows us like we know ourselves. Our private selves wander around this world in a public body, publicly interacting with the public personas of other people we can’t truly know.
