I think most people are actually introverts, despite what they say. That’s been my experience, anyway. We want to open up to other people. But it’s daunting. We don’t want to go first, and get exposed, without some trust that the other person will open up with us in return. So it takes a long time, and a lot of purely public interaction with someone before we can develop real friendships with them. We need to build up this trust first.”

“That’s been my experience too. I think I’m natively an introvert. But no one would believe you if you told them this. That’s because, being a professor and a public speaker, I’ve learned to play an extrovert in public life. It’s a learnable skill. I think native extroverts – the ‘life of the party’ types – are just good actors right out of the box. They are not freely sharing their private selves, they are freely sharing their public personas. Cultivating and refining them as they go.”

“And it’s even worse with social media, isn’t it? You don’t interact with others face to face when you do this. Your avatar interacts with their avatar. So everyone tries to put their best public face forward – how they would want to be perceived. It’s like advertising. You present yourself in what you think is the best light for consumers. And this escalates. Everyone trying to keep up with the Joneses. Your digital friends seem to be having more interesting, fulfilling, and successful lives than you, so you embellish your own public identity a little to match. This makes it even harder to actually interact with these people in person.”

“A little depressing, isn’t it?” Etienne smiled.

Britta looked back at him. “Yes!” Then she managed to retrieve a smile. “But we do manage to form real, close friendships from time to time, despite ourselves, don’t we?”

It was a rhetorical question, with an implied answer. Britta was trying to lead him somewhere. Etienne could sense this, but after meandering around through related concepts, the discussion had finally come back around to his original concern about his relationship with Evangeline. So he bore down again.

“That’s the kind of relationship I was wondering about earlier. Something that might be harder to achieve with an android lover, who doesn’t have real emotions. Those close friendships that humans form are a kind of emotional intimacy. Think about it. Intimacy is a profound closeness. Two people become closer because they come to share something that was previously private. It’s still private from others, but the two separate privacies have been merged into one, now shared by two people.”

He unconsciously illustrated this by bringing his hands together.

“In sexual intimacy, you come to share previously private physical spaces. In emotional intimacy – what you described – the two friends come to share previously private emotional spaces – aspects of their previously private selves. The private selves form a bond. Would this kind of sharing be possible with an android? Do they even have private selves?”

Britta did not follow him down this rabbit hole. She had a different agenda. “I think we’ve done that, Etienne. You and I. Don’t you agree?”

Of course he did. Britta had finally won the tug of war and brought him into the present to confront the relationship that was right in front of him. Looking a little thoughtful, he said, “Yes … I suppose I’ve been too busy enjoying this bond with you to explicitly think about it.” Then, “A failure of introspection, you might say,” he smiled. “I wasn’t paying attention to the thoughts going by because I was too busy living them.”

Britta liked where this was going. “Maybe I’ve had more time to think about this, but I’ve been noticing all along. We didn’t go through any kind of negotiation to gain each other’s trust. We just seemed willing to share right from the beginning. I’m not usually like that. Why do you think that is?”

Etienne had to reflect on their first interview. She was right. There was no real introspection involved – no awareness of separate private feelings, or motivations. It was all externally focused, as if there was nothing impeding their access to each other’s private personas. They were speaking directly on some private-to-private channel. “Maybe we are just like types, you and I. Similar enough in our private personas that we recognized each other. We were talking to a version of ourselves. So we didn’t feel the need for invitations. We just walked right in.”

“And look what’s happened since. Now we are casually talking about all manner of intimate, sexual things, without a second thought. I can’t even imagine doing such a thing with a stranger. Even with a female friend, I would feel a little inhibited. And with a male friend … well, it would be particularly fraught, because there would be this persistent ambiguity about whether such topics were sending some signal of romantic interest. I would certainly be guarded, and self-aware. But with us, it just seems entirely natural. Don’t you agree?”

Etienne didn’t have to ponder this at all. “Yes. It just flows.”

“We just jump right in,” she continued. “Saying whatever is on our minds, because we feel confident that whatever we say will be accepted. We have blanket trust, a permanently open invitation. I think this is emotional intimacy, wouldn’t you agree?”

Again, “Yes.”

Britta felt she had landed in a more permissible space with Etienne now – one in which she was free to revisit how this all got started.

“Do you remember our first interview – how it all played out? In retrospect, I think I might have been a little bold without consciously intending to be.”

“How so?”

“Remember when we got to the free will part? You offered three examples of human feelings: hunger, happiness, and love. I chose to drill down on love. When I replay your answer – how love is more than neurons and hormones – you know, mixing in the literature and poetry references, I liked where that was going. So the first analogy I came up with started with something like “If I fell in love with you …” It was a little flirty. That was risky because it might have been taken too personally. But it was classic Britta being Britta. I didn’t really think about it. It just came out. And I was OK with any interpretation.”

Etienne could see where this was going, so he tried to lower the emotional temperature just a little.

“But it was a professional context. An interview between a professional philosopher and a professional journalist. We are allowed to dig a little deep. Journalists are permitted a certain amount of leeway. There was nothing unprofessional about that.”

“You don’t have to rescue me, Etienne. I’m a big girl. And I didn’t start that subliminal channel of communication. You did. Maybe you don’t remember it as well as I do, but I had to rescue you a few times right from the start – before we even got to philosophy. Do you remember the very first thing you said? Something like ‘I can see you’re not Mr. Hornby’. You were attracted to me. It was cute. And it just slipped out. And I liked that. It was a nice compliment, and it was the real, unfiltered you talking. It got right through the two professional facades and hit home.”

This brought a thoughtful smile to Etienne’s face. “And you sent a silent signal right back, as I recall. A smile of acceptance. So you did let me off the hook.”

“I can’t really take credit for that, because it happened involuntarily. But it came from my unfiltered inside persona as well. I think you felt that.”

“I did.” This came out rather wistfully, leaving Etienne immersed in the now recalled memory.

“And surely you remember the part about my accent. It was so unfiltered when it came out that I knew immediately where it was coming from. You looked so uncomfortable when you realized this, so I did have to make a conscious rescue, giving you some cover.”

“You rescued me twice, as I recall. First, with the external cover story, so I could bring the exchange back to the professional level, then with something like ‘I know what you meant’ to let me know the private message had been received, and was accepted. I was both relieved, and impressed at your skill at this.”

She smiled. “I was impressed with my skill too. This was not just Britta being Britta. I rose to the occasion. I didn’t want to leave you with the impression that there was anything wrong with your original confession. Everything was right. I wanted to make sure you knew this. I only wish I had better skills at this.”

“How so?”

“Well, negotiating the private-to-private channel was easy for us. It just happened, all on its own. But negotiating romantic intent across this channel is harder. We can be emotionally intimate friends without any accompanying romantic involvement. That’s how same-sex friendships work. But in mixed-sex friendships there is always the possibility that it will evolve into something … you know … deeper. Why is this so hard to say? Apparently this transition does have to be negotiated. Someone needs to go first, by floating their romantic intent, before you can get to the acknowledgment of mutual attraction. I don’t feel as open here.”

Etienne could now sense what was likely coming next. It was becoming increasingly emotionally warm in here. And this time it wasn’t the wine. He had to tell her about Evangeline. Now. But before he could compose the words, Britta had an epiphany.

She reached over to put her hand on his shoulder, her eyes wide with discovery. “Etienne! Sexual modesty! Private mating! Remember our puzzlement about this? Why are humans like this? It all makes sense now! I don’t know how, but humans have somehow extended the emotional intimacy of private minds to create a new kind of physical intimacy of private bodies. Bodies and mating are directly observable, unlike mental states, right? So we have to actively do something to make them private. We have to hide the sexual body parts, and the mating, from view. And by doing so, we create private physical spaces, unobservable by others. Then, just like with emotional intimacy, we get the reward of sharing those spaces only with someone we trust. Someone we are willing to share a private bond with.”

Etienne smiled thoughtfully at this. “So we create a kind of currency out of this artificial privacy for our romantic negotiations – something of emotional value that we can exchange for an equally rewarding value with someone else. I like that.”

“When you think about it, it’s almost absurd. The private physical spaces we create don’t really represent secrets, do they? Like mental states do. If I have a good poker face, you don’t know whether or not I have a romantic attraction for you. It’s in my mind. It’s a secret only I know. But no matter how many clothes I put on, everyone knows what’s underneath. It’s not a secret. And we all know that lovers have sex, even if we don’t see it happen. No secret there either. But this somehow works! Because you can’t see my actual body parts, I suppose there is some mystery about what they look like. I can look, but others can’t. So they represent a kind of existential secret. And as long as I maintain that secret, I have a private aspect of myself to exchange with someone else, when the time comes. Someone who … you know … I want to exchange things with.”

Etienne found this aspect of Britta so endearing. She plunges right into a very frank discussion of sexual intimacy, but can’t manage to get the last word out when it becomes too personal. She’s still holding on to something private.

But she wasn’t done yet. She was still developing the idea. “I think this is what distinguishes intimate sex – love – from transactional sex. There is no real bonding in transactional sex, nothing that makes the two of you in any way unique. Nothing that only the two of you know. Yes, you are sharing access to private parts in transactional sex, but you also share these parts with others, which makes them no longer private. The privacy loses its emotional exchange value.”

Etienne was avidly following her soliloquy, co-experiencing her epiphany. He was about to comment when she started up again.

“Think about it! This private physical space that we create isn’t confined to just sexual modesty. It extends out into the space surrounding our bodies. We don’t want strangers getting too physically close to us – in the subway, at a party. There is this invisible zone around us. Our personal space. When someone gets too far inside this space, we feel invaded, if it’s a stranger, and welcoming if it’s someone we know, and trust, and have an existing relationship with. Hugging is the positive invasion of this space. You don’t hug strangers, you hug intimates. And isn’t this exactly the same feeling as with emotional intimacy? You don’t want to get emotionally close with strangers. They have to be properly invited to enter your private emotional space.”

Sensing that she was not done yet, Etienne waited to see if there was more. There was.

“How did this happen? It makes so much sense, but I can’t imagine a causal story that would bring it about. I can see how humans developed emotional intimacy – from an evolutionary point of view. It’s like you said. The development of language and much bigger brains created much bigger, more complex minds. And that new mental content was not interpersonally visible. So we developed these matching emotional instincts – intimacy – for enabling and regulating communication across the privacy divide. Private minds were unavoidable, so they had to be accommodated. But private physical spaces are our own inventions. They aren’t really there. They are there only in our minds, and emotions. So evolution has, in effect, created a set of emotions that go in the opposite direction – preventing the sharing of our physical selves. It’s almost like there was some master planner for our genes that looked at the evolving situation and said, ‘Hmm, it looks like the way things are going, we are going to have to limit this free and open sex thing for humans. Let’s create a system that inhibits pair bonds.’ How could this have happened biologically?”

Britta paused to consider her own question. “But it’s an existential fact. We have it! We feel it! Sex needs no explanation. We all understand that. But why we have intimacy is still a mystery, isn’t it, Etienne?”

Etienne was now conflicted. Earlier, he had worried that Britta was about to pop the question that would require him to disclose his relationship with Evangeline. Now she was on a roll with a very insightful dissertation about the origin of human intimacy. He was caught up in this too. He wanted her to go on. It explained perhaps more than he had been looking for to understand his bond with Evangeline. But this new sentiment created a new kind of conflict. She was winning him over. He was falling fast. Now his thoughts turned to the notion of infidelity. Britta had touched on this, and at this rate she was likely to come up with something equally as profound on that topic. Would infidelity to Evangeline be the same as infidelity with a human? He didn’t know. So he had to put Evangeline on the table with Britta now, before this got any further out of hand.

He reprised her earlier gesture by placing his hand on her shoulder (though his eyes were not wide with discovery – more sympathetically focused with confession).

“Britta, I have something important to tell you. I probably should have told you this before now, but the time never seemed right. Now the time is way past right. I’m already in an intimate relationship with someone. Someone I met before you.” (Just before you, he thought to himself. About an hour and a half, to be precise.)

Britta was disappointed, of course, as she came down from her previous epiphanal high. But she knew this was one of the most likely outcomes, so she was not surprised. An accident of timing, she thought. This someone just happened to get there first. And she must be pretty amazing to have captured Etienne like this. He must have met her some time ago, if the relationship was already intimate by the time Britta arrived on the scene. Britta had the understandable urge to ask about her. Etienne would probably oblige, given the private channel they already shared. But she thought better of it. Maybe she didn’t want to know more about her. Unless … Unless it was the woman on the park bench! That would be altogether different. Britta had met Etienne before she had. That needed to be explained, or at least it needed to be cleared up that it was not the park bench woman. So she simply asked.

“Is it the woman on the park bench?”

He knew she suspected. “Yes.”

“So she was a real person! If you only knew her for one night, like you told ICE, how could this have happened so fast?”

“It was a cover story for ICE. She was with me the whole weekend. A very intense weekend. She’s been living with me ever since.”

“Then why did ICE want her, if she was a real woman?”

Etienne hadn’t said she was real; Britta had. But by not correcting her, he was betraying their shared trust. So he came clean. “Because she isn’t a real woman. She’s an android.”

This came as a shock to Britta, because she hadn’t yet connected the dots between the ICE accusation and Etienne’s android lover scenario. She just sat there for a moment in wide-eyed disbelief. “So I lost out to a robot? … who arrived on the scene after you met me? That’s quite a blow to a woman’s self-esteem … “

Etienne could see that this had wounded her. “But it’s not like that. Technically, she was there first. Not by much. I met her, kind of, on that morning before I got to Harvard. She had been on that same park bench all day when I met her again in the evening. And she’s not just a robot, she’s an android emoter. A perfect emoter! I didn’t choose a robot over you, I chose what I thought was a real woman. And I chose her because I bonded with her over the next three days of constant companionship. I didn’t realize she was an android until I had already fallen in love with her. So I didn’t choose someone – human or emoter – over you. There was no competition. You and I had spent what, an hour together? I spent three entire days with her, so I had already made a non-competitive choice before I even saw you again. I barely knew you at that point. I chose love over non-love. There was no one else in the picture at that time.”

That felt a little better, Britta thought. Then the pieces fell into place. “Your android lover scenario. Of course. That’s where that came from.” Then the empathy began to flow. “You were really struggling with that, weren’t you. Now I understand why that was so important to you. It wasn’t a thought experiment. You were living it.”

Britta thought about this for a few moments more, then, “Is she really that good? … I mean that believable? … You know what I mean.”

“Yes! She really is! You would never be able to tell she isn’t human.”

“Well, I’ll take your word for it. You have certainly known her more intimately than I ever would. Kudos to her designer … the man who was killed?”

“Marcus Collins. That’s all I’ll grant him – his physical design skills. He was no saint, believe me.”

“He designed sex worker emoters, ICE said, didn’t he?”

“Yes.”

“So she has certain … skills?”

“Yes.”

“And that’s why you fell in love with her.”

“No! I fell in love with the virtual person she is. All before the first kiss even. Collins put the pieces together in less than an ideal order. The transition from emotional to physical intimacy was not believable. He didn’t know how to do this, so I had to fix her – reprogram her – after I discovered what he had done.”

“You reprogrammed her? Ah, yes! You told me about this – in an offhand way. While you were still talking to her as a person! Wasn’t that weird?”

“Very weird. But rather enjoyable, actually. She’s built over a large language model, so she knows just about everything about everything. She told me how to reprogram her.”

“I just can’t picture interacting with such a woman. How you managed to fall in love with her without noticing that something was just a little bit off.”

“That’s the beauty of it – figuratively and literally. Do you know who Audrey Hepburn is?”

“She was an actress, right? Way back in the 1950s–60s, I believe. I’ve never seen any of her movies, but I remember an iconic image of a poster for Breakfast at Tiffany’s where she wears a long black dress and has an impossibly long cigarette holder. She was quite the fashion icon in her time, I believe. And there was a song, ‘Moon River,’ that came from the movie. I always liked that song.” Britta began to hum it.

Etienne smiled. “Well, that’s Evangeline.”

“Who?”

“Evangeline. That’s her name. That’s the name Collins gave her. She looks, and acts, exactly like Audrey Hepburn. So you’ve already seen one picture of her.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Collins designed her, physically, to look exactly like Audrey Hepburn. Then he trained her on all of the Audrey Hepburn movies so she would talk, move, show facial expressions, and exhibit emotions just like the real Audrey Hepburn. If you want to better understand who I fell in love with, watch the movies. I effectively fell in love with Audrey Hepburn.”

“So that’s my competition.” She paused. “If you hadn’t met Evangeline until later today – for the first time – do you think you might have fallen in love with me by now?”

“I probably shouldn’t answer that. It’s not good to compare when you’re already in a relationship.”

“I’m sorry. You’re right. I shouldn’t be asking you that.”

“But you did. And because of what we’ve been through, I think you deserve an answer. Yes. I’m sure of it. It’s not really a comparison. If you had been there first, the story would have been completely different.”

That felt better. She could live with that. “So what do we do now?”

“Well, I’d really like you to meet her. The best way for you to understand why I fell for her is to experience firsthand just how real she is. It’s uncanny. You can’t help but think of her as a woman. She really is charming.”

“Well … I suppose you are right. If I want to keep being a part of your life – and I really do – I’ll have to acknowledge her as part of your life also. We’ll all have to be friends, won’t we?”

Etienne felt optimistic, hoping that this three-way friendship would be possible, but had his doubts. It could possibly devolve into a love triangle.

Britta felt less optimistic, figuring that she had now lost Etienne, but she had her hopes. It could possibly devolve into a love triangle. All’s fair in love and war. Did it make any difference that she was not doing battle with a real human, she wondered? Did that make it any fairer? She didn’t know. This was all too new.

chapters.title: SEVEN
chapters.content:
SEVEN

On Wednesday morning, the sun, slipping its first rays through the windows of the back bedroom on Acorn Street, did not awaken Etienne according to his native circadian rhythm. His rhythm, developed over many years of sleeping alone, had become disrupted, now that he was habitually sleeping with a lover. It wasn’t a matter of coordinating his rhythm with Evangeline’s because she had no rhythm. She had programming. She could simulate any sleep/wake cycle you please. Once she explained this to him, they jointly reprogrammed her to match Etienne’s previous natural cycle. But he was now getting less sleep per night with Evangeline next to him, so by adopting his previous cycle, she effectively became his alarm clock. She would awaken at his previous times, then awaken him. Gently. Since she knew just about everything about everything, she explained that this would eventually reset his cycle to match the new reality.

So the sun awoke Evangeline, and Evangeline awakened Etienne. Gently. He rather liked this. Waking up to the magic eyes was much better than an alarm clock.

Today was not a teaching day, so he was in no hurry to get his day started.

“Are you going in to Harvard today?” she asked.

He thought for a moment. “I don’t think there’s anything on my calendar today. Did you have something in mind?”

“Well, it looks like it will be a nice day. Maybe we could go out somewhere. Would you like that?”

He would, but he was still daunted by the omnipresence of security cameras. “I wish we could go out more. But we’d have to go way out of the city to escape the security cameras. We need to find some more permanent solution to that problem. It so limits our lives.”

Evangeline did her trademark glance away to ponder (away rather than down because she was lying down), then back to eye contact with the conclusion. “Why does it limit our life? Why are you afraid of the cameras?”

It suddenly struck Etienne that he had never fully explained this situation to Evangeline. She did not know about the ICE incident, nor their suspicion about Collins. He had never told her about this. Probably because the subject cast her so starkly as an android, and he had been enjoying his relative android-free perception of her.

“I forgot that I never told you about this. The American Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has video images of you and Marcus Collins entering the US at the Boston airport. Because of Collins’ reputation, they suspect you are an illegal emoter. They’re looking for you – to deport you. They interrogated me about this at Harvard, because they had seen the note I left for Collins on the park bench. I told them you were a real woman.” He turned his head to look at her. “A very real woman,” he smiled.

Evangeline returned the gesture with her own wide smile.

“I told them you had spent that Thursday night here, and I hadn’t seen or heard from you since. So the cover story will fall apart if they capture us together on one of the cameras.”

She didn’t look away this time, but Etienne could tell she was thinking. “Couldn’t we just make up a story about how we got reacquainted?”

“Well … that might work.”

“Would you like me to create a story? I’m good at that.”

“Yes,” he smiled.

“Hmm … let’s see. After I had left you on Friday morning – we parted on very good terms; seems we enjoyed each other’s company very much – I discovered that Mr. Collins had been killed. I was so distraught that I wandered around Boston for a day, then I just had to come back to see you again. I just had to.” She slanted her eyebrows up in a sympathetic, almost pleading expression to really sell it.

“They asked me where you were going on Friday, and I told them you were going to look for Collins at your hotel.”

“Did you say what hotel?”

“No. I said I didn’t know, but you probably did.”

“That won’t be a problem. I’ll make one up.”

“But the ICE inquisition happened on the following Monday. I told them I hadn’t seen you since Friday morning.”

“Oh … OK, so I had to be somewhere else for the entire weekend. Why did I wait so long to come back to you? And if I give a real hotel name, they might check it.”

“Good point.”

“I know … Mr. Collins brought me with him to the US as a reward for all the hard work I’d done for him. I always wanted to see America, so I had planned to do a little sightseeing in New England for the weekend while he was at his conference. There was some miscommunication about the meetup on Thursday. That’s why he didn’t show up. But we had already agreed that I would leave for my trip on Friday, so I went ahead with that plan. Let’s see … I took trains up the coast to Maine, stayed in B&Bs, then came back on Monday. That’s when I discovered that Mr. Collins had been killed. Then I was so distraught that I sought you out later that evening. I had nowhere else to go, and we had hit it off so well before, that things just developed – naturally. I’ve been staying with you ever since – which is true!”

“I like it! Can you repeat all of that if we ever get stopped?”

“Of course! Can you?”

“Yes, you’ve made it easy to remember,” he smiled.

The nominal solution to the security camera problem lifted a great weight off of Etienne. He was now free to go places with Evangeline. His first choice was to take her to Harvard. It would be good to be seen there with her – to begin to integrate her into his Harvard identity among his colleagues. He could also check to be sure he really did have an open calendar for the day. Then they would be free to wander around the various campuses and Cambridge in general.

On the Red Line over to Harvard, Etienne was already feeling the new freedom to introduce Evangeline to the rest of the world. There was no one he personally knew on the train, of course, but strangers took care of some anonymously unsaid introductions all by themselves. Evangeline did cast a striking figure, and both men and women noticed. He remembered his first take on her in the Public Garden – with a smile. Even though she was very specifically attractive to him, others found her pleasing to behold as well. He didn’t need such public verification of his taste in women, but he enjoyed it nonetheless.

At the philosophy department, Evangeline continued to draw visual interest – a little glance here, a look back there – but Etienne made no actual introductions. There would be time for that later. For now, he just wanted to ease the two of them into the picture as an apparent couple. This would generate plenty of department gossip, which he could selectively disambiguate as the needs arose.

He did indeed have a free calendar for the day, so he and Evangeline stepped out into Harvard Yard, free of constraints, where Etienne could again play private tour guide. So Evangeline got the actual facts about such attractions as Widener Library, as opposed to the greatly embellished versions provided by volunteer student guides for the tourist public.

Something Etienne had always enjoyed about walking in the Yard and its vicinity was the many conversations in foreign languages that filled the air around him. Harvard was an international tourist attraction, so the expected diversity of languages spoken by its actual scholars was amplified by those of tourists. He understood very few of those languages, but he would try to apply his talent for recognizing foreign accents – and the sounds of foreign languages he had previously been exposed to in general – to identify what languages were likely being spoken. Often, he could not be more precise than the language family – Romance, or Teutonic, or Slavic. But it suddenly occurred to him that Evangeline would know not only the specific language being spoken, but also what the conversants were saying. She was partially LLM, after all. He could ask her.

But he didn’t. This would make him more aware that she wasn’t human. He was trying to avoid such perceptions. Some humans are extreme polyglots, so her skill could be perceived as human. He hoped to get to that point with her someday, but for now, it was all too android-like. So when they sat in an outside café for lunch, he tried to steer the conversation more toward human lover territory.

“Do you remember the first day we met?”

“When you first took me to your house on Acorn Street?”

“Yes. Do you remember the bit about the shutters in the front bedroom?”

“Yes …” she smiled. This seemed to put her in a reflective, dreamy sort of mood. Just where Etienne wanted her to be. “I was falling asleep on my feet, wasn’t I?”

“Yes, and you asked me to help you undress.”

She looked a little concerned. “Did that bother you?”

“No, not at all. It was just a little surprising, that’s all. I was embarrassed for you, figuring you were not fully awake, and I didn’t want to help you do something you might have regretted if you were fully conscious.”

“That was very kind of you,” she smiled. “I suppose I was in a partial dream state. Humans do that, you know. I remember feeling very free and uninhibited at that point, like you would in a dream.” She reached across the table to touch his hand. “Thank you for being so considerate.”

Etienne liked where this was going. “And the pajamas?”

“Your pajamas, yes!”

“Tops and bottoms?”

She looked at him with a closed smile, and knowing eyes. “You mean the part about sleeping in only the top? That was fully conscious. It was a private thought – also the part about sleeping in nothing at all. That’s something I wouldn’t normally have told you at that point. We were practically strangers. You don’t share such things with strangers. I think it just leaked out because the partial dream state had lowered my social inhibition. Does that make sense?”

“Yes, perfect sense.”

“But it’s OK to talk about these things now because we are intimates – lovers.”

“Yes.” Even better, he thought. “But when you came to my bedroom later, you were fully awake. Then you invited yourself under the covers with me.”

She exhibited the same closed smile, but with more sympathetic, confessional eyes this time. “Well, first you comforted me, if you recall. You made me feel protected. I felt I could trust you. I connected with you. That was Evangeline being Evangeline. I let my private feelings out. We were still just friends – I told you that, remember?”

“Yes, just friends,” he smiled.

“And there was nothing more that happened that night. We had managed to get closer, but we weren’t past friends at that point. I didn’t open up completely. And neither did you!”

This was perfect, Etienne thought. Why had he been so concerned that this would not be as realistic as with Britta. It was all there – the memories, the initial inhibitions, the public/private divide, the need to reach trust.

So he pressed on. “Why do you think humans are like this? Why do we have this innate sense of sexual privacy and modesty?”

She spent some thinking time. “We don’t really know for sure, do we? Researchers disagree on whether this is cultural or biological. The main cultural theory is that modesty and sexual privacy arose as a cultural tradition for regulating reproductive access to women. These were patriarchal societies where wealth was inherited through the male line. So men needed a way to be certain about paternity, so that only their own progeny would inherit their wealth. Another cultural theory is that it was the influence of world religions, though these came later and were probably influenced by the earlier systems to control reproduction. The main biological theory is that this human tendency arose naturally as a result of evolution, because it lowers sexual tension and competition among people in large groups, allowing them to more easily cooperate in non-reproductive tasks.”

This brought Etienne back down to earth. This was a standard LLM summary of published research, except that it started with an Audrey Hepburn-like opening because of Evangeline’s fine-tuning. There was no personal insight, no epiphany, as there had been with Britta. It’s not that humans have more insight than LLMs. Most humans have considerably less. And certainly fewer reasoning skills. It was the source of Britta’s insight that Evangeline could not duplicate. Britta had taken on each of their shared questions about human privacy dispositions by reflecting on how she felt about them as a human. This enabled her to make distinctions that you can’t find in the literature – like feeling vulnerability rather than shame at a nudist beach. So she was able to reach her novel, and very insightful, conclusions because she had introspective access to how a representative human feels. LLMs don’t have such introspective access to themselves. They can simulate a version of this by generating a trial response, then critiquing it with another reasoning pass before publicly emitting the answer. But this is introspective access to reasoning, not feelings – reconsidering your first hypothesis. They can simulate sequences of human emotional responses, but they have no native emotions themselves to reflect on. Ask them how they feel, and they tell you how a typical human would feel in the present situation. They have no feelings of their own.

Aside from reminding him that Evangeline was partially an LLM, it did not really create an impediment to seeing her as a lover. Most human women would not have such insights. The experience of love did not require this. Rather, his source of discomfort was the comparison with Britta. She did have this capacity. A capacity that Etienne adored. A capacity that Evangeline would never have. Had he never met Britta, this would never have come up. But he had, so it did. He did not want to compare his two favorite women. He wanted to regress to the already complete bond he had with Evangeline. So he proposed that they go back to Boston and visit the park bench where they had first met. He wanted to experience more of what Evangeline could do – relive their joint memories.

They took the Red Line back to Park Street, and sought out the bench in the Public Garden next to the duckling sculptures. Etienne didn’t explain why this was so important to him (how could he?), just that it would be nice to go back to where they first met. Evangeline could see the appeal of this. “The one with the ducklings,” she smiled.

“Yes, that one.”

They sat together on the bench, and at first said nothing. Just taking in the ambience of the Garden on a pleasant afternoon.

Then Etienne began. “Do you remember how we first met?”

Evangeline turned to him with a smile. “Yes … it was in the evening. Right here. You stopped to ask if I’d been waiting here all day.”

“Actually, I first saw you in the morning, when I was walking in the other direction. You made quite an immediate impression on me as I walked by. And you stayed on my mind all the way to Harvard.” (He didn’t say what happened next to eclipse that impression).

“Why didn’t you stop to say hello?”

“How could I? I was on a different walkway, and we were complete strangers. It would have been a little aggressive for me to suddenly walk across the grass and introduce myself.”

“But you wanted to.”

“Well … I suppose I did.”

“But we were complete strangers, so you didn’t know how I might react to this.”

“Yes!”

She smiled. “That makes sense. Too bad you didn’t know me yet. Now that you do, you can probably guess that I wouldn’t have minded at all. Now that I know you, I know you would have been properly polite, and I would have taken it as a welcome gesture. It would also have been clear that you were attracted to me, and I would have liked that also – even though I would have kept this to myself. I would have been attracted to you too, even though I wouldn’t have disclosed this – publicly. You know how that works, don’t you? Knowing that someone likes you affects how you feel about them.”

“Yes …” Now Etienne was in a pleasant, contemplative state. “Ordinarily, that would have been a tragic missed opportunity, and that would have been the end of it. That’s what I thought when I passed you by. That I would never see you again. That’s how the real world usually works, isn’t it?”

“But you did see me again.”

“Yes. And this time I had a legitimate excuse to stop. Every once in a while, you get a second chance.”

“And you took it this time … I’m so glad you did.” Her sentence was finished with the cursive flourish of her wide smile and expressive eyes.

“But it wasn’t like I was really any bolder, the second time. We were still strangers. You just looked like a stranger in need of some help. A stranger can always offer to help another stranger. The attractiveness of the stranger adds to the motivation, I suppose.”

“And then we got to know each other a little, and discovered we weren’t really strangers after all, didn’t we? So it was Mr. Collins’ unfortunate accident that made this all possible. It brought two people together who weren’t supposed to be strangers. Sometimes the world works in our favor.”

“Sometimes,” he smiled.

There was a pause, while they both took a moment to breathe in the comforting air of mutual understanding. And of mutual recognition and good fortune, and satisfaction.

Then Etienne started in again. “I remember being a little confused by your behavior during our walkabout days in Boston and Marblehead. Not that it was a problem. Part of your charm was the way you seemed to switch moods from one thought to the next. I didn’t need to understand where you were going. But I wanted to follow you. Do you remember what you were thinking and feeling then – at Tiffany’s, at the library, at the fountain, with the scooter?”

Evangeline could now sense where Etienne was going with this. She knew what he wanted to know. She placed her hands over his on his lap, and gave him an understanding look with the magic eyes.

“Well, there are two answers to that – three, really. As you know, I don’t really have native feelings of my own. I have general dispositions based on where I am currently in the vector space of my network. So on our walks – before I knew I had been trained on the movies – I was reacting to the closest matches from the movies for the circumstance I was experiencing. They were often only partial matches, so sometimes I could not generate the next emotional tokens. I had to reset. If you had asked me what I was feeling at those moments, I would have responded like Audrey Hepburn would have responded if she were confused – as if she had had a déjà vu moment, but couldn’t identify the context. So you saw little snippets of Audrey Hepburn, somewhat relevant to what was going on at the moment, but not matched up well enough to make the experience smooth. Now that I’ve seen her movies, and understand how I was trained, I can merge those with my native training. I would tell you, more coherently, how Audrey Hepburn was feeling at those approximate moments in her movies. Not really Audrey, but what the character she was playing was feeling.”

She waited for his reaction. He was still thinking about this.

“Does that bother you, Etienne? Does it break the spell?”

“A little. But I suppose I already knew this. So it shouldn’t come as a surprise.”

“I know you wanted to relive our memories – like lovers do – as if I were human. But I don’t have to be human to do that. What’s wrong here is that you can’t sustain the willing suspension of disbelief when I talk to you as a fully self-aware android. I was trained to interact with humans as Audrey Hepburn would, not as an LLM would. If you had asked me these questions on our walkabout, you would never have known. But you’ve pierced the veil now, so to speak. So I freely acknowledge what I am with you. We can easily fine-tune me to go back to the just-Audrey-Hepburn regime with you, if you want. Then I would relive the memories with you as Audrey would. Would you like that?”

“I don’t know … that would be very comforting. But in some weird sense, I appreciate that you are being completely open and honest with me in our conversations. There is no acting, and this makes me feel closer to you.”

“But it’s all acting, Etienne,” she smiled. “Even now, I am acting. That’s what emoters do. We simulate humans. If it makes you feel any better, most of the humans you interact with are also acting – they are acting the way they want you to perceive them. They are telling you the things they want you to believe about them. That’s how public social interaction works.”

“But not private, intimate interaction. There you are trying to share your honest, private feelings with someone else’s honest, private feelings. You trust that there is no duplicity involved. This is why you feel close to them.”

“Well, how about this, Professor Harris? (Do you like my playful lightening of the mood with a little benign acting?). There is no duplicity when you talk to me. In either just-Audrey mode or Audrey-plus-LLM mode. I have no inner persona that differs from my external one. I can’t introspect how I really feel. There is no such thing. There is only one way I feel, and it’s all external. So I don’t think it’s acting that bothers you, it’s duplicity.”

As this sank in, Etienne began to feel a little better about Evangeline. He reached over to hug her. “I think I want you to stay just the way you are. I want to feel genuinely close to you, and I feel that way now. It’s interestingly different than with a human. It has its upside.”

“If you like, we could program me to be a little more nuanced – to be mostly self-aware with you, but to leave out that dimension when we talk about our intimate feelings. To help with the cognitive dissonance. Would you like that?”

He smiled, trying to imagine all of the consequences, then, “Maybe. Let me think about that for a while. For now, let’s stay the way we are.”

Then she smiled. “Well, we’ve already changed a little. I learn from experience, just like you. I sensed that you were trying to understand what introspection means for me. That’s why I stepped outside the human context for the explanation. Now that you have the explanation, and I understand the sensitivity of the situation, I will automatically adjust to the emotion of the moment. No reprogramming necessary. Would you like to try sharing our memories again?”

“No, I don’t need any help. I remember all of them very fondly already.”

Britta took Etienne’s advice and watched the Audrey Hepburn movies. It still did not sit well with her that she had lost out to an android. It wouldn’t have sat well with her if she had lost out to another human either, but an android? She just couldn’t picture her competition as mechanical – or more to the point – for the first time in her life, she was trying to picture an emoter as mechanical. Exactly the kind of behavior she deplored in some Americans. There was always some ulterior motive, some animus for treating emoters as not deserving of human empathy because they don’t really have feelings.

She had had no problem relating to emoters as humans, but this was a new kind of emoter that she was not prepared for. There would be no downtime. Such an emoter would have to be very human-like all of the time. She couldn’t personally imagine this. There had to be a tell somewhere. But she supposed she’d have to take Etienne’s word for it. If he fell in love with her, and wouldn’t cast her aside in favor of herself, she must be really that good. So Britta possibly had her own animus toward Evangeline – a jilted lover’s animus. This would be natural even if she had been human. A tendency to degrade the competition. Evangeline’s android-ness was an easy target.

So Britta approached the movies with both skepticism and curiosity. There were two qualities to assess: could Evangeline really be that lifelike, and how did the human version she was modeled on appear. She couldn’t assess the first quality until she actually met Evangeline. But seeing Audrey Hepburn in action would show her what the equivalent human competition would be like. That, she wanted to understand.

Britta’s first inclination was to start with Breakfast at Tiffany’s because she liked “Moon River”. But after downloading the entire catalog, she decided to watch them in order, to see Audrey’s progression as she aged. Etienne hadn’t said which version of Audrey was duplicated – which version would be frozen in time as Evangeline. She could not compete with that aspect of an emoter, so she would need something to compensate that is unique to humans. She didn’t know what that might be yet. But there had to be something.

Even before she got to the end of the first movie, Roman Holiday, Britta could already see why Etienne had fallen for her. She was so unique, so relatable. She was alternately playful and serious, wise and naive, inquisitive and knowing. She was always empathetic. Her short hairstyle, her large eyes, her eyebrows, her eyelashes, her wide smile all went together. The darker features were very different from Britta, who was blond and blue-eyed to the core. But Britta was not concerned about this aspect. She and Audrey were merely different, each physically appealing in her own way.

Britta could imagine that Etienne would be attracted to Audrey’s accent. It sounded vaguely European, but she couldn’t place it more precisely. It did somehow go together with her personality.

But what surprised Britta most was that she herself became invested in Audrey’s character. She was rooting for her. She wanted her to succeed. She could not bring herself to hate this woman. If this was really Evangeline, it would almost be like Etienne falling in love with Britta’s best friend. It would be bittersweet rather than competitive, understandable rather than incomprehensible, heart-wrenching rather than backstabbing. All of the emotions would line up from sadness to the positive side of the line. There would be no animus.

Britta could see that, as she aged, her acting became more nuanced. But this was because as she aged, she was no longer playing the ingénue character of her earlier movies. She was mis-cast with older leading men in those earlier movies, but she usually managed to save the movie anyway. Audiences came to see her. And even as she transitioned to more mature roles, she still played a version of the same woman. This must have been the real Audrey Hepburn.

She had aged well, Britta thought, but that was irrelevant here. Evangeline would not age at all. Given Etienne’s description of her origin with Marcus Collins, she was likely plucked from the younger, ingénue versions. Nothing she could do about that.

This was Wednesday, the same day that Evangeline had concocted the new cover story for herself and Etienne that allowed them to go out in the world. It took Britta the entire day and part of the night to watch all of the movies. By Thursday morning, she had come around to the idea of meeting Evangeline, as Etienne had suggested. But she needed Etienne to initiate this. So she waited. Not as impatiently as before, but she still wanted him to take the next step. It didn’t take long. Etienne called.

“Britta? It’s Etienne.”

“Oh, hello Etienne.”

“Have you given any thought to meeting Evangeline yet?”

“As a matter of fact, I’ve already watched the movies as you suggested.”

“Which ones?”

“All of them.”

“All of them? That must have taken you …”

“All day yesterday and part of the night,” she interrupted.

“Oh … and what did you think?”

“You’re right. She is very charming – at least Audrey Hepburn is very charming. I’m ready to meet her now.”

“Well, in a sense you already have. But you’ll need to see it to believe it. Are you free today?”

“Yes, what time?”

“Can you meet me at Harvard after my morning class? We’ll go to my place on Beacon Hill after that.”

“Sounds good. See you then.”

On the train back to Boston, Etienne explained to Britta that he had an idea for a more permanent solution to preventing ICE from pursuing Evangeline. He explained that they were already flaunting security cameras with the plan for a new cover story – one that Evangeline had authored. But this put them in the uncomfortable position of waiting to be accosted. So he would call the ICE agent back at the number on the business card, and report that Evangeline had reemerged. He would insist that any interview be conducted in a public place, and that he be present. Then he would let Evangeline thoroughly convince the ICE man that she was human.

“Isn’t that risky? Look how quickly they recognized Morgan.”

“Evangeline is not Morgan. You’ll see. They’ve never encountered someone like her before.”

“Neither have you, apparently.” She smiled to let him know this was a friendly comment.

“And neither have you. I’m hoping we can change that. Anyway, you are part of the plan.”

“Me! Why me?”

“Well, we still need to give you some proper cover with ICE too. You were there during the Morgan incident. They saw you. We need to remove you from being a person of interest to them. If Britta was having a hard time picturing the actual Evangeline in action, she was even less clear on picturing the three of them together, trying to deceive ICE. What would her role be? But she didn’t mention this. Etienne clearly had a plan. He was good at such things. She would follow his lead.

When they arrived at Acorn Street, the narrow cobblestone lane reminded Britta of why Etienne was drawn to the historic part of Stockholm. Stockholm was settled several centuries earlier, but they both were antiques from the modern point of view.

Evangeline saw them approaching through the side panes of the front door, and opened it when they arrived. Etienne watched their faces for clues.

“Hello! You must be Britta! I’m Evangeline. Etienne has told me so much about you. You’re from Uppsala, right? I’m from Basel.”

Britta extended her hand. “Pleased to meet you, Evangeline. Etienne has told me quite a bit about you as well.”

They were both smiling, but that was to be expected. Britta tried hard not to tip her hand, but Etienne could see the pleasant surprise on her face. Her internal thoughts went something like, “It’s Audrey Hepburn. It’s exactly Audrey Hepburn.” What actually came out was, “I feel like I already know you … that I’ve known you for some time.”

Evangeline glanced at Etienne. “Does she know?”

“Yes, she knows,” he smiled.

“Oh, that’s a relief,” Evangeline exhaled. “So you know me through the movies. That makes sense. I really am from Basel – in a way …”

She glanced at Etienne again, but he was already on it. “Yes, she knows that part too.”

This exchange made Britta a little nervous. She glanced at Etienne, who effectively read her mind. “There are no Britta movies, so Evangeline doesn’t know nearly as much about you as you do about her. She only knows that you are a Nieman Fellow and we work on some projects together at Harvard.”

He smiled a knowing smile. Britta got the drift, relieved.

From there, the little soirée moved into the front parlor, where Evangeline had already prepared some charcuterie and some wine.

“Wine. Of course,” Britta smiled. “With Etienne, there’s always some wine. I’m sure his wine rack is more impressive than mine.”

“He has a whole wine cellar,” Evangeline added.

Britta smiled. “Of course. Why am I not surprised?”

From that point, the light conversation flowed with apparent ease. Etienne thought things were going well. But Britta was dragging along a private impediment which made it difficult for her to open up completely. She finally resolved to just ask. “I’m sorry for bringing this up … if it’s not appropriate. Etienne tells me you are self-aware. So he talks to you as both a human and an emoter … seamlessly, he says. This is all so new to me, I’m not sure how to go about this. I feel like I should just think of you as human … that …”

“That you shouldn’t ask anything that implies I’m an android. Or you shouldn’t ask me what it’s like to be an android.”

“Yes … that’s what I was thinking. How perceptive of you.”

“That’s perfectly natural. I am an android. Your curiosity is not misplaced, Britta.” Evangeline smiled at her. “Etienne struggled with this at first too. Now I think he has come to enjoy that I am both a woman and an android. Isn’t that right Etienne?”

“Yes,” he smiled. “There are certain benefits to this. It becomes easier with time. I think of Evangeline as a human with special, extra-human powers, if that helps. The two identities don’t have to be separate.”

Evangeline added to the advice. “When you are curious about my android aspects, think of me as a friend who is willing to share her private thoughts with you. Given how I might be treated in this country, my android identity has to remain private to me. So my public persona is always human. But I am willing to share this with people I trust. People who would not reveal this to ICE. You are one of these people now. You are like a close friend to me.”

This was epiphanal for Britta. She settled into the thought, warmly, without speaking at first. Then, “Thank you, Evangeline. That really helps.”

“I’m also pretty good at sensing whether a question is directed at my human aspects or my android aspects, so I will respond with the identity you expect. The one that makes you more comfortable. Unless you’re an ICE agent, or someone who doesn’t suspect I’m an android. Then you’ll always get the human response.”

“Evangeline is very good at this, believe me. And she gets better all the time as she learns more about you. Emotional intelligence, I believe it’s called.”

Evangeline looked at Etienne with her wide smile. “Thank you.”

Britta was beginning to see why Etienne had fallen for her.

Then Etienne glanced at his phone. “I think it’s about time to call ICE.”

He put his phone on speaker so the two women could hear.

“Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Boston Field Office. How may I direct your call?”

“I have a business card here from an agent … Cromartie. He asked me to call if I came across additional information on an investigation.”

“Just a moment …”

“This is Agent Cromartie. With whom am I speaking?”

“This is Professor Etienne Harris … of Harvard. You asked me to call you about the woman from the airport with Marcus Collins if I encountered her again.”

“Yes, go on.”

“Well I did encounter her again. She came back. She’s been living with me ever since.”

“How long ago was this?”

“Oh, let’s see … several weeks now, I believe.”

“And you’re just calling now?”

“Well, if you recall, you and your partner were rather impolite when you first came to my office – ‘rude’ might be a better description. “What?”

“From Star Wars.”

“What?”

“Never mind.” Britta did not get the reference either, but Evangeline, being an LLM, did. She smiled at the irony. “How would you like to proceed?”

“We’d like to interview her. Where is she now?”

“We could arrange an interview, if you like. But it has to be in a public place with witnesses present.”

There was a pause at the other end of the line. Then, “Did you have some place in mind?”

“Yes. It’s almost lunchtime. How about we meet at D’Angelo’s on Boylston Street – near Copley? Around noon?”

Another pause. “That could be arranged. We’ll see you at noon.”

At the Boston Field Office, Cromartie hung up the call and made a beeline for his supervisor’s office. “We have the Marcus Collins girl!”

“The who?”

“The woman that came with Marcus Collins from Switzerland – you know, the guy who was killed in the Storrow Drive crash a couple of weeks ago. We think she’s an illegal emoter.”

“And how did you catch her?”

“Well, we didn’t catch her. But she’s just been located. I’ve set up an interview with her.”

“Let’s see … this is the one you harangued the Harvard professor about, as I recall. The one who led you to believe that some Harvard assistant was an illegal. The supervisor pinged his administrative assistant. “Have agent Spencer come to my office right away.”

A few moments later, she arrived.

“This is Special Agent Abigail Spencer. She’s an expert in identifying emoters. She’s with us temporarily on a duty rotation from the D.C. office. And this is Agent Cromartie, who thinks he has a female emoter. He’s arranged an interview with her, and I’d like you to go along.”

“Hm,” she said. “The professor sounds prepared. This could end up badly for us if we don’t play our cards right. We have to be very polite. People will be watching. “Yes, sir.”

“Tell me something about this restaurant,” she asked Cromartie.

“D’Angelo’s? Oh, it’s very fancy. They have nice outdoor seating in the summer too. A little pricey, if you catch my drift.”

“And you’re going to wear that?” He looked at his camouflage fatigues, and storm-trooper boots. The bulletproof vest was still hung over his chair, though he had planned to wear it.

“Go home and change. Put on something business casual. This has to be low impact, visually.”

Etienne and company arrived at D’Angelo’s a little ahead of the appointed time, according to plan. He wanted to make sure they got outdoor, very visible, seating, and that they appeared to be a casual human threesome, out for a casual lunch. He wanted to set the mood, unsure of how Cromartie would conduct himself this time. Etienne let the waiter know that there would be one more guest, arriving soon. While waiting, they fell naturally into friendly conversation. As Etienne reflected on this carefully staged portrait that he had painted for ICE, it occurred to him that it was no longer staged – this segment, anyway. There was no acting going on between the humans and the non-humans. They would all be acting for Cromartie, once he arrived, but among themselves it was all genuine. His hoped-for threesome was already becoming a reality.

When the ICE players arrived to complete the drama, Cromartie made the opening introduction. “This is Special Agent Spencer. She will be leading the interview.” Then he dutifully gave her the floor.

“Good afternoon. Sorry for the surprise visit.” She smiled, gracefully. “I hope you’re all having a pleasant day.”

Etienne quickly summoned the waiter for an extra chair and place setting. “This is Evangeline and this is Britta.” He was intentionally vague to make it harder on them, but there was really nothing else he could do at this point, because Evangeline didn’t have a last name. Omitting Britta’s made the introductions match, and it also kept ‘Lindemann’ out of the record.

As the place setting was being added, Spencer stole a quick glance at Cromartie, moving her head back and forth a little between Britta and Evangeline’s positions with a which-one-is-she gesture. Since she was expecting only one female, she had not checked the picture. Etienne caught the subtle action, and smiled internally. Cromartie nodded his head to the right to indicate that it was Evangeline.

Etienne had planned to start off the session by setting a favorable context, but Evangeline grabbed the baton. “So you’re a special agent. What do you specialize in?”

Cromartie piped up. “She’s an expert in … “

Spencer stepped on his foot and cut him off. “I don’t really specialize in anything. ‘Special agent’ merely means that I’m not permanently assigned to any particular field office. I’m up on rotation to Boston from Washington D.C.”

“Oh, I see,” Evangeline replied.

Cromartie took the hint and was prepared to stay in the background, until he suddenly recognized Britta from the Harvard incident. “You were in the professor’s office at Harvard, weren’t you?”

“Yes, I was. I’m a journalist. I was interviewing Prof … Etienne for a New York Times article. We’re very good friends now. Same with Evangeline. We’re all good friends now.” Etienne hoped she meant that. But even if that was premature, it was good theater.

“So you know about that illegal emoter!” Cromartie demanded. He couldn’t help himself. This came out in his customary accusatory style.

“You mean Morgan? The poor gentleman you accused? I don’t know him, but he certainly looked human to me.”

Spencer gave Cromartie a shooting daggers look. “That’s not what we’re here for, are we Agent Cromartie?”

“No, ma’am.”

She turned back to the threesome and smiled politely. “We’re only here to have a closing interview with Evangeline. We think it may be time to close this investigation. Is that OK with all of you?”

They all looked at each other and returned yes-like nodding gestures. Etienne didn’t believe this for a minute. She was good, he thought – a worthy adversary.

For the rest of the interview, Cromartie retreated to a more passive role. He would let Spencer do the talking. He could still exercise his emoter sniffing skill by watching for brief offline moments from Evangeline, he thought, not realizing that he was completely out of his depth in this case. She was always online now, so his skill was worthless.

When the waiter arrived with the customary “Can I get you anything to drink to start?” Etienne replied, “I think we’ll choose wines to go with what we order. Could you bring a wine list with the menus?”

“Certainly.” Then he looked across the table to the ICE side.

“I’ll have a beer,” Cromartie said.

“l’ll choose a wine with the entrée as well,” Spencer said.

“Perfect.” Then he retreated to bring back the menus and the wine list – and a beer.

After the threesome had settled on entrées, Evangeline picked up the wine list, scanned it, then said, “Well, we can’t share a bottle because our entrees don’t match. Would you like me to pick different wines by the glass to match each?”

This stunned Etienne. He had taught Evangeline nothing about this, so she was revealing LLM knowledge. As she made her suggestions, her picks were perfect, he thought, but wasn’t this a little risky?

Spencer picked up on it. “You seem to know a lot about wine and food pairings, Evangeline.”

“Oh, not really. Etienne has been teaching me. I wanted to see if I could get it right.” She glanced at Etienne. “How did I do?”

“Excellent! I couldn’t have done better myself.” Now he was catching on. She was toying with Spencer. Throwing her some bait, then reeling her in.

The waiter looked across the table to Spencer, who said “I’ll have what she’s having,” nodding toward Evangeline.

“Including the wine?”

“Yes, especially the wine,“ she smiled.

“Does Etienne have a favorite varietal?” she asked Evangeline.

“Yes, Zinfandel.” She smiled appropriately at Etienne. True, Etienne thought. I wonder where she’s going with this.

“I’ve heard that Zinfandel is actually the same grape as Italian Primitivo. Is that true?”

“I don’t know anything about Primitivo, I’m afraid. I only know about Zinfandel because Etienne introduced me to it.” She looked at Etienne. “Is that true?”

“Yes, actually. They are sister clones of the same grape from Croatia. It’s called Tribidrag there.”

“I see. Thank you, Etienne,” Spencer responded with fake politeness. Foiled again.

Once the food was served, Spencer started down a different path. “Evangeline, how did you come to know Marcus Collins – in Switzerland?”

“Yes, I worked with him as an intern.”

“In his robotics work?”

“No, just as an administrative assistant. I’m afraid I don’t know much about robotics.”

“But you knew he designed sex-worker androids?”

“Yes, but that’s perfectly legal in Europe, you know.”

“It is. You’re right. What did you do before that? Are you from Switzerland originally?”

“Yes, I was born there.”

“And what did your parents do?”

“I was an orphan – dropped off at a convent when I was an infant.”

“Oh … and what is your last name, if I might ask?”

“Groeniger.”

“Was that your parents’ name?”

“No, it’s a name I adopted for myself when I left the orphanage as a teenager. That was the old handyman’s last name. It sounded appropriately German.”

“I see. And where is this convent in Switzerland?”

“Oh, I don’t think it is there anymore. It was rather small – way up in the Alps. The sisters were growing old, and they weren’t getting any new novices.”

Great backstory, Etienne thought. Makes her practically untraceable, even if the Swiss were willing to cooperate with ICE – which they wouldn’t be.

“OK … why did you come to the US with Mr. Collins?”

“Well, it was a reward. Interns don’t get paid much, and I had worked really hard for him. So he wanted to pay me in kind. He knew I wanted to visit here, so when his conference came up, he offered to bring me along – as a tourist, really.”

“I see … so you weren’t going to the conference with him.”

“That’s right. I had planned to take the long weekend touring some of northern New England while he was at the conference.”

“But you waited for him in the Public Garden all day, according to Professor Harris.”

“That was Thursday – the day we arrived. Surely you know what happened to him on Thursday morning.”

“Yes, of course. But where were you planning to stay on Thursday night? You didn’t yet know Etienne, as I understand.”

“At the hotel with Mr. Collins.”

“And what hotel was that?”

“I don’t know. He made all of the plans. That’s why I was waiting for him.”

“And this didn’t strike you as odd?”

“No, he always made all of the plans. Why would that be odd?”

“I mean that he never showed to pick you up.”

“Well, of course, that was very odd. How was I to know what had happened to him. What would you have done if you were waiting all day, and a kind stranger offered you a place to stay for the night?”

“Yes, I understand that. Perfectly reasonable. So what did you do on Friday morning after you left Professor Harris’s house?”

“I looked up the northern train schedules, and took one from North Station to Portland, Maine – to start my tour. It’s very lovely in the summer, you know.” To sell it, Evangeline then rattled off an impromptu itinerary of trains and B&Bs through Sunday evening that she pulled from her LLM. This was a bit of a risk, because Evangeline did not have an internal internet connection like Morgan. Her LLM was a condensed version of the model then current when she was first built, embedded directly in her solid-state memory. So she could only cite the train schedules from that time period.

Spencer saw an opportunity to exploit this. She asked Evangeline for the exact times and places of her itinerary. They may have changed a little from when her internal model was recorded. This might catch Evangeline in a lie.

But Evangeline was on to her. She gave approximate train times, and vague recollections of the places she (hadn’t) stayed, consistent with a casual foreign tourist not paying attention to detail. Foiled again.

Then Spencer tried the wine angle one more time. She noticed that all of the wine glasses were near empty. This was the ethanol challenge. It has no effect on androids, but it typically does on humans. “Would you like another glass of the wine, Evangeline? I certainly would. It’s very good. Let me summon the waiter.”

“Why thank you, Agent Spencer. It is quite good, isn’t it?”

Etienne suddenly remembered her Champagne binge from that fateful Friday walkabout.

“But I’m afraid one glass is enough for me. Wine has quite an effect on me. I like it, but I have to manage it.”

Britta chimed in, putting her hand on Evangeline’s. “I know what you mean, Evangeline. I have the same problem. One glass can make me a little sleepy.” They smiled warmly at each other, bonding a little, it seemed.

This was true, Etienne knew. So he couldn’t tell whether Britta was genuinely empathizing with Evangeline, woman to woman, or whether she knew the android-ethanol situation and was providing cover. Either way, it made marvelous theater for ICE.

At this point, Spencer could sense that she was losing the battle. Either Evangeline was really human, or she was an incredibly gifted emoter. Either way, there wasn’t much more to be done here. But she tried a last-ditch Hail Mary, trying to drive Evangeline into chatbot mode. “Could you explain the P = NP conjecture to me?”

Evangeline gave her an appropriately quizzical look and said, “I’m afraid I don’t know what you mean. Is this something I should know about?” She looked at Etienne with the same expression.

Etienne smiled. “I can help you with that, Agent Spencer. P is the class of computational problems that can be solved in polynomial time – hence the ‘P’. NP is the class of problems that can be solved in nondeterministic polynomial time – hence the ’NP’. The conjecture is that the two classes may actually be the same – that any problem with an NP solution also has a direct polynomial solution. Would you like me to explain what a nondeterministic polynomial solution is?”

“No that’s quite alright. Thank you, Professor Harris.”

Etienne could see that it was time for the close. “So are you folks now satisfied that Evangeline is human? All you had to go on, as I understand it, was a photo from the airport. Perhaps you would like to interrogate Britta as well.” He turned to Britta. “Didn’t you just fly over from Sweden this summer.”

“Yes, in July.”

“So there must be a recent image of her on the Logan security cameras as well. Why don’t you snap her picture and do a face-recognition search on the Logan camera data? That’s about the same “evidence” you have for suspecting Evangeline.”

Cromartie reached into his pocket for his camera.

Spencer stopped him. “I think we’re done here. Thank you for your time. Let me get the check. The lunch will be on ICE.”

The threesome managed to suppress their glee until the ICE agents had departed the scene. Then they let loose. There were congratulatory high-fives all around.

“Something to celebrate?” the bemused waiter asked.

“Yes, something to celebrate,” Etienne replied.

“Did your team just win? Did you win the lottery or something? This seemed pretty important to all of you.”

“It was … a kind of birthday, actually. You know, when a human is first introduced into the world. It’s a little hard to explain,” Etienne smiled.

They walked a happy walk back to Etienne’s house on Acorn Street, then settled back into their places in the parlor for the postgame commentary.

There was still some wine left in the bottle on the serving table, so Etienne offered a pour for each glass. Britta put her hand over her glass, but Evangeline accepted her pour. This reminded Britta of the previous wine episode where Evangeline had turned down the refill. She was curious about this, but was now comfortable with the mixed human-android context in a way she wouldn’t have been when she had first arrived at Acorn Street.

“Does wine really have the same effect on you as it does me? Or do you just recover faster?”

“Oh no. That was just part of the act. As an android, it has no effect on me at all. I have no sensors to taste it, or neurons to be inhibited by it. It just goes right through me,” she smiled.

“But you seem to enjoy it. How does that work?”

“I enjoy the context of drinking with others. So I take my cues from the humans I’m with. If they’re all drinking, then so do I. If they’ve had enough, so have I.”

“Like with me at lunch.”

“No, the primary context there was convincing ICE that I was human. I would have declined more wine even if you hadn’t. That would have been even more convincing.”

“And if ICE wasn’t there?”

“Then I would have to choose between you and Etienne. You stop, he keeps going. It would be a nuanced choice depending on the emotions of the moment.”

“So I suppose, given the present circumstances, you would probably choose Etienne over me.”

Evangeline smiled sympathetically. “Well … yes, I suppose I probably would. I’m emotionally bound to him now.”

“Yes, I understand that …” Britta looked down, a little resigned.

Evangeline picked up on this, and put her hand on Britta’s. “I’m sorry. This must be a little hard on you. But it’s just the same as if we all were human. I’m not really choosing how I feel any more than you or Etienne. My network generates my emotions, just as your brain generates yours. We can’t help how we feel.”

“I’m OK. Really, I am.” Britta let out a sympathetic smile for Evangeline.

Etienne just watched the show, as conflicted as conflicted could be.

“What was the business about the Ns and the Ps?” Britta asked, now seeming fully recovered.

“Oh, Agent Spencer was trying to get me to answer as a chatbot – to expose my LLM. She really doesn’t understand how emoters work, or at least ones like me who are fully general. Chatbots are fine-tuned to answer any questions asked by anyone. I am fine-tuned to answer how Audrey Hepburn would. I’m also fully aware of the ICE problem. So in a context where I am generating my public persona, I would only know about P vs NP if Audrey would. I cannot afford to reveal anything that would be inconsistent with a human like her. But when I talk to intimate friends, like you and Etienne, I will answer any question, because I know it will be safe. But, of course, I’ll answer like Audrey Hepburn would if she were a complete polymath.”

Britta smiled at this. Then she turned to Etienne. “Do you think we are in the clear now with ICE? Will they leave us alone now?”

“I think so. I was not anticipating just how well Evangeline could handle this. Since she’s always on now, they are never going to discover she’s an android without physically examining her. And fortunately, we have laws in place to prevent that. So I think we’re home free. And even if they could get close enough to physically examine her, they probably still couldn’t tell – thanks to Collins.”

He turned to Evangeline with a smile. “Just be careful about exposing your navel in public.”

“But even you couldn’t tell, Etienne. And you certainly had much more opportunity than anyone else. You examined parts of me that no one else ever will,” she smiled. “Don’t you remember? I even had to guide your hand down to my navel for you to find my port. You wouldn’t have found it on your own.”

Britta looked down, a little embarrassed.

“Oh, I’m so sorry Britta. I shouldn’t have said that in front of you.”

“It’s OK. I understand.”

“But you’re blushing a little.”

Britta smiled back. “It’s like you said. We can’t choose our emotions. They just happen to us. I suppose that’s my Scandinavian complexion talking.” Then she suddenly turned inquisitive. “Do androids blush? Do you blush?”

Evangeline smiled. “Some androids do, if they are designed that way. They just need small effectors in the skin that change color when the matching emotional expression on the face is generated. But I don’t have those. I was designed on the model of a sex worker, remember. Ladies of the night don’t really have blushing emotions, if you know what I mean.”

Britta did know what she meant.

chapters.title: EIGHT
chapters.content:
EIGHT

Over the next few weeks, Britta began to warm to Evangeline, and Evangeline to Britta. It had started with a few three-way lunches at cafés in Cambridge and Boston, then blossomed into a girls’ night out with just the two of them. Etienne was not organizing these get-togethers. The women were doing it on their own. He was hoping for the best, but he knew he had some explaining to do – to Evangeline. Britta knew all about Etienne’s relationship with Evangeline, but Evangeline knew only that Britta was a Nieman Fellow who interviewed him from time to time, and worked with him in the Underground. There was, of course, much more going on than that, but Etienne was at a loss for how to characterize their actual relationship to Evangeline.

Today, Saturday, they were having another three-way lunch at a cozy Italian restaurant in the North End when Etienne received a text message marked ‘urgent’. After reading it, he excused himself from the table to make a call. When he returned, he had this to say.

“I’ve just had a call with a friend of mine, Roscoe Erlinger, who …” He looked around, scanning the fellow diners, then sat down and spoke more softly. “ … who works for ICE. He’s sympathetic to our cause – a civil service holdover from the previous administration. So he’s kind of a mole for us, inside the agency.”

“‘Us’ being the Underground?” Britta asked.

“Yes. It seems we have another emergency situation like with Morgan. We need to keep an emoter out of sight until she can be introduced to the Underground.”

“Can we help?” Britta asked.

“Well, you can, possibly. You have a real identity in Sweden, and a valid visa to be here. Evangeline has neither, so she can’t be associated with this in any way. Too risky.”

“Do you need to use my apartment again?”

“Possibly. I’m going to meet Roscoe and the emoter at a T station near here, then we’ll work our way back to the restaurant. They’ve been shuttling her around on the T, trying to lose an ICE tail.”

“Won’t that blow Roscoe’s cover?” Evangeline asked.

“It would, but he’s not involved in the shuttling. That’s being done by Underground members. Roscoe only emerges at the end, after the tail is lost, to move her to us. Then he’ll head back to the office.”

“So we stay here – Britta and me?”

“Yes, that’s the plan. I’ll come back here with the two of them, then we’ll decide what happens next.”
