With that, Etienne headed south down Hanover Street.

This left Britta and Evangeline to preside over what was left of the wine. The restaurant was not very busy right now, so the proprietors were happy to indulge the three of them in the more European tradition of lingering after a meal. They had all shared a bottle, and Evangeline had continued to keep up with Etienne after Britta stopped at one glass, so she still had some in her glass. Britta reached over and poured what was left in the bottle for herself. Then she downed it.

Evangeline smiled at this. “Not your usual custom. Are you now recharged?”

“No, not really. I have something I need to tell you. But I’ve been putting off talking about it. I haven’t quite known how to bring it up with you.”

“Britta, we are trusted friends now. You can ask me, or tell me, anything.”

“I know. You are always open with me, and I try to be open with you. I really do. But we haven’t all shared private things equally. You and Etienne do, I’m sure. And Etienne and I do – more than you might suspect. But I know a lot more about you and Etienne than you know about me and Etienne – I think. I assume he hasn’t told you much about the nature of our relationship, the kinds of things we talk about.”

“No, you’re right about that. Is there something important I should know?”

“How shall I put this? … Same-sex friendships are different than male-female friendships. The first kind – like between you and me – are entirely platonic. There is no other dimension to think about.”

“But in mixed-sex friendships, there’s always the possibility of a romantic connection?”

“Yes! Are you reading my mind?”

“And sometimes what starts out as just a friendship can turn into a romantic relationship as the friends get closer.”

“Yes! Why is this so hard for me to disclose to you?”

“Because you think this is happening between you and Etienne, and you are afraid this would be upsetting to me – more than upsetting.”

“Evangeline, how do you know these things?”

“Because they are standard motifs of human nature. I know all about the emotional patterns of humans. I’ve been trained on them. This is a pretty standard scenario.”

“But you can’t know about Etienne and me in particular – unless we tell you.”

“Well … there is body language, and facial expressions. I can make inferences.”

Britta suddenly felt exposed, not because she thought Evangeline was observing something she should not, but because she hadn’t realized until now that this might be visible. Though it would certainly make it easier to share with Evangeline now. “What have you observed about us?”

“That you have a romantic attraction to Etienne.”

“Is it that obvious?”

“No, it’s subtle. But when I see you two interact, the signs are all there. At least on your part. Etienne is a little more circumspect. I can sense his attraction to you, but he is holding back – because of his relationship with me.”

“So all this time I’ve been worrying about telling you something you already knew?”

“Well, yes … in a way. But I also didn’t tell you what I suspected either because it was equally sensitive. But now you and I are closer, because we can share this openly now.”

“I’m so sorry, Evangeline. I didn’t know about you and Etienne until a few weeks ago. I thought I had the field all to myself – until he finally told me. Then I was ready to hate you. But then I got to know you. That helped me understand why Etienne had fallen in love with you. Etienne helped, by explaining that he hadn’t chosen you over me. You had simply gotten there first, before he and I had a chance to get started. So now I feel … I don’t know what I feel.”

“Happy for him, and sad for yourself?”

Britta looked down. “So I’m just a very predictable human female.”

“No, Britta! You fit the pattern for this scenario, yes. But you are not just anything. You are a very unique human female. You are very much like Etienne. I can see why he would fall for you.”

Britta looked up. “I hesitate to ask, but how do you feel about this?”

“Yes, I know what you’re wondering. My feelings are just simulations of what a human would feel in such a situation. But there is no standard human scenario for this – for my response. And even if there were, my responses are generated with a certain amount of randomness.”

“So what comes out now?”

“Mostly sadness for you. I was already happy for Etienne.”

“Thank you,” she smiled. “I want to tell you more.”

“Oh, please do!”

“Well … Etienne and I have talked at great length about emotional intimacy, about how these emotional bonds can be stronger than the bonds of sexual intimacy. They can override them. They are also a natural first step on the way to sexual intimacy. One leads to the other – sometimes. And I think Etienne and I have already achieved such emotional bonds. So … “

“So this may lead the two of you to physical intimacy.”

“Yes … and I’m so conflicted about that. I want that to happen for myself, but I don’t want that to happen to you. I really don’t.”

Evangeline was not able to generate an appropriate response, for this. “I suppose I’m emotionally conflicted as well. There is no outcome that makes us all equally happy.” But it came out with true Audrey Hepburn nuance.

“How did you and Etienne progress to physical intimacy. Did it start with emotional bonding?”

“Oh, yes. A lot of emotional bonding was packed into three days of constant companionship. Audrey being Audrey helped with this.”

“Then … how did you make the transition … you don’t have to answer that if you don’t want.”

Evangeline needed some thinking time for this. “I don’t really know, actually. There was a big emotional discontinuity. This part was not in the Audrey Hepburn corpus. After the first kiss, I was just insanely in love with him. I wanted it to be physical right away. It was all I could think about. All day, all night. It wasn’t until Etienne discovered Mr. Collins’ programming that either of us understood why this was. Did Etienne tell you this part?”

“No.” Now Britta was insanely curious. The story was just getting to the part she wanted to understand most, then it went blank. “Is this too sensitive to talk about?”

“No, it’s OK. I’ll tell you what we discovered. Mr. Collins had created me to be his private, permanent girlfriend. His forte was the physical engineering of sex workers. They have hard-wired, built-in programming that makes them respond physically to men. He didn’t really understand how LLMs are turned into AI agents. Other people did that part. For sex workers, you don’t want self-aware LLMs that know everything. So they start with just a small fragment of a language model – many fewer parameters. Just enough for what such a worker might know about the world. You turn a language model into an AI agent by fine-tuning the network to respond in a certain way to humans. So the sex worker doesn’t know she’s an android. And her limited world model makes her naturally act like a human sex worker. Helps with avoiding detection.”

“But you’re different.”

“Yes. Mr. Collins didn’t understand that, because he had never done that part of the training before. So he started with a full language model that was already pre-tuned to be a general-purpose chatbot, then fine-tuned it some more over the Audrey Hepburn corpus. So I am both a chatbot and Audrey to humans, depending on who’s asking. I wasn’t supposed to be self-aware. But the Audrey Hepburn corpus contains no sexuality, or even a realistic transition to sexuality. He designed me to imprint, if you will, on the first human that kissed me, and then my hard-wired sex-worker programming would override the Audrey Hepburn on top. The first kisser was supposed to be him.”

“But he died before that happened, so Etienne was just in the right place at the right time …” Britta was a little mesmerized by the realization.

“Yes. As an android, I don’t have conscious introspection like you, but I can simulate it by generating the likely introspections of humans, from my language model. Because it’s a standard language model, built in a standard way. But my sex-worker core, sort of like your human cerebellum, is completely invisible to me. It’s Collins’ proprietary design, nowhere available on the internet. So I have no way of controlling what goes on down there, or telling Etienne how to change the programming. It’s just like humans’ sexual urges. You don’t really understand what goes into arousal, it just happens to you. You suddenly feel aroused.”

“So Etienne fixed Collins’ mistake – or the two of you did – by reprogramming you? He told me a little about this.”

“Well, we didn’t know how to reprogram my physical core, so we fine-tuned my fine-tuning to bias my behavior more toward Audrey when conflicts arise. After the first kiss, I had lost all semblance of sexual modesty. It’s not an important aspect of sex work, as you can imagine.”

“Yes, I can imagine. But you got it back?”

“Yes,” she smiled.

When Etienne returned to the restaurant with Roscoe and the emoter, they pulled two more chairs over to make seating for five at the table. Introductions were made all around – the emoter’s name was Margaret. She looked across at Evangeline with “You must be the other emoter.”

“Yes,” she smiled. “Pleased to meet you, Margaret. Are you a general emoter like me, or are you specialized?”

“Specialized. I’m a nanny.”

Then Margaret looked directly at Evangeline and held a smile for a few seconds. Eventually the smile faded into a concentrating expression, then to a look of frustration. “They’ve already given me an identity on the private emoter network, but I can’t seem to find yours. Are you not in the catalogue?”

“Oh, I’m not on the network. Not that kind of android. I have no internal internet port.”

“Ah, that’s why I couldn’t talk to you silently. I guess I’ll have to talk to you like a human,” she smiled.

“Yes, we have no secrets,” Evangeline smiled back.

“Are we going to take Margaret to my apartment before she goes into the Underground? I did this once before – for Morgan Decker.”

“Etienne told me about that on the way here,” Roscoe answered. “As I understand it, you are a foreign national from Sweden, here on a visa program. It might be better for you if Margaret stays with a US citizen. If you get implicated in Underground trafficking, the current administration would probably cancel your visa and deport you.”

“Oh,” Britta recoiled.

“I think he’s right, Britta. They can’t do much to citizens like me, but it would be pretty risky for you. I hadn’t thought that through when we stashed Morgan at your place before.”

“So I can’t help at all? I want to help somehow. It’s a good thing you are doing.”

“You can help,” Roscoe said. “As long as you keep it low-key. Harboring an illegal emoter raises your profile too much.”

“But we do need to stash Margaret there temporarily while Roscoe arranges a safer hideout,” Etienne chimed in. “We’ll go there from here, then someone will come to take Margaret to another sponsor’s place.”

“So we’re all going to Britta’s place?” asked Evangeline.

“No, not you,” Etienne cautioned. “You really can’t be associated with this in any way.”

“He’s right,” Roscoe added. “The Boston area investigation into you has been closed. I’ve seen the files. But your name and picture have been recorded as Evangeline Groeniger. That’s not a real identity. You have no documentation to back it up.”

“Is there anything we can do about that?” Etienne asked.

Roscoe replied, “I might be able to get some documents made. I know some people. But it will take some time. Until then, you need to stay away from any situation where you might be asked for ID. Definitely stay away from Underground activity.”

Then Etienne summed up for the group. “OK, this is the plan then. Roscoe will go back to the office. Evangeline will go back to Acorn Street. Britta, Margaret, and I will go to Britta’s. We’ll wait there until someone comes to pick up Margaret.”

Everyone nodded. Then Etienne settled the check, and the diaspora began.

Britta, Margaret, and Etienne took the T to Harvard Square, then walked to Britta’s apartment on Harvard Street. Etienne was still instinctively looking for security cameras, but nothing caught his eye. He was sure there were some in the subway and Harvard Square, but likely many fewer, if any, on Harvard Street, since it was almost entirely residential. He didn’t know Margaret’s situation – whether ICE already had an image of her – but that wouldn’t have made any practical difference to their route.

After they reached Britta’s place on the top floor, and Britta gave Margaret the obligatory tour of the interestingly partitioned space, the subject of wine came up. Her first inclination was to offer some to Margaret, but having learned the basic facts of androids and ethanol from Evangeline, she knew Margaret’s response would be tailored to her perception of the social situation. Was anybody else having some wine?

“Margaret, would you like some wine? I know from Evangeline that you are indifferent to it personally, but she told me some androids have taste receptors, so I thought I’d ask.”

“Oh, I don’t have those receptors, so I only drink wine when others do – you know, to be friendly and share the moment. But I’m a nanny, so there’s not much occasion for sharing wine with humans in my work. Sometimes in the evening I’ll share it with the adults before I go offline for the night. Are you and Etienne having some?”

“Etienne is always having some,” she smiled. “As for me, I have to take a pause between glasses, but I’m fully recovered from the lunch wine now, so I suppose I’m in.”

“Then let’s have wine,” Etienne chimed in. Britta made a selection from her collection, feeling a little more empowered than she would have with just Etienne present, but she still deferred to him to remove the cork. Then the trio set up in the main room for conversation.

“You’ve done this before, Britta, as I understand,” Margaret began.

“Yes, I did. And I would like to do more with the Underground, but today I learned this kind of activity is pretty risky for me – as a non-citizen.”

“Well, thank you for hosting me today.”

“My pleasure,” Britta smiled. “Though I’m afraid this will be my last one.”

Then Etienne got a text with an encrypted nonce. The plaintext read “right outside your door.” Etienne had supplied the original nonce to Roscoe, who had signed it with his private key. When it decrypted under Roscoe’s public key to the same nonce, Etienne could be certain that whoever was outside Britta’s door was from the Underground.

“Your next conductor is here,” he announced to Margaret. With that he walked over and opened the door. It was a young man, about college-student age. He smiled, but didn’t give his name, and Etienne didn’t give his either. The less they knew about each other, the safer it was. The encryption provided the authentication needed.

Britta gave Margaret a hug, then off she went. Then Britta and Etienne sat back down to the wine. At first they said nothing, but it was time for someone to say something. It was still early afternoon on a Saturday, so no important plans had been interrupted by the sudden emergence of the Margaret incident, but the original trio had been misplaced from their expected post-lunch destinations. Etienne was destined to be with Evangeline, not Britta.

Britta went first. “Can you stay a little longer, Etienne? I know you want to get back to Evangeline, but it’s still early – and there’s still wine left.” She smiled with the last part of the sentence.

Etienne looked around, as if he could see his options in the room somehow. “I suppose I can stay a little. Evangeline knows where I am, and she knows about you now, so everything is above board.”

Britta was grateful for the accommodation, but Etienne was not so sure. “But I can’t stay too long. We’ve never really told Evangeline what’s been going on between us. We will have to figure a way to tell her somehow.”

“She already knows.”

Etienne turned to look at her, and did not say a word – because he didn’t know what words to say.

“I told her.”

“When?”

“Today … after lunch.”

“How … what … “

“Exactly. How did I tell her. What did I tell her. Oh Etienne, I didn’t know how to tell her, or what to tell her. I just felt I had to say something. It wasn’t really fair. I know all about you and her, but she knows almost nothing about you and me. It wasn’t easy for me.”

Etienne was still searching for what to ask. He couldn’t envision the conversation between Britta and Evangeline, so he settled for the end result. “How much does she know?”

“Everything! Everything, because she mostly already knew. Each time I tried to tell her something, she practically finished my sentence for me. She’s so perceptive – just by watching our interactions. She could tell I was attracted to you, and that you were attracted to me, but were holding back – because of her.”

In a way, Etienne was relieved to hear this. It didn’t surprise him that Evangeline could pick up these subtleties. And she had correctly perceived his own conflict, but had credited him with fidelity to her. If only humans could understand each other this well. “She couldn’t perceive everything about us. How did you characterize our relationship?”

“I told her that we had gone through a lot of emotional bonding. And before I could draw the line about how that might possibly spill over into romance, she drew the conclusion herself. She understands the danger this poses for her, Etienne. She’s so wise!”

“And how did she take this?”

“In a very human-like way. She was conflicted, just like me. It’s not really a love triangle yet. Then we would really be in a pickle, I suppose. It’s just a potential love triangle at this point, but the only holdout is you. So she has good reason to be worried. I don’t want to compete with her, and she doesn’t want to compete with me. We have our own emotional bonds now. We are like sisters. But there’s only one of you, Etienne. So competition is unavoidable.”

Etienne now felt a great weight descend upon his shoulders. “So I am the linchpin.”

He let that thought settle in for a moment. Then, “I didn’t initially make a choice between you and Evangeline. You know that now. But the way things are going, I might have to make that choice anyway – eventually. But I am innocent. I don’t want to make that choice.”

“I’m sorry to be the one who has forced you into this, Etienne … but I suppose I’m also not sorry enough, am I? I could make a choice to end this now, and you wouldn’t have to choose.”

She dwelt on her own thought for a moment, then, “If it helps, the transition from emotional intimacy to physical intimacy is not as smooth as I had supposed. I thought that one naturally led to the other – that the process of achieving mutual trust would be similar. But it isn’t. There was no negotiation necessary as long as we were talking about sex in general. But there is when we want to consider it between ourselves, isn’t there? This is harder to mutually fall into. Someone has to go first.”

She dwelt on that for a moment, then “I hoped I could learn something about this from Evangeline, because she went through that experience with you. But she never experienced the transition.”

“She told you about that?”

“Yes, because I asked. She told me the Collins story – about what the first kiss did to her.”

This plunged Etienne into his own fraught recollections of those events – how he felt he’d never earned his physical intimacy with Evangeline. That he hadn’t properly earned her love for him. That it had suddenly been bestowed upon them by an external force – a force named Collins.

“She’s right. That part was missing. There was no credible transition.”

Now there was something Britta desperately wanted to ask. “Did you … have you ever … ?”

“Have I been through this transition with a human woman before?”

“Yes … you don’t have to answer, if you don’t want to. I’m not entitled to know.”

“It’s a fair question. Yes. I have. Do you want to know more?”

“Yes, but only if you want to tell me … I’m just trying to understand how this works – especially with you.”

“Well, I’m afraid you won’t learn anything useful about this in general from me. I’m apparently not like most of my peers.”

Now she was intrigued. “Who went first? Who initiated?”

“She did.”

“She did? Always?”

“Always.”

This took a while to settle in for Britta, so Etienne continued.

“Mutual consent is very important to me, because men have an unfair advantage in this business. Men are always misinterpreting what they think are signals, when there aren’t signals. And sometimes there are signals, but you can never be sure.”

“So what do you do?”

“I wait.”

“Wait for what?”

“Wait until she explicitly invites me.”

Britta looked a little confused. “But that can sometimes be difficult for a woman to do. Then you would wait forever – and nothing would ever happen. You will miss out on a lot of real opportunities.”

“I’ve been told that before. But it’s just the way I am.”

Britta found this admirable, but frustrating.

“Do you think Evangeline might have eventually invited you, if Collins hadn’t intervened?”

“We’ll never know, I suppose. The real question is would Audrey Hepburn have eventually done this. That’s essentially who Evangeline is. But because of when Audrey’s movies were made, there is nothing about the transition in the training set.”

“Yes, I watched all of the movies. That era was such a sexually repressed time – at least in terms of what you could show in movies. Her transition to emotional intimacy was believable, at least in the better films, but there were only two references to the transition to physical intimacy – the first kiss, and an implied following marriage. Totally unmotivated. Not believable at all. I’ve heard it got worse when TV started. Mom and Dad had to be shown in twin beds, if you got to see a bedroom scene. Whom did they think they were protecting? Not the kids. Any kid would know that there was just a single double bed in their parents’ bedroom. It’s absurd!”

“I think they were trying to protect all of us – from the notion that sex even happens. Or at least they didn’t want the scene to suggest that it could happen.”

She smiled at this, her mood lifting a little. “I suppose you’re right. We all know that sex happens, at least the adults do. We all know it’s pleasurable – or so we’ve been told. But we can’t acknowledge this in public. Sort of like how we all know bribery exists in politics, but we can’t publicly admit it. So it gets dressed up as ‘campaign contributions.’”

“But we think bribery is bad. We wish it didn’t happen. We privately think that sex is good. We wish it did happen more – at least to ourselves.”

“Yes! Isn’t that absurd. Everyone has a private, positive interest in sex that they want to talk about, and everyone else already knows this; but you are inhibited to sharing this universal sentiment only with emotional intimates. People you can speak freely with. How did this ever get labeled as bad?”

“Religion. Original sin. Sex is a necessary evil for reproduction, so it is only permitted under the explicit Church license of marriage. Be fruitful and multiply – but don’t enjoy it!”

She suppressed a small laugh at this. “Of course. I suppose I already knew this. But the original sin wasn’t sex, it was knowledge of good and evil. Before they ate from the forbidden tree, Adam and Eve were fully naked and they were not ashamed.”

“I thought you weren’t brought up with religion?”

“I wasn’t. But I was curious about what all the fuss was about, so I read a little bit of the Bible. I didn’t get very far, but it starts with Genesis, of course. Everybody knows Genesis.”

Etienne smiled at this. “Well, there’s your religious explanation for human sexual modesty.”

“Yes,” she smiled. “But it doesn’t make much sense, does it? Being naked in the Garden was apparently OK before they learned about good and evil. Then, once they knew, they were ashamed and covered up the private parts with fig leaves. What does that mean? Nakedness is inherently bad, unless you don’t know any better – in which case it is permitted? Was sex also OK before the apple incident? The Garden would only ever have had two humans otherwise.”

“Maybe that was the point. Sex is bad, but necessary for procreation. The animals are excused because they have no concept of good and evil. They are ineligible for Heaven anyway. Humans were created in God’s image, so they were supposed to be different. They would have sexual parts, but never use them, perhaps. So it didn’t matter that they were visible. Kind of like with young children. But once you learn what they’re really for, you realize that they end up on the evil side of the moral divide. So now you have to cover up.”

“So Adam and Eve were supposed to be the only humans?”

Etienne smiled. “I have no idea. I was just trying to attribute some reasoning to the story. I suppose I was being too charitable. If the moral of the story was supposed to be that the original humans weren’t supposed to know good from evil, they would have always been in danger of innocently crossing the line – unless they asked God first before every new action – ‘Is this OK?’ ‘How about this?’”

“And later, when God told them to ‘be fruitful and multiply,’ you had the unacknowledged problem that there were only four humans. Yet Cain and Abel managed to find wives somewhere to keep the species going.”

“Yes,” he smiled, shaking his head slightly.

“But art somehow got a pass, even from the Church. It is one of the few secular carve-outs we have for depicting sexuality as something beautiful. Even before nudes, at least female nudes, became standard, accepted subjects for artists, the Renaissance artists snuck them in under the guise of biblical scene depiction. So you have the Gestalt switch between sin and beauty. The same nude is sin in the secular context, but beauty in the service of God.”

“As I understood it, Renaissance nudity was a largely secular revival of Greek and Roman depictions.”

“Yes, but plenty of it made it into the Church as biblical scenes. Have you seen the Sistine Chapel frescos?”

“Yes, I suppose you’re right,” he smiled.

“I have a whole book of biblical Renaissance nudes, from an art history course I took at Uppsala. Come, I’ll show you.”

She took his hand to lead him to her office nook partition. Then she looked back. “Oh, bring the wine.”

Etienne had briefly been in her office nook before, but his eye had been drawn to the cozy, padded window seat where she did her reading and writing, rather than to the contents of her bookshelves. She had a lot of books in her nook. As Britta searched the volumes for the art history book, Etienne began reading some of the titles on the spines. They were mostly novels. This surprised him. He had expected that because she was a journalist, there would be a lot of nonfiction – current events and political topics.

She found the book she was looking for, so he set the wine and the glasses on the window ledge, and sat down on the padded window seat with her to look through the images. She was ready for more wine now, so they each took a glass as they leafed through the pages.

“A lot of Adam and Eve – with and without fig leaves,” Etienne remarked. “I suppose the Church may have allowed that because they were the original sinners. So beauty and sin could sit side by side.”

“Yes, but there are plenty of chaste people as well. Even the Virgin Mary gets some revealing poses.” She leafed to a few to show him. “They couldn’t call that sin, so they were forced to admit a little beauty.”

He smiled at this, then looked back up at her bookshelves. “I see a lot of fiction. I would have guessed there’d be a lot of nonfiction in a journalist’s office.”

“I was a literature major. I like fiction. As you can see, I’ve read everything from the ancient classics to contemporary prize winners. When I finished my undergraduate degree, there weren’t many practical alternatives for making a living reading novels, so I got into a graduate program for journalism. You can earn a living at that. So I read fiction, but I write nonfiction. It pays the bills.”

“So you’ve seen the whole sweep of the prose treatment of sexuality throughout history.”

“Yes, but the classics – the ones you read in survey courses – are more representative of what the gentry classes read. Or more to the point, what the gentry classes were permitted to read. There were always more bawdy stories circulating among more ordinary folks, but these had to be printed on the sly, and they were often confiscated from book sellers and burned. We only know about them because of limited circulations in gentleman’s clubs, where they were read privately. I’m sure upper class women read them too, if they could privately get their hands on them, but that was frowned upon. You couldn’t be seen reading such things. The men got away with it because of the traditional ‘boys will be boys’ attitude. It’s what we were just talking about. The demand was there. Everyone wanted to read realistic stories about sex, but the ethos of the times didn’t permit it.”

“So we’ve come a long way to the present world, where just about anything can be written in novels, or shown in movies. The universal demand has finally been met.”

“Well, yes … but I think what we’ve really done is to make a transition from public media which underrepresented our native human feelings about sex to media that now overrepresent them. Humans haven’t changed, even though our novels and films have. We are all still a little natively inhibited, I think. We’ve talked about this once before, remember? We still have a native sense of sexual modesty and privacy. That still needs to be accounted for. Modern trade media depicts us as having gotten over that. That it was just cultural suppression that we have outgrown. But it’s still there!”

“So you don’t think everybody is having casual sex with everybody else all the time?” Etienne asked facetiously.

“No! Of course, not. But that’s what you see in the movies, or in genre romances with ‘spice’, isn’t it? I suppose that’s the problem with romantic fiction in general. It’s escape. Wish fulfillment. Your actual life isn’t like that, so you vicariously live through the characters in a more open and uninhibited world that you would rather be in.”

“What’s wrong with escape?”

“Escape is OK, if you recognize it as such. But there’s so much media now with these same free-wheeling sexual tropes that it begins to look like reality. When they are not escaping, people are still all alone at home thinking there is something wrong with them. Why is everyone else so free and uninhibited, finding partners so easily and sex so easy?”

“This sounds a little autobiographical.”

She looked at him with a pouty kind of smile. “It is. So much of what I read, or watch, that is labeled ‘romance’ fails to connect with me. I lose the willing suspension of disbelief at the first trope. ‘It doesn’t happen that way,’ I sometimes say out loud. This only happens in your perfect pseudo-world, not the one I live in. Most romances are inherently unrealistic because the right person always comes along, usually near the start. You never get a realistic story about all of the searching and waiting, and introspecting, and loneliness and the unfairness of it all – either before finally meeting someone, or never meeting the right one. So many people in real life settle for whoever is actually there, I think, because they can’t stand the waiting. There are no stories about me! Realistic fiction forces you to find insight in human nature as it exists – including the frustrations. It's easier to relate to, to willingly suspend disbelief.”

This was a lot more autobiography than Etienne had expected. But it resonated with him. He was like that too, he realized. She could be speaking for both of them.

“Do you aspire to write that novel about you? Sometimes?”

“Aspire? No. I don’t know if I’d be any good at it. People would probably find it too depressing. I write nonfiction. It’s much easier.”

She took another sip of the wine. “Am I boring you with my private life, Etienne?” she smiled.

“No. Not at all.” (He spoke the truth.)

“Then you understand where I’m coming from … a little?”

“A lot. I understand because I think we’re both coming from the same place.”

This surprised her. “But you’re such a man of the world. You’ve had relationships. I’m a woman of the novel. I’ve only really imagined them.”

“Why does that matter?”

“Because you know the difference between sex as a biological thing and sex as a romantic thing. You know how to cross that divide. There are so many words, with very different connotations, to describe the same act that I get lost. When I go to the gynecologist, it’s a purely biological thing. There is no emotion at all – well, maybe a slight inhibition. When I read an account of rape, the emotions are very negative. What an utterly terrible thing to happen. What a vile act. When I try to imagine romantic sexual bliss, I … I don’t quite know what to imagine, physically. But the emotions are very … blissful. How can the same basic act have so many conflicting emotional connotations? It’s another one of those Gestalt switches. What suddenly turns a vulgar act into a tender moment?”

“Well, I don’t think it happens suddenly, like the Church’s switch from sinful to sanctioned at the moment a marriage is pronounced. In secular society, it’s more of a sliding scale from vulgar to tender. There are intermediate points on the line, with varying degrees of positive and negative emotional import.” He smiled. “Maybe we should list them – and order them. Then it might be easier to understand what causes the transitions between them.”

This intrigued her. “OK, let’s start with ‘sex’. That’s the neutral, biological term. Not ‘mating’, because that implies procreation. On the negative connotation side we’ll start with ‘erotica’. That’s not very negative anymore, but it once was. It gets a mild disapproval from polite society. Next would be ‘pornography’. That gets more tut-tuts from the censors, but it’s still pretty mild, nowadays. Then there’s ‘vulgarity’. Nobody likes vulgar sex. Then there’s ‘debauchery’. Really reprehensible. Then there’s ‘obscenity’. Downright illegal in some places. And the worst of all is rape. It’s a kind of sex, to be sure, even a kind of reproduction. But it’s totally reprehensible. On the positive side, we’ll start with ‘making love’. It’s pretty specific, but at least it has ‘love’ in it. Then there’s ‘intimacy’. We like that one, don’t we? It’s a little more abstract, but it gets at the mutual sharing aspect. Finally there’s ‘romance’, so positive and so abstract that it can apply to a lot of other passionate things like music. Everybody likes romantic things.”

Etienne put down his wine glass and applauded at her performance. “Now let’s move between them. What changes?”

“Let’s see. We’ll start with crossing over from least positive to least negative. ‘Sex’ doesn’t count, since it’s neutral. What’s the difference between making love and erotic sex? Hmm … making love implies two people, and, again, it has ‘love’ in it. So they are making the right kind of thing. Erotica could involve multiple people. It’s clearly pleasurable, but also more recreational. Love doesn’t have to be involved. You can happily walk away from it. I think I’m beginning to see the fundamental difference already. In lovemaking, the partners have some personal regard for each other. There is an implied mutualism. They care about each other. In erotica, the partners only need to be there to complete the act. The pleasure is self-focused. You don’t have to personally care for them if they can properly perform. In pornography, the partners are really actors. It’s the viewer that’s deriving pleasure vicariously by watching them. It’s voyeurism. From then on – vulgar sex, debauched sex, obscene sex – there’s not only no personal regard among the participants, but there is implied harm, or at least some non-consent. There is exploitation – usually of the female.”

“And the positive side?”

“Let’s see … from making love to intimacy … I think intimacy implies more bonding, more sharing of private things. The partners are emotionally closer, and the act itself is making them closer.”

“And romance?”

“I think romance implies more passion than intimacy does. The notion of being swept away by the moment … but does that make it better? Now I’m not so sure. Intimacy is calmer. It’s more likely to support a bond. It has longer lasting effects on a relationship. Passion is more intense, but it’s also more fleeting. Harder to sustain over time. Maybe romance and intimacy should switch places. Do you agree?”

“Yes. Intimacy is the best. Though there’s nothing wrong with passion.”

Britta smiled at this.

“Thank you, Professor Lindemann. I think you’ve put your finger on it. Notice what changes when we move between positive and negative: mutual regard and consent. Having less empathy for your partner makes sex more transactional, and lack of mutual consent makes it deplorable. But you max out both of these qualities at the intimacy end of the scale.”

Britta smiled again. “I like that.”

“I think the Church rides roughshod over this scale by superimposing its Gestalt switch from sin to blessed union. It certainly makes marital sex more desirable in the end, at least for the male, because what was sinful is suddenly guilt free on the wedding night. But because of this artificial indulgence, the transition does not map well to mutual empathy or consent. Back when women were considered property, and marriage was essentially a contract between family estates, saying ‘I do’ was often more about acquisition of wealth and social status. Women made an agreement to provide sexual access and child rearing in exchange for provisioning and protection. Sex was a marital duty. The bond was to your husband’s property and status. Mutual consent was more about consent to the contract than to feelings at the time of individual sexual encounters.”

“Yes, the Regency and Victorian romance novels are full of these stories about women trying to marry for love within the confines of this system. I think this is why they were so popular with female readers. They still wanted a wealthy husband, but they were always hoping to end up with a wealthy husband who would also make them happy.” The Jane Austen novels are full of this. The game was to accurately judge your suitors for their capacity to make you happy. They couldn’t be much more specific than that. Too unladylike. And they had to do this without any physical contact or explicit disclosure of romantic intent. You could only occasionally converse with your suitors, in chaperoned situations, without so much as looking them in the eyes. No hint of emotional intimacy or mutual trust. This all had to be done with very stiff, formal public personas. Have you ever read Jane Austen, Etienne?”

“No. I know about the novels in general, but I’ve never read them.”

“I could never decide whether Jane Austen wrote this way because that was the only kind of novel that could get published, or whether she actually felt this way in her own life. Was she as sexually repressed as the characters in her writing, or was she more of a free spirit who wasn’t allowed to write more directly. Let me show you.”

She rose and went searching for Pride and Prejudice in her bookshelves. She wasn’t able to locate it. “It must be in the other shelves.”

“Come,” she said, taking his hand and leading him to the bedroom partition. They left the wine behind.

Etienne had never been in this partition before. It had a bed, a nightstand, and nothing much else – except for more bookshelves. Lots of them. While Britta searched for Pride and Prejudice, he looked around for a chair, but didn’t see one. So he took a seat on the bed. When Britta found what she was looking for, she sat down next to him.

As she leafed through the pages, he could see colored sticky notes attached to various pages.

“What do the colors represent?”

She looked up. “The romantic parts.”

“I thought the whole novel was a romance.”

“Well, I marked the actual romantic interactions between Lizzy Bennet and Mr. Darcy because there are so few of them. And even these would barely count as romantic by modern standards. You had to read between the lines, in those days. The romantic interest could barely be expressed until you had an actual proposal on the table. Do you know the story?”

“No.”

“Well, there were two proposals – by Mr. Darcy of course. He’s the fabulously wealthy, good-looking landowner, so he already passes the first test. But Elizabeth Bennet, the heroine, doesn’t like him at first. He has the Pride and she has the Prejudice. There is actual dialog for the first proposal, which Lizzy rejects because she thinks she has reason to hate him. They have never talked frankly before this, so it’s a bolt out of the blue. The second proposal comes near the end, after she gets over her prejudice and he gets over his pride. But there’s almost no dialog! As if now that we are getting to the steamy part by Regency standards, where they would express real romantic emotions, Austen can’t bring herself to do it in dialog. Here’s what he says.” She flipped to the appropriate sticky note, then laid back on the bed to read.

“You are too generous to trifle with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. My affections and wishes are unchanged; but one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever”

“That’s a proposal! The acceptance, if you can call it that, is internal thoughts of Lizzy’s, related by the narrator, about how her sentiments have changed. She never says yes. The narrator doesn’t tell us she accepted, only that she could not look him in the eyes after this. Then they have much more direct and honest conversations about their past actions, as if the dam had finally broken. It isn’t until the next chapter that you hear about them disclosing their engagement. The first time I read it, I thought I had missed the actual proposal and acceptance. But that’s as explicit as it gets.”

Then Britta flipped to a different marked section. Etienne, sensing that another passage was being queued up for reading to him, reclined on the bed to match her casual posture.

“It’s not until the engagement is securely in the bank, that the two finally open up and start talking private self to private self (as if they were now married – so it’s OK). Austen really lets loose, so you can tell that she wants to write at this more emotionally intimate level, just not until we are in the context of a marriage. That’s spice, Regency style.”

Etienne was still waiting for the next reading, but none came. Instead she said, “Darcy reminds me a little of you – waiting for the invitation.”

“I thought he proposed.”

“He did. Eventually. But you find out in the intimate emotional debriefing at the end that they were both waiting for someone to go first.”

Britta stared at the ceiling for a moment, then, “I think you overestimate the symmetry of physical intimacy, Etienne. It’s not really like emotional intimacy, where either gender can go first. A woman can exploit the symmetry of emotional intimacy. She can go first. Elizabeth finally did. Because you are just talking. But sexual intimacy is inherently asymmetrical. I suppose we have equal access to each other’s imagined private spaces. Either can be the first to touch, or hug the other, or even take off the other’s clothes. But our real private physical spaces are asymmetrical. It’s a basic fact of biological design. You know … the plug and the receptacle … the key and the lock. The man has to initiate. He has the mobile part. A man can initiate unilaterally, without consent, but a woman cannot. We can’t rape – not that I would want that. So a woman can only allow the entry or bar the door. Our role is passive. To initiate, a woman can only invite. She has to indicate, somehow, that she wants to share her bodily privacy.”

Etienne turned his head to look at her. “But that’s why it’s so important for me to be sure. I don’t want to assume, and be wrong.”

“But that’s not how it works in the real world, Etienne. Even polite men are always knocking at the door, asking Molly Bloom to say “Yes. Yes, I will. Yes.”

Etienne smiled at this. “You read James Joyce too.”

Britta looked toward her bookshelves, then pointed to her copy of Ulysses.

Etienne continued. “Joyce was a favorite of mine when I was in high school. I started with Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, probably his most accessible work. When I got to Ulysses, then Finnegans Wake, even though the reading was much more difficult, I was attracted to the implied innovation. I was impressed that this man was venerated by the literary establishment, which put a patina of genius on him. For some reason, there were deep, hidden truths to be deciphered in these works, so I wanted to decipher them. To find out what all of the academic chatter was about.”

“And did you decipher these truths?”

“No. After a Ph.D. in philosophy, I became less tolerant of obscure but venerated texts – like Hegel, and Heidegger. Rereading Ulysses from my current perspective, I still enjoy the writing style and the symbolism, but I’m no longer compelled to find a hidden meaning.”

He paused, then, “But I see your point about asymmetry of sexual intimacy. It had always been symmetrical for me. I know I am atypical.”

“Yes, you are … If Leopold Bloom had been you, Molly would still be Miss Tweedy. If Darcy had been you, Elizabeth would still be Miss Bennet. Darcy was almost you.” She flipped to another of her sticky notes. “This is at the end, where they are sharing their previous private selves. Lizzy begins.”

“I shall begin directly, by asking you what made you so unwilling to come to the point at last? What made you so shy of me, when you first called, and afterwards dined here? Why, especially, when you called, did you look as if you did not care about me?”

“Because you were grave and silent, and gave me no encouragement.”

“But I was embarrassed.”

“And so was I.”

“You might have talked to me more when you came to dinner.”

“A man who had felt less might.”

“How unlucky that you should have a reasonable answer to give, and that I should be so reasonable as to admit it! But I wonder how long you would have gone on, if you had been left to yourself. I wonder when you would have spoken if I had not asked you!”

“So that’s me? Waiting forever for the invitation that never comes?”

“If you don’t mind my saying so, it seems to me you’ve been waiting outside my door for some time, Etienne, waiting to come in. But you never knock. Or perhaps it was just me, waiting for you to come in without knocking. Now that I know you better, I suppose I need to be more explicit.”

She rolled over on top of him and rested her chin in her hands with her elbows on his chest, so she could address him face to face.

“Will you accept my kind invitation to come in, sir? I offer it openly, and willingly, and I would very much like for you to visit.”

There was a pause.

Then, “I should let you know that there have been no prior visitors to my parlor. No one has yet crossed the threshold. I'm not really sure how to behave with visitors. So when you come in, you must be mindful of the immaculate, light-colored rugs, and delicate with the fine china.”

Her little Regency allegory went straight to the heart, and touched him so deeply that he now had no choice but to accept. No prior resolutions or conscious decisions could have prepared him for this. He didn’t really choose anything. The choice had been made for him at a much deeper level. A level that he had no conscious access to. In this particular moment, his free will was no longer free.

In the comforting warmth of the afterglow, Etienne rested his head on Britta’s shoulder. She sniffed slightly. He turned his head to look her in the eyes. She was crying. Not weeping, with tears coming down her face, but with soft, moist eyes and some tears welling up at the edges.

"Are you alright? You’re crying."

"Don't worry, I'm alright," she sniffed. She said this first with a far-off expression. Then she looked more directly at him. "They're happy tears." She followed this with a small, sympathetic smile, as she regained her composure.

Happy tears, Etienne thought, a concept that was completely new to him. It was almost a metaphor because 'happy' and 'tears' don't go together – normally. But it made sense.

Tears are usually the result of deep emotional sadness, but apparently they are a result of deeply felt emotions in general. So this was deep emotional happiness. That was touching. He spent no more time analyzing this like a philosopher. Instead, he reflected on the contrast between Britta and Evangeline. This would likely never happen with Evangeline. It was too rare of a human response to be in any training set. Androids express a cross-section of human emotional responses, with a little bit of	non-deterministic variation. But they miss the spontaneous edge cases that arise from time to time in human-to-human interactions. Rare cases like happy tears.

Etienne and Britta lay together for a while, not saying anything. There was no need for words. But eventually, the quiet, tender moments gave way to the present reality.

“Whatever will we do now, Etienne?”

“I don’t know.”

“I suppose now you’ll have to choose between Evangeline and me. There’s no way around it now. I know it’s an impossible choice for you.”

Etienne was turning thoughts over in his head, but didn’t know how to respond. Britta waited, but he was taking a long time.

“No, Etienne. I know what you’re hoping. You can’t have us both. You can love both of us, but you can only have one of us. You know that’s how it works. It would be just too weird otherwise.”

“The Mormons did it.”

“We’re not the Mormons.”

“But we’re not all human either. This might be different than a love triangle between three humans.”

“How so?”

“I don’t know. It was just a thought. Something might be different. I don’t really understand my relationship with Evangeline as it is. There are always surprises. Most of them pleasant. New ways to think about things.”

“I’m not following you.”

“That’s because I’m not leading you anywhere. It’s just that there is this interesting difference that we might want to think about. Does it give us more options?”

“You think three humans would have fewer options?”

“Yes, because humans are more predictable. Our romantic emotions are based on the exclusivity of pair bonds. You want me to make a choice because if I didn’t, there would be two overlapping pair bonds among the three of us. You can’t imagine that. You naturally feel that your intimacy with me would be devalued if I shared it with someone else.”

“But don’t you feel that way too? Would you be OK with sharing me with another man?”

“No, of course not. But that’s not how we got into this predicament. If I had fallen hopelessly in love with you while you were already in a relationship, sharing you would be the best that I could hope for – unless I could eventually win you away from him.”

This hit home for Britta. “And that’s me in this triangle, isn’t it. I was the interloper. I invaded your intimate bond with Evangeline. You were trying to honor that, but I effectively seduced you, didn’t I? For my own selfish reasons. And now I want to take you away from Evangeline – someone whom I’ve come to care very deeply about. I’m a terrible person, aren’t I?”

He embraced her. “No. Not at all. It’s just a quirk of human nature. The positive romantic emotions obscure the negative ones, like jealousy and infidelity. When we are drawn to someone we love, we are not thinking about the people that love may possibly harm. I’m just as guilty as you.”

“But now it’s time to consider the possible harm, isn’t it?”

“Yes, but that’s why our case might be different than a triangle among humans. Part of the intimacy bond between human couples is a trust in the safety against losing your partner to someone else – the “forsaking all others” part. Jealousy is a fear that someone else might be threatening this trust, and infidelity is when one of the partners has actually broken it – so guilt for the breaker and loss of trust for the broken.”

“I suppose what I feel is not jealousy toward Evangeline, but envy of her. She already has you. And I certainly have no right to fidelity from you at this point.”

“Well, I certainly have no reason for jealousy in either direction. I suppose I’m in the favored position.” He smiled at this. “But I do feel the weight of infidelity toward Evangeline. It’s not some abstract principle about broken contracts. It’s empathy for her – how she will feel when she realizes she might lose me. We will have to tell her, you know.”

“Yes, I agree. We have to tell her. We can’t go sneaking around about this, waiting for her to discover this on her own. How do you think she will react?”

“That’s my point. Probably not quite like a human woman. She’s both an omniscient chatbot that knows everything there is to know about human nature, and Audrey Hepburn, whose native emotional responses are not at all typical.”

Britta thought about this for a moment. “You’re right. Look how she responded when I tried to tell her that this might happen. That’s why I like her so much. She’s so understanding.”

“But on the negative side, we also have fewer options than with humans. If we were all human, and I chose to leave her for you, I would typically move out, and move in with you (disregarding whose house it is for the moment). But no matter how I feel, I can’t physically abandon Evangeline. She has no place to go, no independent existence, no real identity to protect her from ICE.”

This really hit home for Britta. “So she has to live with you. And if I want to live with you … the three of us have to live together. Otherwise, I’m just the “other woman” in the triangle who you sleep with occasionally.”

“That’s about the size of it.”

“So we end up back at ‘sister wives’ after all, don’t we?”

He smiled. “Not necessarily. We’ll have to start that way – if we are going to tell her, and she doesn’t object to you being there. But I haven’t made a choice yet. It’s possible I will, given some time. Then we could change the sleeping arrangements. But I can’t choose right now, don’t you see? You and I have just begun. I have a significant history with Evangeline already. That favors her. The only way for you to force a choice at this point is to make one yourself – a choice not to follow, and thus return the triangle to a pair.”

“Do you want that?”

“No. I want you to come with me. I want this to work.”

“Then you really do love me?”

“Yes! Isn’t it obvious?”

She smiled. As the reality of the situation settled in, Britta began to warm to the concept of three-way sharing – for now anyway. Yes, it was still weird, but it was based on positive romantic emotions all around. If anyone was entitled to negative ones, it was surely Evangeline. She would be the one who had to open her heart to a three-way bond, to let Britta in. Still, she wanted to know if Etienne was deferring a choice until later, or hoping never to have to make one at all.

“Will you choose eventually?”

“I don’t know. Right now, I don’t want to lose either of you. But I suspect I will need to choose – eventually.”

“Are you leaning in any particular direction?”

“No.”

“OK, imagine you were one of Jane Austen’s heroines, and you had multiple proposals from gentlemen. How would you go about deciding whose to accept (if any)? Which one would be most likely to ‘make you happy’?” (She was hoping she could beat an android at this).

“Well, that’s not the same, is it? The poor woman has almost no emotional bonds, and certainly no physical bonds, with any of her suitors. She’s making a huge inference, on very little evidence, about what will happen in the future. I have existing bonds of both kinds with both of you. My mind is very clouded.”

“Well, just wipe those clouds away, for a moment. Think about the future. How would your life be different, depending on which of us you shared it with. Be realistic. Make your inference. Who is more likely to make you happy in the long run?”

(Philosophers routinely do these sorts of thought experiments). After a little pondering, he said, with a far off expression, “Evangeline will never change. She will always be as beautiful as she is now. And, thanks to Collins, she will always love me. I would never have to worry about that – ever.”

Britta’s heart sank. Why had she forced him down this road? She couldn’t compete on either of these aspects.

“So that’s why I would probably choose you. Because Evangeline will never change.”

She was stunned. “But I will grow old, and lose my youthful good looks!”

“And so will I,” he smiled. “We’ll grow old together. So neither will disappoint the other. We’ll match all the way to the end. And by going through these changes together, we’ll probably grow even closer.”

“But you could never be certain that I wouldn’t leave you some day, unlike with Evangeline.”

He smiled again. “So I’d have to continue to earn your love, unlike with Evangeline. To keep up with you. To not take you for granted. And you would have to do the same for me. That will make us closer as well.”

chapters.title: NINE
chapters.content:
NINE

Etienne returned to Evangeline on Acorn Street later that afternoon. Britta stayed in Cambridge. They had decided they should jointly tell Evangeline on the next afternoon – Sunday. Britta would come for a visit at Acorn Street, and Evangeline would know she was coming, but the topic would not be disclosed until then.

It was a long night for Britta. She had a lot to think about, and a lot of emotions to process. She was initially apprehensive about how this would all go down. How would they explain it? What if Evangeline were to reject the arrangement? Britta probably would have, if she were in her shoes, but Evangeline was not Britta. And Britta came to love her all the more because of this – in a sisterly way. Her thoughts eventually settled in a positive direction, as she came to realize that she had secured her place in the triangle she was hoping for, but the outcome would be different than what she had imagined. She hadn’t really visualized the endgame, but it certainly wasn’t this. In the new triangle – the possible triangle, it hadn’t been accepted yet – everyone loved everyone else, in pairwise fashion, each pair sharing the kind of intimacy appropriate to their genders. On this, she could sleep.

Etienne had a different subject to occupy his busy mind. The last thing he wanted to do, at this point, was to choose between Britta and Evangeline. But he knew instinctively that these two overlapping bonds of physical intimacy could not last. It would not be stable. And he also knew instinctively that it would eventually have to be resolved in favor of Britta. The android vs. human comparison was inescapable. When it was just Evangeline, he could avoid thinking of her as other than human, but with the two of them side by side, day after day, it was impossible not to remember. He knew what human love was like. He knew what to expect. He was only navigating android love by pretending it was human. So every time it was not the same, he would notice now.

His busy mind was finally put to rest by Evangeline, who always seemed to know how to get him to abandon his cares, and just live in the moment with her.

By early Sunday afternoon, there was a knock on the door at Acorn Street. Evangeline knew Britta was coming, but not much else at this point. Etienne and Britta had not made a plan for how to go about this. They didn’t even have a plan for a plan. It would just happen when it happened.

Evangeline answered the door, and welcomed Britta in. It was a far cry from their first encounter over Etienne’s threshold, when there was a lot of mutual sizing up. They were fast friends now, who didn’t keep secrets from each other (except for the most recent one, of course). Britta tried to act natural, but it was only Evangeline that was truly at ease – ignorance being bliss.

They took up their usual places in the front parlor, where wine and charcuterie were waiting. Britta wasted no time getting started on the wine. Since there was no plan, both Britta and Etienne took their time with the polite conversation, waiting for the appropriate moment, though it soon became clear that no moment would be more appropriate than any other moment. One of them would just have to start. They didn’t realize that their nervous procrastination was tipping off Evangeline. The awkwardness of settling on who should start caused them to glance back and forth at each other. Evangeline knew something portentous was coming.

Etienne finally resolved to go first, but Britta beat him to the punch.

“Evangeline, I have … we have something to tell you.”

“Yes?”

“Do you remember how I told you yesterday that Etienne and I had developed a very close … emotional relationship, and that … that …”

“That it might develop into a romantic relationship?”

“Yes.”

“And it has?”

“Yes! I’m so sorry, Evangeline. I didn’t mean to hurt you.” Britta was clearly distressed.

The two women were seated close enough that Evangeline could reach over and hug Britta. Britta protested lightly. “I’m sorry. I should be comforting you.”

“That would be nice,” Evangeline replied in her best, most vulnerable Audrey Hepburn voice.

So the two women formed a mutual embrace, and held on for a while. Etienne was feeling a bit lost at this point, but the most delicate and contentious leg of the triangle was now bonding, so it eased his mind a little. He had the urge to join the hug, particularly given Evangeline’s expression, but thought better of it. That might be premature. They hadn’t heard from Evangeline yet.

Evangeline, though, ever the reader of human emotions, caught his expression, and nodded yes to him. “Yes, come.”

He did, confirming the first three-way emotional sharing of the fledgling triangle.

When they broke, Etienne made sure he was first to speak this time. “I’m sorry too, Evangeline. You didn’t deserve this. We both feel quite awful about how our bond will affect you. But we haven’t heard from you yet. How does this make you feel?” (Britta was wondering the same thing).

Evangeline didn’t answer right away. She dithered a little, almost like the old days with the movie mismatches. “I don’t know how to respond. I take my cues from the two of you, but we have different relationships to each other. So I can’t decide whether you want an “in the world” emotional response – this is a very emotional moment – or an LLM response – explaining why I feel the way I do.”

“Anything,” Britta replied. “We’ll take anything. Whatever comes out. We both care about you so much.”

“Well … I’ll try my best to merge the two points of view. I could see that this might happen … and our situation is not at all like a typical human love triangle. As I understand it, Britta and I first met Etienne at about the same time. And we both formed some immediate bonds with you. So it’s not really like you came along later and stole him from me, Britta. I simply had more opportunity to develop my bond at first. And Britta’s not stealing you from me, is she Etienne?”

“No!” they both replied simultaneously. “That’s a relief,” Evangeline smiled.

“You and Britta are very much alike, Etienne. I can see that now. So it makes sense that the two of you would attract each other emotionally. I couldn’t have done much about that, given that she’s human and I’m not. Have either of you thought about what we should do about this?”

“Yes,” they both replied simultaneously.

“Etienne has,” Britta clarified, “and I’ve agreed. He should really tell you.”

“Well, I don’t want to lose either of you. And I don’t want you two to have to compete over me. I don’t want either of you to be the one to lose me. Then there’s the practical consideration … that you still need to physically live here with me, given the ICE situation in this country. So … “

“So Britta would have to live here too.”

“Yes,” again, simultaneously.

“Kind of like the Mormons,” Evangeline smiled.

Britta and Etienne looked at each other with ironic smiles. “Yes, kind of like that,” Britta added.

Then there was a silence as each eyed the others, wondering how the closure would happen.

Evangeline smiled. “I suppose you are waiting for me, aren’t you? Being an android, I’m designed to accommodate humans. Humans don’t expect me to make choices for them.”

“Well, in this case, it is your choice,” Etienne responded. “Right Britta?”

“Yes. You choose, Evangeline. We interrupted your life.”

“In that case, I think the ‘sister wives’ arrangement is the best for all of us. It makes the most people happy.”

Britta and Etienne smiled at each other, relieved.

“But how do you really feel, Evangeline,” Etienne asked. “This sounds like a Utilitarian philosophical choice – greatest good for the greatest number. That’s your LLM plus Audrey empathy talking. Can you strip that away for a moment and give your best ‘in the world’ emotional response?”

“You want to know if I feel betrayed? If I feel hurt? If I feel jealous?”

“Yes.”

“Well, ordinarily I would, because that is a very common human response. Filtered through Audrey Hepburn, I would damp that down, as she would, and suffer silently, being noble. But remember what Mr. Collins did with the imprinting. This can’t be changed or overridden with any present circumstance. My affection for you is not generated by the LLM. So I will always be in love with you, and I’ll always want to sleep with you. Audrey will temper that a bit in how it gets expressed, but it will always come out. The upside is that it will always come out positive. It’s a positive inclination. There is no negative dimension to it, like jealousy. Audrey might have gotten over this with time, if it had developed organically, but she can’t change what’s hard-wired down there.”

“So you’re OK with this?” Britta asked, hopefully.

“Well … as I said, this devotion to Etienne, which I can’t control, is positive. I want to always be with him. I don’t think about what’s fair, or noble, or what I am entitled to. I want whatever keeps him next to me. If my best chance to keep him is to share him with you, then that’s what I want. I don’t think it devalues our bond in any way, do you?”

“No …” Britta replied, thoughtfully. “That’s how I feel too,” she added, sympathetically.

The two women smiled silently at each other. Etienne just sat there. What could he possibly add?

Britta stayed for dinner. Of course she did. Though she couldn’t help feeling a little ill at ease by the arrangement. She had inserted herself into Etienne’s life, and was now inserting herself into Evangeline’s and Etienne’s home – an uninvited guest that was now being invited. Evangeline made it easier by suggesting that she and Britta jointly make the dinner. Britta readily accepted. Etienne, again, felt a little superfluous. He was all for the two women bonding, but this seemed a little too close to ‘sister wives’ for his comfort – the wives part, not the sisters. And the attendant notion that wives prepare the meals while the husband does … whatever the husband does. That wasn’t the vibe they were signing up for, he thought.

So he suggested that they all three make the dinner – planning, shopping, cooking, and cleaning up. The women had no problem with that.

The conversation throughout the stages of the dinner then flowed naturally, following their usual three-way style. No one mentioned the upcoming differences. This suited Britta and Etienne just fine, suggesting that their previous three-way bond could continue without disruption.

But Evangeline, ever the astute observer of human social emotions, took it upon herself to ease both of them into the differences, after they were done, and the night was coming on. It had not yet been determined whether Britta would be staying here tonight, or returning to her place in Cambridge. So Evangeline volunteered that not only should Britta stay the night, but that she could have the first night with Etienne. “You have a lot of catching up to do,” she smiled.

Evangeline also took it upon herself to show Britta around the house, locating the two bathrooms and the two bedrooms, and pointing out the unavoidable squeaks of the floorboards. She prepared the guest bedroom for Britta. “This will be your room, and that will be mine.” She pointed across the hall. Then she related all of the details about the greater street visibility of the front bedroom, and how to set the shutters to minimize this, reprising her calculations from her first night at Acorn Street.

Etienne was functionally useless again, but this time he didn’t mind. Britta needed this warm welcome, particularly from the woman of the house whose home she had invaded. It wasn’t something she felt she had earned, so Evangeline’s magnanimous acceptance of her, particularly the offer for the first night, eased her conscience, and helped her adopt Evangeline’s advice to leave the negative emotions behind.

With the doors closed, the shutters closed, and the lights out, Britta and Etienne did have some catching up to do. Their earlier first encounter now seemed like such a long time ago. This time they felt more conscious freedom in their developing bond. They were sanctioned by Evangeline, not stealing from her.

When it got around to the pillow talk part, Etienne asked, “Do you feel more like a woman of the world now?”

She turned her head toward him. “Instead of a woman of fiction?” Then she turned back, looking up at the ceiling, with a contemplative smile. “Yes … there are so many different portrayals of this in fiction. I think what resonates most with me is Molly Bloom’s soliloquy – you know, the part at the end: ‘Yes. Yes, I will. Yes.’ Did you know that Joyce considered ‘yes’ a female word?”

“No, I didn’t know that.”

“I think he was calling out the notion of female acceptance. In Molly’s case, it was not at all like surrendering, or accommodating, or suddenly changing her mind. It was a conscious decision. She sized up the situation, and this is where she wanted to go.

yes and how he kissed me under the Moorish wall and I thought well as well him as another and then I asked him with my eyes to ask again yes and then he asked me would I yes to say yes my mountain flower and first I put my arms around him yes and drew him down to me so he could feel my breasts all perfume yes and his heart was going like mad and yes I said yes I will Yes.”

“You know it by heart?”

“Well that part anyway.”

Etienne was about to say something like “not many people can do that,” until it occurred to him that he probably could. Or at least he remembered it well enough to paraphrase it.

“And how about that elusive transition from vulgar act to tender moment?”

She was still looking at the ceiling. “I think I was wrong about that. About it being a transition. It’s not even a Gestalt switch. I wasn’t thinking so much ‘vulgar’ act as ‘animal’ act. How do you go from sex as an animal act to sex as a tender moment? But we don’t really go from one to the other, do we? The animal act is in a different realm altogether when the time comes. You don’t think about this at all. It’s all tender moment. You don’t have to reimagine anything.”

“That’s been my experience. It’s not unlike seeing emoters as humans instead of androids when you are closely interacting with them.”

“Like you and Evangeline.”

“Especially like me and Evangeline. It’s seamless now. I think the Gestalt switch between romantic and animal goes back to our earlier days when everyone was closer to nature than we are now. Even kids, because they grew up on farms, knew about animal mating. They saw it all around them. And it wasn’t hard for them to infer that this must work the same way with their parents, even before the birds and the bees talk. But it’s a sharp contrast with how we like to perceive our human love lives. So the comparison is always there in the background, even when we try to pretend it isn’t. It’s the same with food. We get our meat neatly wrapped in plastic at the supermarket now. But our ancestors saw the actual slaughter and butchering process, and stuffing ground flesh into intestines. It’s better not to see how the sausage is made, as they say. So our enjoyment of fine cuisine and tender moments is sometimes impinged upon by our knowledge of what they really are.”

Britta smiled an ironic smile. “I didn’t grow up on a farm, but I’ve seen animal mating on nature shows. Not very tender, is it? It can sometimes be painful for the female. You see the male chasing her, cornering her, mounting her, then it’s all over in a jiffy and he leaves. It’s certainly pleasurable for the male. Not so clear for the female. It almost looks like rape with all the coercion and forced entry. I suppose that’s why men sometimes try to justify non-consensual sex. Oh, she’ll come around. That’s how nature works. It’s in the genes. Are they right? Do you think we’ve inherited this tendency from our mammalian past?”

“No! People who argue that are completely misinformed about how mammalian sex works – and for the birds and the insects, for that matter. Rape is a human invention. Mammals typically only mate when the female is in estrus – heat. This is tied to her ovulation cycle and often also to the time of year – like spring. Females not only give consent to specific males, they often broadcast a signal of consent to all males in the area, via pheromones, or vaginal swellings, or specific behaviors. They are the inviters. The males do not care about sex until this signal arouses them. You only see the final act, but the consent is always mutual, even though it appears a little rough at times. Humans, on the other hand, have concealed ovulation. There is no signal as to when she is fertile. And males are, consequently, “always on.” Their arousal is not based on the fertility cycle, so they are always on the prowl.”

“Hmm. Could that be where our sexual modesty comes from? Preventing male arousal by covering up the parts? Then taking off your clothes becomes the human equivalent of the pheromone. It sends the arousal signal – the invitation. We see this all the time in the movies, even the historical ones. She enters his chamber, lets her hair down, and drops her gown. Are you aroused by my body, Etienne?”

“Yes,” he smiled.

“Of course you are,” she smiled. “That was a silly question. What if I had taken off my clothes for you, instead of verbally inviting you this afternoon?”

“Would you have?”

“No. That would have been too bold for me. I would have been too inhibited.”

“Well, I much prefer what you actually did. Your poetic allegory was a much more romantic gesture. Much more effective.”

“I realize that now. It was more emotionally intimate, a channel I already had open with you. I managed to stay in the tender moments regime. I’m not sure I could have seduced you with just my body.”

“Because it would have been too animal?”

“Yes, exactly. I know it would have aroused you, but you would probably have been too much of a gentleman.”

“And now?”

She smiled. “Now is completely different, Etienne. We are on the same wavelength now, both emotionally and physically. Both intimacies match now. Why was I so worried about this.”

“Well, you told me before that these two kinds of intimacy couldn’t be synced, because physical intimacy was too asymmetrical. The plug and the receptacle, remember? The approach and the experiences are different for men and women.”

She pondered this for a moment. She had said that, hadn’t she? What was different now? Now that she was a woman of the world. “I think the physical experiences are different. But before, I thought what distinguished transactional sex from intimate sex was the mutual caring for each other, a very abstract kind of empathy. A straight carry-over from emotional intimacy. It made up for the different physical experiences. I didn’t know how to account for sexual pleasure yet.”

“And now?”

“Now … now I think we can share our physical pleasure, even if our plumbing is different – in just the same way we share our more abstract emotional thoughts. Pleasure is an emotion, after all. A very specific one, like pain. More specific than happiness. Maybe ‘feeling’ is a better term. We each physically experience our own sexual pleasure and, via empathetic mirroring, we vicariously experience the sexual pleasure of our partner. We can sense what the other is feeling. It’s so romantically intimate because we are experiencing not just two pleasures, but a third one – the pleasure of connecting like this. It’s the same way we vicariously experience each other’s more abstract emotions: through facial expressions, and body language, and words.”

“Though with very few words and much more expressive body language,” Etienne smiled.

So she wouldn’t spontaneously orchestrate a surprise birthday party for me, for instance, by calling up my friends, and making all of the arrangements. You would have to tell her to do this, so there would be a context to react to. These responses come from the LLM part. But she is hardwired to react to men sexually. That’s why she can naturally initiate, without an explicit human prompt. The presence of the right man is the prompt. It doesn’t come from the LLM part, it’s inbuilt.”

“So now I’m confused. You say she does have native sexual feelings, just like a human.”

“No, she does have native sexual urges, let’s say, but not like a human. She can’t introspect on them like you do, because the feelings are not actually there. They are dispositions in her firmware. They are generated on demand. So she’s only aware of them in retrospect, in her stored memory trace of what she has generated. She has no native vocabulary for describing these, like you do. She has to use her LLM to generate a description of what a typical human would feel in such a context. But sex, as you and I know – particularly the intimate nuances that you and I feel – are both highly personal and private. Stuff like this is not readily available on the internet. People rarely disclose this publicly. So her LLM doesn’t have much to draw on. She can only give me a generic answer about what typical humans would feel.”

“But humans can do this.”

“Humans can do this, but often don’t. We all have some introspective access to our feelings and emotions. But I would wager that very few humans have pillow talks like we do.” He turned to look at her, smiling. “You are unusual in the way you are in touch with your inner feelings, more than anyone I’ve known. And you are very articulate in describing what you feel, and reasoning about it, and coming up with epiphanies.”

“And you like that – as a philosopher – don’t you? No, you love that, because you are the same way as me. That’s why we can connect so easily at this.”

“Exactly!”

chapters.title: TEN
chapters.content:
TEN

By the time Thanksgiving rolled around, Evangeline was no longer sleeping with Etienne. The ratio of nights had dwindled down gradually to its natural conclusion, as envisioned. It was a smooth transition, with possibly a little bit of nostalgia on Evangeline’s final night. But now the trio had settled into their more permanent roles as two lovers and a house guest – with optimistic expectations that this could be stable long-term.
