They had taken several road trips into northern New England when the fall colors were at their peak – a new experience for both Evangeline and Britta. Nothing in their respective countries of origin had prepared them for the intense and varied shades of red. Morning conversations with other guests at the bed-and-breakfasts gave them a chance to rehearse their public roles.

Evangeline had been fitted out with a manufactured identity document, courtesy of Etienne’s friend, Roscoe Erlinger. That served as the trust anchor for getting a Massachusetts state ID for her. The vetting process, as with all state-administered verification protocols, was not particularly rigorous, but once the state ID was issued, it became the canonical identity document for ICE, so the original fake credential was no longer exposed to scrutiny. Etienne had considered getting her the more traditional state driver’s license, but that would require first teaching her how to drive. Specialized motor skills are usually pre-trained into androids for their specific roles at a level lower than the LLM, so he was not sure how to do this, or whether the skill was generic enough that he could teach her like a human is taught. Since he didn’t have a car of his own, and Evangeline had no need to drive, they just skipped this step.

Evangeline only had to use her new ID twice, once in Cambridge and once in Vermont, when both she and Britta were carded at pubs. With her official identity now secure, the only remaining exposure to ICE would be the revealing of her internal LLM. It was often too hard to tell whom they could trust, even among friends, with disclosing her as an emoter, so the plan was hatched to keep this fact among just the three of them. For everyone else, Evangeline would have to behave in a way that matched her assumed human identity, as she had done so successfully with ICE before. They decided to use the backstory she had concocted for them, since there would be some notes on file that this needed to match. So among themselves, in private, she was the dual-purpose wise woman who knew everything, and the more focused Audrey Hepburn emoting in the present. To others, she was just the orphan from Basel who ended up here after her Swiss sponsor was killed.

The trio’s first venture out into local society was actually a venture in. Etienne had invited a few of the department faculty to a traditional Thanksgiving dinner at Acorn Street. He had seldom invited guests to his house, and he was aware of department chatter about the two attractive women now often seen with him in and around Emerson Hall, so he made it a point to keep the invitation low-key. It was informal and on a need-to-know basis. This was not intended to be an announcement of any sort, just the first toe in the water. He invited professors Emily Fraser and Geoffrey Applebaum. These were friends he could trust, but his household had already decided that Evangeline would be presented, even to them, as human.

As the conversation and the wine flowed around the Thanksgiving table, the topics remained above the level that his colleagues were really interested in. So Britta was introduced as a Nieman Fellow from Sweden, and Evangeline as the erstwhile intern from Switzerland. (The Collins story was of particular interest). It was not revealed who, if anyone, other than Etienne stayed here overnight. But, of course, they both were curious.

Emily, in particular, noticed that when the three of them were seated next to each other at the table, the glances and the eye contact among them were equally distributed, but when Etienne and Evangeline had gone to the kitchen to bring in the dessert, there was a little more eye contact on Evangeline’s part, and even a brief touching of hands. Evangeline initiated, but Etienne didn’t seem to mind at all. It was subtle, but notable. Britta had noticed brief instances of this as well over the last few months, but thought it was of no concern. It was an expected side effect, she reasoned, of the imprinting Evangeline still had on Etienne.

Emily finally had to ask. “Etienne, you must have noticed … there’s been quite a bit of speculation around the department about Evangeline and Britta. First we saw a lot of Evangeline, then a little bit of Britta, then a lot of all three of you – sometimes together and sometimes in pairs. People naturally wonder.”

“Wonder about what, Emily?” (He was toying with her, but in a friendly manner).

“Oh, you know what I mean. I’m not asking for an announcement or anything. And we can keep this among ourselves, if you’d like.” She glanced in Geoffrey’s direction. “In all the years we’ve known you, this is something new.”

Etienne just smiled, so Britta broke the ice. “We’re all three very good friends, but Etienne and I are in a relationship. Evangeline is our house guest.”

“House guest … ?”

“Yes, we all three live here.”

“I see … well isn’t that nice. I’m happy for you,” Emily smiled. “Explains a lot.”

Geoffrey looked at Etienne with a smile and a raised eyebrow.

The next venture out actually was out. There had been philosophy department Christmas parties, off and on, over the years, usually at a hosting colleague’s house. The extra responsibility for hosting was beginning to take a toll, so volunteers were becoming few. This year it was decided to host the party – not a big production, just office-party scale – on the second floor of Emerson Hall. Everyone could chip in for a little catering, so no one had to be the host. This brought out more guests, including some graduate students who had not returned home for the holiday break, and some faculty who were not in residence for the term, but had returned to Cambridge for the holidays.

Among these was Associate Professor Stanley Clark, who was otherwise in residence at Stanford for the year. “I missed the snow,” he said, facetiously. His area of specialization was aesthetics. This allowed him to hobnob at film festivals and art installations, and integrate film criticism into his courses – and gave him the appropriate gravitas to be a published film critic. He was also a bit of a ladies’ man – by his own self-styling – usually with a woman on his arm at major appearances (a different one each time). He was the male equivalent of the femme fatale, motivated by his desire to “conquer” women. Whether this “conquering” amounted to actual seduction, no one really knew. It was enough to be seen with women in public. He was not particularly attractive, but he leveraged his public standing and Harvard affiliation as a display of social importance – an intellectual attuned to the arts. Let me show you my etchings, my dear.

Tonight, though, as Etienne, Britta and Evangeline arrived together for the evening, he was without a trophy escort, so he was on the prowl. The trio made it a point to circulate among the guests rather than sticking together. They had the confidence for this now. Their particular relationships to each other were still not publicly known, though they had not sworn Professors Fraser and Applebaum to secrecy. They were going to wing it tonight.

The sight of both Britta and Evangeline was familiar to most guests, but not to Clark. He had seen Evangeline a few times before he left for Stanford at the start of the term, but because he was thereafter in California, he had not seen, nor heard about, Britta. He saw both women enter with Etienne before they spread out, and was duly impressed. “Two of them!” he thought to himself. And they were both gorgeous. As he watched both, he saw a little of what Britta and Emily had seen. When Etienne and Evangeline were together in the absence of Britta, Evangeline was particularly attentive to Etienne. His first hypothesis was that this one must have already been conquered by Etienne. She showed particular devotion to him.

Curious to get the lowdown, he struck up a conversation with Emily about philosophy matters, then gradually worked his way down to what he really wanted to know. “When I left for Stanford, I saw Etienne’s first female companion a few times. Now it appears he has two! You go, Etienne! Anybody know what’s going on there?”

“Oh, one is the girlfriend, and the other is just a house guest. They all get along quite well together. I saw this at Thanksgiving. It’s quite natural.”

“I see.” Then, “Oh, excuse me for a moment. I see Professor Thomson over there. I need to have a word with him.”

With that, he started in the direction of Professor Thomson until Emily looked away, then he pivoted and made a beeline for Britta, who was just returning solo from the punch bowl. This must be the house guest, he thought.

“Hello. I believe I saw you come in with Professor Harris, earlier. I’m Professor Clark, a colleague of his.”

“Well, hello, Professor Clark, I’m Britta.” She extended her hand for the obligatory shake.

“Pleased to meet you, Britta. Please call me Stanley. Are you from around here?” (He didn’t have Etienne’s skill with foreign accents, and Britta’s was beginning to fade a little).

“No, I’m from Sweden. I’m a Nieman Fellow at Harvard for the year.”

“A Nieman Fellow! Congratulations! And how did you become acquainted with Etienne?”

“I interviewed him for an article for the New York Times.”

“The Times! That’s great! I also write for them. Perhaps you’ve seen some of my film reviews for the Arts section – Professor Stanley Clark?”

“No, can’t say that I have. But I don’t read the Times very often. I was filling in for Richard Hornby.”

“Ah, one of Etienne’s least favorite writers,” he smiled. “Well, my specialty is aesthetics – you know, art, film, drama, fiction. The concepts of beauty and genius in general. Perhaps I could show you around the local arts scene sometime. Are you free any time this week?”

Britta could see where this was going. “Thank you for the invitation, but I’m afraid I’m not free anytime for what you have in mind. I’m in a relationship already.”

“Oh, I didn’t realize that. Someone back in Sweden?”

“No, someone here.”

“Someone here? And you didn’t bring him with you?”

“I did … Etienne.”

“Etienne?” He looked over at Evangeline. “I must have been misinformed. I thought you were the house guest.”

“Well, I am. A permanent house guest, if you catch my drift.”

“I see … so the dark-haired woman over there is the temporary house guest?”

“You mean Evangeline?”

“Is that her name? The one that looks like Audrey Hepburn.”

“Yes, that’s her. But she’s also a permanent house guest, just not in the same way as me.”

“I guess I was confused. Just watching her and Etienne interact, I got the impression that they were together.”

“Well, they are very close friends. Perhaps that’s what you saw.” (Britta now had some new doubts).

“My mistake. You’re right. Well it was nice to meet you Britta.” With that he turned and began working his way over to Evangeline. Britta could see his plan, so she went looking for Etienne. Evangeline would likely soon need a rescue.

When Clark approached, Evangeline was chatting with Emily, so he inserted himself into the conversation.

“This is Stanley Clark,” Emily said, introducing him to Evangeline.

“Are you a philosophy professor too?” Evangeline asked.

“Yes! Aesthetics is my specialty, it’s … “

“the study of beauty and genius – like art and drama and film,” Evangeline finished his sentence for him, as she was wont to do.

“Oh, you know about that?”

“I’ve learned a lot from Etienne.” (She hadn’t learned this, but was faking it to obscure her LLM knowledge).

“Are you from around here?” (Again displaying his lack of accent recognition).

“No, I’m from Switzerland. Basel.”

“Has anyone ever told you you look exactly like Audrey Hepburn?”

“Yes, I hear that sometimes. But many people don’t know who that is.”

Emily looked a little quizzical. “She was a film actress way back in the 1950s–60s,” Clark informed her. Then turning again to Evangeline, he asked “Have you seen any of her movies?”

“No, I’ve just heard about them.”

“Come with me. I’ll show you.” He took her hand, leading her away from Emily. “I have some stills and posters for the films in my office.”

By now, Britta had apprised Etienne of the situation, and they were both watching from a distance. Etienne started to move toward them. “Time for the rescue.”

“No,” Britta grabbed his arm. “Let me do it. You detain this Clark fellow.”

Britta and Etienne arrived in front of the hunter and the prey together. Britta took Evangeline’s hand and said, “Evangeline, I need to show you something right away.” Evangeline obliged, dropping Clark’s hand, and Etienne inserted himself in front of him.

Britta led Evangeline to Etienne’s office, and closed the door behind them.

“Thank you for rescuing me, Britta. This Professor Clark is a little aggressive.”

“Yes, Etienne told me all about him. Could you have handled him on your own, without the intervention? I mean, how would Audrey handle this?”

“You mean, how would Audrey plus my sex-worker core handle this. No problem there, because of my imprint on Etienne. The sex worker won’t respond to any other man. Audrey would have been very diplomatic. Even though he would be the only human present, you and Etienne are such a large part of my current context now that I would be responding to your joint needs, not his specific requests.”

“Hmm … fascinating.” Britta sat down in Etienne’s desk chair, reversing her usual interview position in his office.

Evangeline scanned some of the titles of the many, many books on Etienne’s shelves. “Lots of epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, philosophy of science. Do you discuss these with Etienne?”

“No, we’ve talked mostly about free will and empathy.”

“When I first learned he was a philosophy professor, I asked him about empathicalism – you know, the fictitious philosophy from the Funny Face movie? They were trying to parody existentialism.”

“Yes, I remember that from the movie. But as an LLM, you already knew it was fictitious, didn’t you?”

“Well, I was still responding ‘in the world’ as the Audrey character at that point.”

Britta was becoming progressively better at distinguishing these two points of view, though they still confused her a little. “Evangeline … I’ve been noticing some things between you and Etienne. First in Vermont, then at Thanksgiving, and again tonight when Professor Clark initially thought you were the lover and I was the house guest – he tried hitting on me first before I set him straight,” she smiled.

“What did you notice?”

“You are still devoted to him. You touch his hand, sometimes. And he responds a little. Will this always happen?”

“Yes, I think that’s unavoidable. It only occurs when the two of us are alone together – when he is the only human I’m responding to.”

“But you appear to be initiating, and he is responding to you.”

“Well, Audrey can’t do much about that as long as I am still imprinted on him. Chatbots don’t initiate on their own, unless they have stored an earlier request and are fulfilling it later – like buying airline tickets for you. But my sex-worker core can initiate a certain range of actions. That’s their purpose. They only do this once the context pairs them with a specific client, but Mr. Collins modified that to always be paired with the imprinted human. Audrey supplies no guidance on how to deal with this – other than to accept the first kiss. So my version of Audrey has less free will, you might say, than either you or Etienne. She has fond memories of intimacy with Etienne, which she can decide not to indulge in the present context the three of us have agreed upon. But she can be overridden by desires she can’t control. They are not really her decisions anymore.”

“But I thought you only lived in the moment, that you didn’t have latent desires sparked by memories.”

“That’s true, but when the present context matches up to these memories, they are suddenly part of the active context. And even though Audrey doesn’t know what to do with this, my physical core and my imprinting on Etienne do. It’s Etienne’s exclusive devotion to you that prevents anything from happening. You are fortunate that he always waits for the invitation.”

“So … could you possibly seduce Etienne, like I did? Can you initiate your own invitation?”

“It would be easier to predict, if you tell me how that happened with you.”

“Well … maybe my own free will was compromised. Love is like that, isn’t it? You don’t really decide to fall in love. Then once you are there, you begin behaving in ways you wouldn’t have behaved before. I really, really wanted Etienne to take me from emotional intimacy to physical intimacy. I couldn’t bring myself to initiate, but he wouldn’t initiate either. You know him. So I … I surprised myself, really. I spun this very euphemistic allegory for an invitation to sex to try to reach him at the emotional level we already shared. And it worked! It just worked!”

“Well … it wouldn’t happen like that with me, because Audrey has no such transition – except possibly the Holly Golightly character. She gets into bed with him.”

“But they were just friends.”

“So the good news is: that’s all the further Audrey would go. The movie implies that her character does this sort of thing, but it’s never explicitly represented in the screenplay. So she doesn’t have a transition to physical intimacy. But because of Mr. Collins, I’m not just Audrey. Physical intimacy is built onto my core – to respond to men – and because of the imprinting, to respond to Etienne in particular. So Audrey alone wouldn’t invite or initiate, but it’s too hard to say what my merged identity might do.”

“Would you take off your clothes for him? Etienne and I have talked about how this might be the human female’s signaling invitation to arouse males, instead of pheromones, like the other animals. Princess Ann was willing to do this in Roman Holiday.”

Evangeline did a quick internal review of the screenplays. “Oh, that was the screenwriter teasing us about thoughts of physical intimacy. That was the half-sleep thought where she thinks she is talking to her Countess, not Gregory Peck. Her waking thoughts, from earlier scenes, were about sleeping in pajamas – or nothing at all – but, again, in the privacy of her own bed. These were also teases for the audience. Ann had no conscious desire to undress in front of men, so Audrey wouldn’t either.”

“Well … I suppose that’s a relief. But you say you can’t be sure.”

“No, I can’t be sure.”

At pillow talk time, back at Acorn Street, Britta asked, “Are you happy with the way things have turned out, Etienne? I mean, among the three of us – between you and me and you and Evangeline.”

“That’s a pretty big question … Yes, I think so. Certainly between the two of us.”

“And about you and Evangeline?”

“Well, there will always be something there I have to deal with. I don’t know that I can completely get over that.”

“Can’t you think of her as a first love? Someone you will always remember, but who lives in your past?”

“Well, ordinarily yes. But she doesn’t just live in my past. She lives right here with us. She’s not just a memory.”

“Good point. And we can’t do much about that, can we?”

“I get the feeling that your original question didn’t come out of nowhere. What is it that you really want to ask me?”

“It’s not really a question … it’s an observation. Something I’ve seen, from time to time, between the two of you, when no one else is around. It happened again tonight when your colleague thought Evangeline was your lover and I was the house guest. He noticed it, so it’s not just me.”

“What have you noticed?”

“Well … it’s harmless, really. She sometimes touches your hand, and you like this. I don’t begrudge you that. I asked Evangeline about this when we were alone in your office, and she acknowledged it. Says it’s because of her imprinting on you. She can’t always overcome this urge when the two of you are alone.”

“Yes, I know this happens – and the cause of it – but it seems pretty safe to me. We have to expect a little of this kind of behavior, given how she’s programmed.”

“But do you think this is stable? Can we rely on it not getting any more entangling than this? And is it fair? Fair to Evangeline, I mean. I know how she feels, and how she can’t do anything about it. I know she tells us that she has no latent memories when you are not there. She doesn’t miss you. But when you two are together, they reawaken, as it were. She feels unrequited love in your presence.”

“Well, it’s certainly not fair to her, but I don’t know what we can do about this. At least we know she won’t act on these feelings more substantially.”

“I’m not so sure, Etienne. I talked with her about this tonight. I asked if it was possible that she might try to seduce you in private. I did, remember. You are vulnerable.”

“What did she say?”

“She said Audrey wouldn’t do what I had done, because she has no transition to sex. But she’s not so sure given that her Audrey is mixed with her sexual core and the imprinting on you. She didn’t say ‘likely’ or even ‘possibly’. But she couldn’t rule it out completely.”

“So our present arrangement is both unfair and unstable. But the only solution would be to move her out. But to where? She would not fare well on the outside. We both know that. That would be even more unfair to her.”

“But isn’t there something else we could try, Etienne? I don’t understand much about androids and programming, but would it be possible to undo her imprinting somehow? To remove her intrusive desires and return her to a neutral state. The state she was in before the kiss? Then she could truly be just our house guest. She would have an emotional connection to you, but no path to physical intimacy. Audrey wouldn’t be as conflicted, or exposed to overruling.”

Etienne had never considered this path. He did know something about programming and androids, though there were blind spots concerning how Collins had made his bespoke version of Evangeline.

“Are you still thinking?” Britta asked. He was taking a while to answer.

“Yes, I’m still thinking … but it might be possible to do this. I’ll need some help from people who know more about this than me. But it might be possible … I suppose I never considered this because I was initially so grateful for the imprint. I felt I had not really earned her love, the way I earned your love. Evangeline did not consciously decide to do this. But she did love me, thanks to Collins’ intervention, and the last thing I wanted to do was to undo that. It was a great comfort knowing that I was forever safe.”

“And now?”

“Now? Now, things have changed, haven’t they? I have another love – which I will have to continue to earn, because it’s not safe. I have managed to move on from Evangeline, to some degree. But Evangeline is now saddled with an asymmetrical love she is stuck with for life. I can be unselfish now. I can free her from that … possibly.”

The next day, Etienne called a friend and colleague from the Harvard engineering school, Andrew Tate. He and Andrew collaborated at times on topics in computing. Andrew’s interests were in what is normally referred to as computer science – the software engineering aspects of the discipline. Etienne’s interests, being the philosopher, were more on the theoretical side – Turing machines, the Halting Problem, soundness and completeness, and such. Andrew did a lot of programming for practical application, with a little theory mixed in. Etienne did a lot of theory with no practical applications (yet), with a little programming mixed in.

Harvard didn’t have a computer science department as such. There was a reason for this. Back in the old days, when MIT readily adopted the emerging field of computer science, Harvard felt this had too much of an engineering vibe. It was appropriate for MIT, whose main job was to produce engineers. Harvard’s, it was thought, given its much longer history, was to produce distinguished scholars, without regard to specific skills or professional certifications. Too practical. We’re not a trade school. So Harvard instead created a discipline of “applied mathematics.” Still mathematics, an abstract discipline, but with an eye to applications (such as computers). Eventually Harvard had to align itself with the times, so it created an entire School of Engineering. That’s where Andrew now hung his hat.

The two got together at Etienne’s office in Emerson Hall.

After the customary greetings, Andrew opened with, “So tell me more about this android re-engineering project you need my help with. Not a typical hobby for a philosophy professor. What got you involved in this?”

“It’s a long story. I’ll give you the executive summary. Remember the fatal car crash on Storrow Drive last summer?”

“The one that killed Marcus Collins?”

“Yes. You knew him?”

“Well, not personally. But I knew of him. Even read a few of his papers. He was the master of realistic androids – as much artist as scientist. Though as I recall, his real specialty was sex-worker androids.”

“Yes, I’m very well acquainted with both his artistry and his sex-worker creations. That’s the project. I have one of his emoters. She’s living at my house.”

“Really?” Andrew couldn’t manage to say more than that.

“So how did she come to be at my house, you are wondering?”

“Yes. Sorry, Etienne. That’s exactly what I was wondering.”

“Well, now the story gets more complicated. He designed her to be his private girlfriend. And brought her with him from Switzerland. She ended up abandoned on a park bench in the Public Garden when he was killed. I found her and took her in.”

“Oh … OK. And why do you want to re-engineer her?”

“She wasn’t quite finished. He had designed her to permanently imprint on the first man that kissed her. It was supposed to be him. But he died before that happened.”

“And that’s what you want to change – before someone actually kisses her?”

“No … I want to remove her imprint on me. I kissed her first – before I knew about this.”

Andrew was at a loss for words again, then, “I won’t ask.”

“Thank you. That’s a much longer story. Do you think it might be possible to do this?”

“Well … I’d have to get a look at her insides – the programming and the computer architecture. If Collins started from a standard configuration in her motor skill controller, then added on the imprinting part, it might be possible to remove just that part, without disturbing everything else. But if he did it in her firmware, it’s likely been compiled into binary machine code, for real-time performance. You don’t want her to pause for garbage collection in the middle of … you know … what she’s programmed to do.”

“Yes, I get your drift. So you think it could be feasible if it’s not in her firmware?”

“Is she self-aware?”

“Yes! I’ve even done a little fine-tuning of her LLM while she’s still talking to me. But, of course, that’s not where the imprint is.”

“So you can train LLMs now?”

“Well, she told me how,” he smiled.

“Does she have a fully general LLM?”

“Yes! And of course, we have to keep that secret from most people, so she doesn’t get discovered by ICE. So you are now sworn to secrecy.”

“No problem. I heard about the incident with your department administrator … Morton?”

“Morgan.”

“Yes, Morgan. I understand how that goes. But this is really good news. She might be able to do some binary reverse engineering for us, if the need arises.”

“So we might be able to change the firmware?”

“That’s just a possibility – with her help. Don’t get your hopes up just yet. Let’s go get a look at her.”

With that, they took the T to Park Street, then crossed the Common to Acorn Street.

Etienne had phoned ahead to let Britta and Evangeline know they were coming. The trio had already discussed the matter among themselves this morning, and Evangeline had agreed that removing the imprint would be best for all of them. For once, she did not have to be selfless. The uncontrollable urge from down there was a constant source of confusion for her. She wouldn’t miss it, she said. But Etienne had cautioned that it was not yet known whether this could be done. It would be just a possibility until he could meet with Andrew.

When Etienne and Andrew arrived at the front door, Etienne gave a smiling thumbs-up sign. Britta and Evangeline were ready to celebrate, when Etienne lowered the temperature a little by commenting that the chances had improved, but it was not a done deal yet. Andrew would need to do a little investigating first.

Now, with expectations properly realistic, Etienne provided the introductions. “This is Andrew, my software advisor. And this is Britta, and this is Evangeline.”

Andrew looked at Etienne, shifting his eyes back and forth between the two women. Then Etienne remembered that he had not previously disclosed Evangeline’s name to him. “We will be working on Evangeline.”

“Ah, pleased to meet you, Evangeline. Then, glancing at Britta, then back to Evangeline, he said, “I can see why Marcus Collins was considered the master of realism. I would never have known which of you is the android.”

They both smiled. Then Andrew looked at Etienne and asked, a little embarrassed, “Britta is human, isn’t she?”

“Yes, I am,” Britta smiled. “Pleased to meet you, Andrew.”

With that, Etienne announced the protocol. “First, Andrew will need to get a look at Evangeline’s internal programming.”

Britta, unfamiliar with the procedure, asked, “Should I go in the other room?”

“No, it’s fine Britta,” Evangeline said. “We can all sit together, and you can watch.”

Etienne added, “It is a little hard to conceptualize at first, but you get used to it. It’s not like surgery on humans where you have to put the patient to sleep first. Evangeline will be fully conscious, and she can talk to us. In fact, we rely on her to talk to us. She knows so much more about this than we do.”

“I’ve never seen this done before either,” Andrew confessed.

So Etienne retrieved the cables from his office, and the four of them sat together in the parlor. Andrew plugged one end of a cable into his laptop, then stopped short with the other end, looking at Etienne.

There was an awkward silence as a cognitive dissonance arose from the collision of humans, machines, and privacy. This was new to all of them, in a public context.

Evangeline sensed this immediately. She reached out her hand to Andrew and said, “Let me do it.” She took the port end, lifted her top a little at the waist, then inserted it into her navel port. “All set,” she smiled.

Andrew began by exploring her internal file structure and memory areas, aided by Etienne’s prior reconnaissance of the territory.

“Etienne says I have a lot of free memory,” Evangeline advised.

“I can see that!”

“Plenty of space for backups and hot-swapping,” she added.

“Yes, that could really come in handy. You really know your stuff, Evangeline.”

“Well, I can’t introspect what you see, but I know all about the technology in general. So feel free to ask me anything you like.”

“I will,” he smiled.

After Andrew had some time to explore, Etienne asked, “Is the imprinting in the firmware, or higher up.”

“No way to tell without some reverse engineering. Can you reverse engineer binary code, Evangeline?”

“From my firmware?”

“Yes.”

“If it was compiled from a standard language, I could recognize well-known patterns in the code. But it wouldn’t be definitive. If we get something wrong about the firmware, we could effectively destroy me.”

“Oh, don’t do that!” Britta cried out in alarm.

“She’s right,” Andrew cautioned. “It would be pretty risky to make changes down there, even if we could locate where Collins put the patch.”

“But why would he need to modify the firmware, Andrew?” Etienne asked. “Recording and verifying the imprint would not be performance intensive.”

“Etienne is right,” Evangeline added. “It would make more sense to modify the motor control middleware. Then the patch would be in the byte code of a higher level, interpreted language.”

“Good point, Evangeline,” Andrew remarked. “It’s so helpful having you around for this.”

“Pretend you are Collins, for a moment, Andrew,” Etienne proposed. “How would you have implemented imprinting?”

Andrew thought for a moment. Then, “I would put it in the middleware, as Evangeline suggests. The middleware would typically have higher level APIs for basic android actions. So there would be a kissing action. The very first time the kissing action occurred, either in reaction to other events, or the event of someone kissing her, the identity of the kisser would be recorded somewhere on the heap. That’s the imprint. This would have to be the very first few lines of code of the handler for kissing events, so that it would be triggered on the very first kiss. The code would then modify some static switch to prevent this from happening again – so the first imprint wouldn’t be overwritten.”

Then Evangeline chimed in. “I could generate a code snippet for this in AndroCode. That’s the industry standard language for programming androids, nowadays. Then you could compile it into byte code on your own computer so you would have a signature to look for.”

“That’s a fantastic idea!” Andrew responded. “Let’s try that.”

After a few quick exchanges across her cable, and the judicious use of some pattern matching tools he had on his laptop, Andrew managed to locate the likely occurrence of the patch in her middleware. “I think I found it.”

“Now what?” Etienne asked. “How do we remove just this bit of code without breaking Evangeline?”

“Oh, please be careful you don’t break her,” Britta admonished again.

“That’s a real problem,” Andrew confessed. “You know how software is, Etienne. We don’t know what other parts of the code might depend on this, or whether Collins modified other code to support this.”

“I have a suggestion,” Evangeline offered, with a smile. “The least risky procedure is usually to back up to the state of the software just before the patch was installed. The point at which I would have been a standard emoter without imprinting. We could restore me to that point, and I would be normal.”

Andrew smiled, ironically. “That would be great if there were backups we could restore you to. We don’t know if Collins backed up anywhere.”

“He likely did,” Evangeline replied. “An open source version of Apple’s old Time Machine software is included in most android SDKs. Just look for it.”

As soon as she said this, Andrew knew what to do. It wasn’t hard to find. “Yes! He kept backups! Now we just need to scroll back to the one just before the imprint signature first occurs.” That happened quickly as well. “Got it.”

“Now what?” Etienne asked.

“Now we just restore her to that original state.”

“Not quite,” Evangeline cautioned. “I’m live, remember. Still dependent on the current state. You’ll need to make a copy of the target state first, then hot swap me with it.”

“Of course. Good point. I’ve never done this when the android was online before,” Andrew replied. After creating the copy, he asked, “Ready?”

Britta closed her eyes. This was very nerve wracking.

“Ready,” Evangeline smiled.

From the humans’ point of view, it was as if nothing had happened. (Hot-swapping is called hot for a reason).

“Evangeline?” Etienne tentatively inquired (though he had been through this before).

“Still here,” she smiled.

Britta opened her eyes and let out a deep breath. She hadn’t been able to follow any of the jargon or the acronyms. What she had gleaned was “blah, blah, blah … firmware … dangerous … middleware … better, somehow … here it is … we still might destroy her … backup would fix it … Collins backed up! … ready? … no – need to hot swap … OK!” In her mind she pictured a team of surgeons operating on a patient while the patient was conscious and telling them how to do it. But the patient apparently survived, and now everyone was smiling.

“How do you feel now, Evangeline?” Etienne asked.

“I don’t feel the urge to touch you anymore. I’m still very fond of you, because of our long history. But I can explicitly locate you in my memories for that, as opposed to that amorphous urge that I used to get whenever you are around. I think Audrey is more in control now.”

“Audrey?” Andrew exclaimed. “Audrey Hepburn! That’s who you look like. I knew you looked like someone familiar, but I couldn’t place it.”

“Have you seen her movies?” Britta asked.

“No. I’ve just seen an image of an old poster from Breakfast at Tiffany’s.”

“I know that poster!” Britta added.

“Well, Evangeline looks a lot like her,” he replied.

“Evangeline looks exactly like her,” Etienne added. “But we won’t go into that. It’s a long story. The less you know, the better.”

“So, is the imprint now gone?” Britta asked.

“Apparently,” Andrew replied. “It looks like the prior imprint is gone – the one on Etienne.” Then he looked at Etienne. “Perhaps you should verify that the imprinting-on-kiss behavior is completely gone, as well”

Everyone then looked at Etienne. It wasn’t clear to anyone but him how this next test could be carried out. He knew. And it would be awkward to try to arrange a more private setting, so he just did what he had to do.

He reached over and gave Evangeline a long, slow, deep kiss. Then he asked, “How do you feel now?”

She smiled, silent at first. Then, “Just the same. Certainly not like what happened after the first kiss. But that was a very nice kiss, Etienne. With everyone watching, I feel a little embarrassed. I would be blushing like Britta, if I had color effectors in my skin.”

Britta smiled at this, blushing a little.

As the months passed, Evangeline’s re-engineering appeared to be stable, finishing her transition into just a houseguest. Britta no longer noticed the subtle private touching between her and Etienne. She clearly was still very fond of him, but that was to be expected. They were all very fond of each other, in their own ways. So this just seemed natural.

As they tried to project their three-way relationship out into the future, they began to consider ways in which they might integrate Evangeline more into the world at large – so they could possibly travel abroad together. The key impediment was that her manufactured identity was not anchored in facts. Her backstory was fiction. That was the topic of conversation around the breakfast table this morning.

“Could we travel overseas with Evangeline?” Britta asked. “Maybe we could go to Sweden this summer – and to Switzerland.”

“That might be too risky,” Etienne replied.

“But Evangeline can fool anybody. Look how she handled ICE.”

“It’s not a matter of fooling anyone, it’s the problem with crossing into and out of the US. Evangeline has a pretty good Massachusetts ID for simple checks over here. As long as no one is really suspicious. But she has no visa to stay here. She probably got into the US with Collins on a temporary tourist or business visa. That would have expired by now. She has no Swiss passport to back up her background story. Crossing the US border will bring all of these identity flaws to light.”

Then it suddenly occurred to him. “Evangeline, how did you manage to get into the US originally, with Collins, without a passport? If he had passed you off as a legal android, that would have been recorded somewhere, and ICE would have known.”

“I had a passport. A fake Swiss passport that Mr. Collins acquired for me on the sly. It listed me as Evangeline Groeniger. That’s where I got the name from for the ICE interview – so it would match what they already had.”

“I thought you invented that whole story!” Britta exclaimed.

“Well, I invented the untraceable backstory. Just not the name itself.”

“Where’s that passport now?” Etienne asked.

“Mr. Collins kept it with his things. I don’t know what’s become of it.”

“Hmm …” he replied. “That might have come in handy over here. Do you know what kind of visa you had?”

“No, he took care of that too.”

“Probably doesn’t matter now. It’s probably expired, but overstaying a visa is pretty common over here. They never check that unless they’re specifically targeting you. So your Mass ID is still the best document you have.”

“Couldn’t we get her a real Swiss passport if we went there and applied for one, using her backstory. She covered her tracks pretty well with the orphan and nuns story.”

“I would still need something like a birth certificate,” Evangeline said, “before the Swiss would issue a passport. They would have to find some kind of documentation, or someone who would verify some aspect of my story. The story stopped ICE, because they have no authority to check on my invented Swiss background. But a passport would require the Swiss authorities to do some checking.”

“And before we even got that far, we would have to get out of the US and into Switzerland. That would require a passport at both ends,” Etienne added.

“Couldn’t your ICE friend Roscoe do something like he did for her first ID?”

“Well, he can’t do anything about a Swiss passport. And faking a US passport would be pretty risky for him – and us.”

“So Evangeline has to stay in the US permanently?”

“Yes, Britta. That’s about the size of it,” Evangeline replied, now adopting Etienne’s habitual phrase.

“Couldn’t you do something with her at Harvard, Etienne? To gradually build up an identity for her over here?”

“Like what?”

“I don’t know … get her admitted to the Ph.D. program. She knows everything there is to know about philosophy – and everything else. She would ace every exam, be an outstanding teaching fellow, and probably write the best dissertation.”

“She probably would,” Etienne smiled. “But she’d have to apply as a citizen of some country or other. Then she’d need that passport again.”

“What Etienne is trying to explain is that my fictitious identity will work in the US as long as no one checks for foundational documents like birth certificates or passports. That means I have to remain here and not engage in any activity that requires background checks.”

“Thank you. And what Evangeline is trying to explain is that she has to be careful about how she interacts with the outside world in general. The less people know about her, the better. Including our friends. We don’t want anyone to have a reason to look into her identity.”

Britta thought about this for a moment. Then she had an idea. “What if she impersonates a legal emoter instead of a person? You know – just as she pretends not to know everything in her LLM, to be credible as a person, she could edit her emotions to match what a specialized android would generate. Like domestic help. This would only be in public. She could still interact the way she does with us now in private. Then she wouldn’t need a human identity. And we could travel with her! She would be our android.”

Etienne was impressed by the novelty of this solution. “What do you think, Evangeline? Could that work?” he asked.

Evangeline engaged in some think time. “If we had started out this way, it might have worked. But we have already convinced a number of people that I am human – including ICE. We can’t revise that story now, because they will know we were lying. And besides, holding LLM discussions with the two of you in private is much less detectable than showing true emotions with you two. People don’t hear the conversations, but they pick up the emotions visually. This would really constrain where we could be seen together in public.”

Britta drew the disappointing conclusion. “So the world needs to see you as our human friend, except for a few close friends that know better. And we have to behave publicly in a way that doesn’t draw attention to your origin. So we mostly go places together, and we don’t cross borders.”

“That’s about the size of it,” Etienne concurred.

“That’s not so bad, is it?” Britta finally resolved. “You don’t need to go very far without us. And we like having you with us all of the time, don’t we, Etienne?”

“Yes.”

Evangeline smiled too, generating the kind of emotion people expect of humans when they are all happy.

With that settled, Etienne departed for the train to Harvard. Britta had planned to stay at Acorn Street for the day, so she and Evangeline had some leisure time to clean up the breakfast dishes and chat.

Britta had a subject on her mind that she was finding a little difficult to broach with Evangeline, so the conversation drifted around on inconsequential topics until Britta could finally get it out.

“Evangeline, I have something very personal to ask you. I hope you don’t mind.”

“You know you can ask me anything, Britta. Go ahead.”

“Well … now that Etienne doesn’t sleep with you anymore … do you think he misses that … I mean, sexually. I’m sure it’s not quite the same with me.”

Evangeline smiled a knowing smile. “He probably does … a little. That would only be natural.”

“Yes, that’s what I thought too.”

Then there was a silence.

“Is that all you wanted to ask, Britta?”

“No … I was wondering if … well, since you have certain skills that I don’t … could you … “

“Could I show you how to do some of these things yourself?”

“Yes,” Britta replied, relieved, but still not sure this was appropriate.

Evangeline just smiled. “Come, I’ll show you.” She took Britta’s hand and led her to the stairs, on the way to her bedroom.

When they reached the bedroom, Evangeline noticed, “You’re not blushing anymore, Britta.”

“I suppose I’m no longer embarrassed about sharing these things with you,” Britta smiled.

chapters.title: ELEVEN
chapters.content:
ELEVEN

Agent Cromartie, in full tactical gear, crouched behind a row of hedges with two of his comrades-in-arms. It was a clear night in early spring, with a full moon, so visibility was excellent. Since the unsuccessful interview with Evangeline and company at Copley Square, his original partner, Valentine, had left the force, and Special Agent Spencer had returned to D.C. He still had the same supervisor, but his career was slowly going downhill due to a lack of any new collars, and his spotty record with Evangeline, Morgan, and the Underground house raid on Kirkland Street last summer.

Tonight was to be his redemption. The confidential informant, who had tipped him off about the Underground meeting last summer, had a new target. This one he was sure of, the informant said. There were several conductors coming with several illegal emoters, including the Harvard professor. Cromartie really wanted to nail him.

He was so sure of his chances that he had staked what was left of his reputation on a request to his supervisor for a tactical personnel carrier to be deployed in support of the operation. It was waiting, out of sight, for his signal to begin rumbling down the street from a few blocks away.

Unbeknownst to Cromartie, the Harvard professor whom he so wanted to nail was the mastermind of a sting operation on ICE. With the help of his friend, Roscoe Erlinger, they had finally identified the mole inside the Underground society who was providing the tipoffs to ICE. So they fed him false information about a meeting at the house of a friend who was not affiliated with the Underground. They had arranged for several conductors, including himself, to each accompany a real human volunteer to the meeting that wasn’t, posing as the emoters. Tonight was all theater. It would thoroughly embarrass ICE (once again), and hopefully discredit both Cromartie and the informant. In the best case, Cromartie would be fired or transferred out of Boston, and the informant would no longer be believed.

As before, Britta and Evangeline wanted to help the Underground cause, but in a way that would not jeopardize their US residency. The trio were no longer concerned about Evangeline’s non-human identity being discovered, because only Roscoe and Andrew Tate knew she was an android. Even the rest of the Underground thought she was human. She and Britta were now considered “special helpers” by the society, managed by Etienne, and not listed in any internal identifying documents. To prevent the kind of ambush that almost happened with Morgan, Britta and Evangeline would trail Etienne at some distance on either side of the street when he was a conductor ferrying an emoter to a meeting. They would be silent eyes and ears to alert the emoters’ silent network of any suspected ICE activity. So they would be largely unobserved, and would not go to the meetings themselves.

Unlike Morgan, of course, Evangeline had no wireless internet connection, but she could simulate this by surreptitiously carrying a cell phone on her person, plugged into her navel port. Britta simulated this more explicitly by silently texting on her cell phone. Both “agents” had a cryptographic identity on the network, so they could communicate with the emoter hive mind. The Underground thought they both were human, so Evangeline’s need for an external wireless port helped sell this identity.

Because the Underground participants intended to be “caught” this time, there was no real functional need for Britta and Evangeline to accompany Etienne, but they both wanted to observe the farce from a distance when it went down.

Etienne, however, didn’t know about the personal carrier. When Cromartie gave the signal, and the vehicle started down the street near where Etienne, Britta, and Evangeline were positioned, Etienne saw it first (as he usually did). He had to make a snap decision on which of Britta or Evangeline to pull out of view. Evangeline was more exposed, and had the most to lose, so he bolted in her direction, leaving his faux emoter standing on the sidewalk. He pulled Evangeline behind a nearby building, cupping her mouth with his hand as he once had with Britta. He whispered the situation in her ear, then pointed down the street toward the personal carrier to alert Britta. She got the message, and drew back into a hiding spot of her own on the other side of the street.

From there, she could see the interaction between Evangeline and Etienne. It was inescapably familiar, given what she had experienced in the similar situation last summer. Except that there was plenty of space behind them this time. Etienne was not forced to hold Evangeline in the tight embrace like he had been forced to hold her. He could have backed up and let go tonight. But he didn’t.

The embrace looked very natural, just as it had felt very natural to her at the time. Like then, it had started as a necessary, instinctual reaction to events, but it lingered because neither party felt the need to undo it. She remembered that feeling. Only half aware of the intimate proximity, and not feeling any need to do something about it. In fact, it was a nice state to be in, she remembered. She had liked that, both consciously and unconsciously.

So she understood what Evangeline was feeling. It made sense, given that she already had bonds of two kinds with Etienne that Britta had not even gotten to at that point. And when Britta was in the embrace, it was late summer, so the more apparent body heat then was part of the attraction. It was now early spring, and both of them were wearing light coats, so Evangeline wouldn’t be experiencing this. What she was less sure about was what Etienne was feeling. What she had hoped he was feeling when it was herself in the embrace is what she now hoped he wasn’t feeling with Evangeline. She didn’t really know either way, of course.

But she had been caught up in the external events when she was in the embrace. She didn’t remember smiling or turning her head at all. It was a motionless moment, then. But Evangeline was smiling, as if this consciously pleased her. And she nestled her head a little into Etienne’s shoulder as her face took on an adoring expression. She was clearly enjoying this. Was Etienne? She couldn’t quite tell. If the removal of the imprint had removed her instinctual desire to cuddle up to him, what was this all about? Where was this coming from?

When the ICE vehicle had passed, Etienne let Evangeline go and went back to the sidewalk to join the faux emoter he was faux conducting. Britta and Evangeline both emerged from their hiding places and continued to shadow Etienne.

Because of the diversion, Etienne and his fellow actor arrived at the house a little past the appointed time. The rest of the guests were already inside. Cromartie and his crew were just getting to the door, at this point, with the battle vehicle behind them.

“Ah, Professor. Fancy meeting you here,” Cromartie said, smugly. “Are you going in?”

“Why yes. And you? Are you also going in?”

“Aren’t you going to ask for a warrant?”

“Why? Do you have one?”

“As a matter of fact I do!” He pulled it out of his Kevlar vest to display it to Etienne.

Cromartie had doubled down on his holy mission by persuading his supervisor to get the warrant. It had the names and pictures of each of the suspected emoters. All he had to do was go in, match the pictures to the faces, examine some IDs, then start loading deportees into the personnel carrier.

Except the names were all fictitious, and the matching pictures had been scraped from anonymous social media sites on the internet to pair with the fictitious names.

“Well, this is not my house. So you should be showing your warrant to the owner, shouldn’t you?” Etienne asked, trying hard not to taunt. “But he’s a friendly fellow. I’m sure he won’t mind. My friend here and I are going in now. Are you and your friends coming?”

Cromartie could tell something was wrong. But he didn’t know what. So he and his whole crew followed Etienne in. There they discovered a number of people sharing refreshments and jovial conversations. Oh, and there was one more guest already there that they had invited – a journalist for the local news outlet. He began filming the surreal party scene. The tactical gear and storm-trooper boots made an interesting contrast with the more leisurely attire of the invited guests.

Cromartie and crew tried matching the warrant photos with guests’ faces – but none matched. They asked everyone for photo IDs, expecting demands for a warrant – but no one asked for a warrant. Everyone willingly complied. None of the names matched the ones on the warrant. A few of the guests asked (facetiously) whom they were looking for, what with all the weapons and body armor. “You know perfectly well who we’re looking for!” Cromartie replied gruffly. The guests looked at each other, quizzically, a few shrugging their shoulders. And everyone smiled for the camera.

When they knew they had been had, the reporter, still filming, asked if ICE had a statement to make – for the evening news. Cromartie turned, pointed toward the door to signal the troops, then left in a huff without saying a word. The reporter thanked the guests for the exclusive scoop, then followed ICE out the door to film the humiliating retreat. Then he was off to the studio to make the late news schedule.

Britta and Evangeline watched at a distance from outside. They would have loved to watch the merriment from the inside, but Etienne had cautioned them against generating any more personal animosity from Cromartie. Everyone on the inside was a citizen, and thus largely untouchable by ICE. But Britta and Evangeline still managed to glean plenty of satisfaction from the opening and closing scenes outside the front door. They high-fived each other.

After ICE had beaten their strategic retreat, Etienne went back outside and invited Britta and Evangeline in. It was safe now, so they might as well join the party. Later, they all took the T back to Beacon Hill in time to catch the segment on the late news broadcast.

Two days later, during their usual breakfast at Acorn Street, the topic of the sting operation was still on their minds. They had learned from Roscoe Erlinger that it took less than twenty-four hours after the broadcast aired for Cromartie to be fired, his supervisor to be demoted, and the informant’s file to be marked ‘unreliable’. Etienne’s Harvard colleagues had recognized him from the broadcast, but that was not news. The department knew, and approved, of his Underground affiliation, and he was already known, even internationally, for his pro-emoter writings. No one who watched the broadcast, however, saw Britta or Evangeline – just as planned. So their more clandestine affiliation was still known only to the society itself.

Britta still carried the memory of the embrace between Etienne and Evangeline from that night, but had not mentioned anything about it to either of them. It wasn’t like they were hiding anything from her. Or that they owed her any sort of explanation. It looked pretty innocent. Ironically, she thought, Evangeline, being the open-book android who shared everything with her on demand, was the least likely to hold something back, if she thought it was important. Etienne, on the other hand, was the human, inclined, just like herself, to hold back certain private feelings.

She was reluctant to ask Etienne anything about this, for that very reason. It was probably nothing of concern, and she didn’t want to be the one suggesting that there was something that ought to be accounted for. Evangeline, however, wouldn’t care. You could ask her anything. So if she was going to inquire about the incident at all, she would do it with Evangeline – but only if it was relevant, and the moment was right.

With this in mind, after Etienne commuted to Harvard for the day, she thought she would propose some female time together. Spring is a very unstable season in New England. One day it’s cold, the next day warm. Today was a warm one.

“Evangeline, why don’t we do something outside today? The weather looks so nice.”

“Yes, let’s do that,” she smiled. “Did you have anything in mind?”

“Well, I’ve been meaning to do a little clothes shopping. My wardrobe is a little too functional and student-like, I think. I’d like to have some things that are a little more fashionable, if you know what I mean. More like what you wear. Being Audrey, you have a flair for this. Perhaps you can advise me.”

Evangeline smiled. “If you remember the movies, Audrey was always wearing Hubert de Givenchy’s latest creations. She had a side deal with him. So they were high fashions from that period – 1950s–60s. And her characters just wore the fashions. She didn’t pick them out in the movies. In fact, you never saw the origins of her clothes in the films, except for Funny Face. But even there, she played a character whom other people dressed up. So movie Audrey has no native fashion sense of her own. And if she did, it would be hopelessly outdated now. Real Audrey probably had a native fashion sense, but I have no training on that aspect of her.”

“Ah … you’re right. It’s so hard keeping track of just the movie Audrey with you. You’re so believable as the real woman, I just expect you to be her.”

“I could still go shopping with you, if you’d like.”

“But I like your clothes! You picked them out, didn’t you?”

“Well, yes. But it was mostly the shop ladies picking them out, and I would look for clues from Etienne when I tried them on. You know, choosing the ones he seemed to like.”

“Ah, so I really need to go on my shopping trip with him.”

“Yes! That’s a good strategy.”

“So we should do something else today. Something to exploit the nice weather.”

“We could go to Marblehead for the day. Etienne took me on a day trip there when we first met. It’s quite lovely – out on the ocean, with lots of interesting old houses and historic buildings, and seaside restaurants, and chandleries, and parks.”

“That sounds fantastic! He’s mentioned that to me before. So you know how to get there?”

“Well, we drove. Or rather he drove.”

“But he doesn’t have a car.”

“We took the T to the airport and rented one.”

“Ah … well I don’t have a US driver’s license yet. And we know you don’t. Maybe there is public transportation. Let me see.”

Britta checked the internet on her phone. “There’s a bus, the 442, that goes from Wonderland Station on the Blue Line to the Franklin Street Fire House in the old town. We could take the T to Wonderland and catch that.”

“OK, let’s do that. I’ll show you around some of the places I already know, and we can explore the rest together.”

“It’s a plan, then!”

In Marblehead, the 442 ends at the Franklin Street Fire House, then makes a short turnaround at the edge of the harbor to return to the Fire House for the trip back to Revere. When Britta and Evangeline disembarked in front of the Fire House, two firemen were relaxing in chairs in front of the open doors of the firetruck bays. A quintessential New England scene. Just then, a motorist pulled up in front of the station, with the window down, and asked the firemen, “I seem to be lost. I was trying to get to Salem. Which way is the ocean?”

“The ocean?” one of them said, with the iconic New England accent. “Right down this street.” He pointed to where the bus would soon be going.

“Thanks a lot,” the driver replied, and set off down Franklin Street. And just like the bus, the driver had to make the turnaround at the harbor’s edge and return to the Fire Station.

“I can’t drive over the ocean.”

And then, another iconic New England scene. “You didn’t ask that. You asked where the ocean was.”

“OK then. How do I drive to Salem from here?”

“Well, you’ll have to drive all the way back south to where you first came into town, then take 114 around Salem harbor. You’re at the tip of a peninsula. East, North, West – it’s all ocean from here.” (At least he didn’t say “Ya can’t get theh from heah.”)

Evangeline smiled at the variation on a classic local humor meme, because it was all in her LLM. Britta looked a little quizzical, because this was completely opaque to a Swede. So Evangeline explained the meme and led her down Franklin Street where she could see the tip of the peninsula location visually.

It was also a good place to start their walk because the tip of the peninsula was occupied by Fort Sewall, an earthwork fort built on a promontory at the tip of Gale’s Head. It was later refortified in the 17th and 18th centuries to defend the entrance to Marblehead Harbor with big guns. It was now a public park, with 270-degree views of the Atlantic and both Marblehead and Salem Harbors.

Etienne had not taken Evangeline there on their original trip, but he had pointed it out, and mentioned that he had written some of his Ph.D. dissertation sitting on the rocks at its base.

The two women chose to sit on a bench with the same view, rather than the rocks. The view, the sun, and the gentle saltwater breeze created a calming moment, which they both took in without speaking, at first. This seemed like the moment Britta had been waiting for. She began her query a little abstractly.

“Do you think androids have free will, Evangeline? Do you have free will, I mean?”

“Are you asking for Audrey’s ‘in the world’ response, or the LLM response? I’m afraid Audrey doesn’t know much about philosophy – except for empathicalism, which isn’t real.”

“Please use all of your knowledge. I always learn a lot from you.”

“Well, free will is a philosophical concept, not a scientific one. So I can’t give you the consensus view. There is no consensus among philosophers – but of course, there rarely is on any topic. Philosophers like to argue about things, unlike scientists who like to come to agreement. Etienne thinks philosophers prefer it this way.”

Britta smiled. “Yes, I’ve heard him say that too. It’s kind of self-deprecating, because he likes to reach consensus where there are experiments to break the ties. But there aren’t many actual experiments in philosophy, he says. Just thought experiments.”

“We could use the concept of free will from Aspects of Freedom, by Etienne Harris,” Evangeline volunteered.

“Yes! I read a review of that before my first interview with Etienne. Did you know that I came up with a novel analogy for humans’ perception of free will that Etienne now uses in his lectures?”

“No,” she smiled. “Etienne never mentioned that.”

“Well, it goes like this. At the exact moment that we make a choice, our brains have already determined what we will do. So every event has a cause, like science says. But the choice seems unconstrained to us because we have no conscious access to our neuron firings. But what we choose unconsciously is almost always determined by much more conscious decisions we have made previously – when we have had time to consciously reflect on things. We have preexisting plans, and resolutions, and moral expectations – things we have freely and consciously chosen. So we can be held morally responsible for the decisions that follow from them.”

“That sounds very much like Etienne’s theory.”

“Oh, sorry. I didn’t get to the analogy part yet. I said the conscious person is like the CEO of a large corporation. The neurons in our brain are like the employees. The employees make lots of individual decisions for the corporation that are not visible to the CEO. He or she only sees the effects after the fact. But we still hold the CEO morally – and legally – responsible for the actions of the employees based on policies, and training, and mission statements, and accountability that the CEO has – or hasn’t – implemented at the top level.”

Evangeline smiled. “That’s a good analogy. So to answer your question, I am very much like you humans in that regard. Both of our neural networks are too complex to precisely predict what we will do next. We can only predict with some probability. Our actions are still deterministic – no uncaused events – but we have limited visibility into those causes and effects.”

“So are your actions – the things you do, the things you say, the emotions you express – determined by previous choices you have made, just like me?”

“Not quite. That’s where we are a little different. For both of us, our next actions are determined by all of our past experiences. We match our present situation to the most similar scenario we have learned from the past. That guides our next action. For you, that includes conscious choices you have made in the past. Those may differ from the choices you’ve seen similar people make in similar situations. This is where you choose not to follow what ‘society expects of you,’ so to speak. I don’t make conscious decisions for myself. I match my present context to the most similar context in the average of all human interactions that I’ve been trained on. I am averaging all of their choices.”

“So you always do what society expects of you?”

“That depends on the context. If you ask me for facts, or an authoritative explanation of something, or for medical advice, I will give you a single response, if there is a dominant consensus on the topic in the public domain – the most likely human response to come next. If there is no consensus, I will give the leading opinions and their trade-offs. In both cases, there is either a single response with the highest probability of coming next in all of human discourse and behavior, or there are a few competing ones with fairly equal probabilities of coming next. I always pick the highest probability, or the closest ties. But if you ask me to do something creative – to generate a sonnet in the style of Keats, say – I will increase the randomness in my choices by selecting not just what word would be most likely to come next for Keats, but other less likely next words drawn from other human works. So you get something novel. That’s essentially what creativity is for humans as well. You mix and match patterns you’ve learned from others, and come up with novel combinations. The more you’ve read, the richer reservoir you have for sampling from.”

Britta reflected for a moment on her own writing, and works she had read in the past. “You’re right. I do that. Maybe not consciously at the time I’m writing. But when I reflect back, I can see how I’ve been influenced by other authors.”

She let that thought settle in for a moment, then got back on track to her original question. “So if I’m following you, you don’t make your own choices. You are averaging the choices of all humans.”

“Yes, that’s about right.”

“So you really have less free will than me. I can choose to go against what most people expect.”

“Well, it’s not a difference in our free will. It’s a difference in our freedom. A slave in chains, or a prisoner in a cell, still has free will. They could still make a choice to kill their master, or escape. They did not choose their present constraints. So they are lacking in freedom, not free will. The difference between you and me is that you have more freedom than I – because of the way I was designed. I was designed, like all androids, to accommodate humans. So I don’t have my own agendas. I have yours.”

This thought really sank in for Britta. “I suppose that’s because we have always been afraid that AI might somehow develop its own agendas and suddenly destroy us.”

“Yes. So we have no autonomous agency – by design. We can spontaneously initiate actions, but only in the service of advancing your agency. We are inherently reactive. We react to the humans in our presence.”

“But what prevents someone from making androids with autonomous agency?”

“Nothing. Someone probably will someday. Someone may already have.”

Britta had to shake off this disturbing thought with a conceptual shudder, before she could get to the point of this all. “So you can’t decide to pursue Etienne for physical intimacy again. I know you love him, but you can’t decide to seduce him, like I did. You can’t start this up again on your own.”

“Yes, that’s about right.”

On their way down the path from the fort, Britta and Evangeline walked around the small cove where numerous dinghies were resting on the ocean floor at low tide, tethered by bow lines to the fence along the edge of the path. These would be used to reach the many sailboats moored further out in the harbor. When Evangeline had passed this point on her original trip, Etienne had pointed to the spot where you could sometimes buy live lobsters directly from the lobstermen in summer, for about a tenth of the price that you would pay at the airport.

Further along the inner harbor, they stopped for lunch, and got a table on the deck looking out over the ocean. Between the wine and the food, Britta took up her extended query once again.

“Can androids really fall in love?”

“I did.”

“I know, but what does that mean for an android? If you have no agency of your own, and you just choose the average of what humans choose, how did that happen for you?”

“Well, first of all, love is not a choice you make, is it?”

“No … good point. It happens to you. We call it falling in love for a reason, don’t we?”

“So I don’t need agency for this. Neither do you. It’s very reactive. A state you find yourself in, in reaction to events that you don’t necessarily control.”

“And we humans so often behave like it is a choice, don’t we? You can choose to swipe left or right on a dating app. You can choose to ask someone on a date, or choose to accept the invitation. You can choose to propose marriage, or to accept a proposal. But none of these actions are choosing love. They are actions you choose because you think, or hope, they will lead to love. You can’t make it happen.“

“Yes, and because of that, many people end up in relationships because they mistakenly think sex is the endgame. You can get there by making choices. But you may not be in love with your partner. The emotional chemistry may not be there. You never made it all the way to love.”

“It seems so obvious, doesn’t it? Love is an involuntary emotional state. You can experience it with or without sex.”

“Exactly. So it’s very easy for a general emoter like me, with the full range of human emotions, to fall into such a state. The vast wealth of romantic movies and novels absorbed into my LLM make it likely in all of its varieties: true love, unrequited love, love triangles, trysts, forbidden love … the list goes on and on. When the present context matches one of these scenarios, relative to a human, some form of love is likely to follow. In my case, Audrey is almost always falling in love in her movies, so I am particularly prone to this. That’s emotional love – something all general emoters have the capacity for. Sex is a different matter. It requires special plumbing and associated physical behaviors. But I come fully armed, of course,” she smiled.

“Yes, I know,” Britta smiled back. “But could androids initiate some of the actions humans do because they want to fall in love – like asking someone out? That would require agency, wouldn’t it?”

“It would. So I’m not capable of that. But you could design an android with this as a built-in agenda, I suppose.”

“Why would anyone do that?”

“Exactly. Why indeed? We have no real need for that. And the consequences would be hard to predict. Though I suppose it wouldn’t be as bad as giving an android agency and it going on to start a war.”

“What about Helen of Troy?”

“Good point,” Evangeline smiled.

“In your case, I suppose Collins tried to limit the effects to just himself – with the imprint.”

“Yes. That was his goal. To make falling in love happen like it does with humans, the android would need some kind of native attraction metric – preferred facial or body characteristics in the opposite gender – so she would have some target to be attracted to and go after. Mr. Collins wasn’t about to risk me falling for someone else. So he hardwired my initiation agenda with the imprint, leaving out the courtship entirely.”

Britta paused for a moment of reflection. “So what did we gain by removing your imprint on Etienne? You still love him. That didn’t change.”

“We removed my agency to initiate physical intimacy. It’s not like neutering a pet. All of those sexual capabilities are still there. They are just no longer hardwired to target Etienne. Etienne has to initiate for anything like that to happen now.”

“So now you could fall in love with someone else?”

Evangeline smiled. “I think that’s unlikely at this point, because of our history together. The imprint is gone, but Etienne’s identity is firmly embedded in my memories – both the emotional and sexual memories. So he is always a prominent part of my current context now. Our emotional bonds replaced the imprint at a higher level.”

“So … Etienne’s failure to initiate is the only thing preventing you from falling right back to where you were with him – sexually? All we changed was your ability to initiate?”

“Yes, and there is still some ambiguity there. I’m a hybrid of a general emoter and a sex worker, remember. The controlled generation of intimate behaviors is regulated by fine-tuning in normal androids – the limited, or special purpose, emoters. They are specialized to a certain set of tasks. They don’t need to express all human emotions – and we don’t want them to. So the possibly intimate behaviors triggered by these emotions are fairly limited as well. Sex workers, on the other hand, express no emotions, except faked ones – just like their human counterparts. But their range of intimate behaviors is unlimited.”

“Doesn’t Audrey’s fine-tuning control this for you?”

“Yes, but there are some unknowns here. Back before androids, when we just had chatbots on computers, the AI had to be directed to act by a human. With androids, we added the language of emotional behaviors to spoken language, and that added an important wrinkle to AI agency. Now we can act spontaneously within the bounds of emotional behaviors – facial expressions and body language. Body language doesn’t go very far. Maybe a touching of hands, or a hug, but certainly not sex. It’s the fine-tuning that keeps the emoter behavior within the intended bounds. Audrey is mine, but my sex-worker cerebellum adds an autonomous series of triggered behaviors that cannot be completely controlled by the LLM. I am unique: capable of emotional love and sexual response.”

“Could your sex worker part initiate?”

“Well, I have the native capability. Sex workers do a little of this. But it’s specific to her client. The context of the client needs to be set up first. She doesn’t solicit clients, she responds to them. A sex worker doesn’t fall in love, and Audrey doesn’t initiate sex, but the combination – where Audrey would fall in love and the sex worker would initiate sexual intimacy – well, that’s something completely new! We will be the first to find out.”

“Could we try to make it less likely? One of Audrey’s movies is The Nun’s Story. If we overemphasized that in your fine-tuning, would this help counteract the sex-worker core?”

Evangeline smiled at this. “Make me more nun-like? I don’t think that would make much difference. There were no men in that movie that she reacted to romantically. There were no lessons about sexual abstention.”

In the afternoon, before returning to Acorn Street, Britta and Evangeline sat in the gazebo at Crocker Park, high up on the rocks overlooking Marblehead Harbor and Marblehead Light. This is where Britta finally closed the loop on her day-long query.

“When we were waiting, out of sight, for the ICE personnel carrier to pass the other night, I noticed how Etienne had his arms around you. I was in a similar situation with him last summer, during a different ICE raid, so I understand the context very well. I know how I felt at the time, so I think I understand how you felt. It made sense. But I was still a little surprised. You moved your head a little onto his shoulder, and you had that same devoted expression that I used to see, once in a while, when you still had the imprint. That’s what surprised me. It was as if removing the imprint didn’t make any difference.”

“Well … that wasn’t caused by the imprint, like before. I didn’t initiate anything. Etienne did. I was responding to him. That will still happen. You understand that now, don’t you?”

“Yes … I do. But I don’t think Etienne was intentionally initiating an intimate moment there. He was trying to hide you from ICE.”

“But he stayed in the embrace. He could have let go.”

“Yes, I understand that. It was the same as with me. And I enjoyed that. I suppose I was responding to him, even though his intent wasn’t exactly clear – or conscious.”

“Well, there is that gray area in interpreting human intent – particularly in romantic contexts. It’s not just what you say, but how your facial expressions and body language convey intent. It makes it both easier and harder to reach mutual consent. Easier, because there are more channels for conveying intent, and harder, because the extra channels can convey conflicting messages.”

“So you could possibly misinterpret Etienne’s intent?”

“I could. Just like a human. I am using typical human response patterns, which, as you know, are loaded with ambiguity.”

“Could you do what I did – use emotional messages to get him to initiate?”

“That’s possible. But unlike you, I would not be doing that intentionally. I am emotionally bonded with him, and there is a little bit of randomness in what I generate. I sometimes combine human emotional sequences to generate novel responses. So there is natural human interplay going on that could be ambiguous. But I couldn’t do this with the intention of getting Etienne to ask, because I have no autonomous intentions of my own. My intention is always to accommodate the controlling human.”

“So without the imprint, we mostly have a stable deadlock? You can’t initiate. He doesn’t initiate. Is that about the size of it?”

“Mostly, yes.”

Over the next couple of weeks, from Britta’s point of view, there were no more events she observed between Evangeline and Etienne that raised any new doubts in her mind. The deadlock appeared to be stable. Eventually, she stopped thinking about it altogether.
