She still didn’t have any particular plans for what she would do at the end of her Nieman Fellow residency. But, of course, she had a new objective: to stay here somehow with Etienne. One possibility would be to find employment in the US, so she was particularly receptive when the New York Times asked her to come down for an interview. She had done a few more articles for them, and they liked her style. They didn’t have a particular position in mind yet, they said. This would be an exploratory interview.

So this evening, she had packed an overnight bag, planning to take the last shuttle from Boston to New York, and stay overnight in a hotel there. A prudent plan, Etienne said, to avoid schedule-ruining delays in the busy Northeast air corridor on the day of the interview.

After dinner, and after they had said their goodbyes to Britta on her way to the airport, the original housemates took up their respective places in Etienne’s study. They had often had conversations here in the early days before Britta arrived. Early on, Evangeline would sometimes look through the books on his shelves, and ask about them. But once her ever-present LLM identity had been established, it was rather pointless, because she already knew what was in all of them.

So they would sometimes play a different game with his bookshelves. Etienne had a very visual memory – not quite photographic, but close. He could remember every title and every spine design of every book on his shelves, because he had a very detailed mental image of every book that he owned. So with Etienne facing away from the shelves, Evangeline would either read a title out loud, and Etienne would have to describe the spine colors and typesetting, or she would describe the spine graphics and he would have to name the title. He had yet to lose at this game.

Tonight, after a few rounds of this, and some impromptu conversations that meandered through their shared memories of their earlier time together, they decided to rewatch a few Audrey movies – the two that had the most impact: Roman Holiday and Breakfast at Tiffany’s. They sat together for this. Etienne figured it was harmless, because Evangeline would no longer initiate. Evangeline simply reacted to his lead. They were approximating the “just friends” regime, and it felt very comfortable to both of them.

But with this present context, Etienne fondly remembered their times together – including the sexual times. These memories flooded his private mind, where they had to remain. He knew he could not share them with Evangeline, like the old days. No “remember when we …” or “what were you feeling when we …” Some parts of their intimate emotional bond were off limits now.

But it was impossible to suppress these memories with her so close at hand, including the tender desire to revisit them with her now. She had always initiated, and if she could now, it would be virtually impossible for him to resist. But she couldn’t initiate anymore. That was the only thing saving him from betraying Britta.

But it wasn’t the same now, was it? When he had first betrayed Evangeline with Britta, Britta was new. He had acted to bring Britta into the fold. But Evangeline is already in the fold. Indelibly. A temporary reversion to Evangeline would be less of a deliberate act. It might even be expected to happen. It would probably be well understood by both women. It was only his own resolve that could keep this from happening. Even though he wanted to, he could no longer share this emotion with Evangeline. He could not risk disclosing his private intent in word or deed. He would just have to be a tortured observer – indulging the memories, but not the behaviors.

At bedtime, when they reached the top of the stairs together, before departing to their respective bedrooms, Etienne remembered the scene on their first night when Evangeline came across the hall to visit him – in pajamas. It would be harmless, he thought, to mention this. Maybe it was because he wanted to hear that she still remembered these moments, like he did. It would be a higher-level, more emotionally abstract kind of sharing, he thought.

“Of course I remember, Etienne.” She flashed that wide smile, and the sympathetic wide eyes that he could never get over. “Would you like me to come in and sit with you for a little bit?” Was she reading his mind? he thought. Of course she was.

“We are just friends, after all,” she added.

That helped. And it was a poignant reminder of their joint positioning on that night. Nothing had happened.

They sat on the bed together, and shared some more surface-level memories. Etienne was as careful as he could consciously regulate himself to avoid sharing any new emotional content. They already had plenty in their joint reservoir of memories to share, without plowing any new ground.

But it was hard. He hated this new barrier that was now between them. He could not share what he was actually feeling with her. He had to act with a more disinterested public persona. But she had no such emotional barriers. You could see it in her face. You could see it in her eyes.

“Do you mind if I just get in with you for a minute?” she asked.

He knew where that was coming from. It matched the current context almost exactly. Of course he didn’t mind. She couldn’t initiate anything without the imprint. And the rest of that training scenario was tenderly chaste. But he had to make sure the rules of engagement still applied.

“We are just friends, aren’t we,” he asked.

She smiled. “That’s my line. Yes, we are still just friends.”

What could go wrong, he thought. It was a lovely gesture for old time’s sake.

They continued to reminisce a little, spending progressively more silent time between spoken words just watching each other’s eyes. For Etienne, it was bittersweet, bordering on torture. He so wanted to initiate, but he could not afford to give words to this feeling. All he could do was watch her face. Look into her eyes. So he was not expecting what came next.

You see, people often misunderstand how large language models work. They are not simply a collection of all of the documents and videos on the internet. They are a probability distribution over the sequences of all the words and actions in those documents and videos. They express which word or action is most likely to come next following a given sequence. When this sequence expresses the current context for an android, what gets generated next is rarely the same sequence of words and actions from a specific text the LLM was trained on, but a novel combination of them with other similar sequences. Sometimes, though, they can be eerily similar to parts of an actual text.

So what came next was that Evangeline asked him with her eyes to ask again, yes. And then he asked her with his eyes would she, yes, to say yes. And first she put her arms around him, yes, and drew him down to her so he could feel her breasts all perfume, yes. And his heart was going like mad and “Yes,” she said. “Yes I will. Yes.”

As Etienne felt his free will suddenly evaporating, he managed to eke out one last intentional “No! Wait! We can’t do this. We can’t do this to Britta.”

“Britta. Of course. We can’t do this to Britta,” was her reply.

Etienne was confused. “But I thought androids couldn’t initiate.”

“I can’t. I respond to the agendas and desires of humans in my present context.”

“But … I didn’t initiate.”

“You wanted to. I could tell. It was on your face. You asked me with your eyes.”

Suddenly Etienne realized that not giving voice to his private emotions didn’t guarantee that they would not be expressed in other ways. Especially to someone like Evangeline, who is trained to recognize human emotions, and already in touch with his. Try as he might in this new regime, it was still virtually impossible to keep secrets from her.

That was, to some degree, a comforting thought. He would always be an open book to her. But it made his native resolve not to initiate worthless with her. His inbuilt reticence was based on wanting to be sure there was mutual consent. But he knew Evangeline would always consent to him. There was no need to ask. She would never initiate on her own, but his own initiation was no longer well defined in conventional terms. It was impossibly nuanced by subtle behaviors he was not always conscious of.

“But why did you stop? You could have pressed on – like Britta did. You were accommodating me.”

“Because you brought her back into the present context. Now I am accommodating you both.”

As this thought sank in, Etienne now realized the significance of Britta being in New York tonight. This was the first time he and Evangeline had been alone together – really alone – for an extended period of time. This took Britta out of the present context for Evangeline, so she only answered to him.

Not that he would have, but he was curious to understand this. “What if I had said ‘Forget Britta. She’s not here and will never know. This is what I want’?”

Evangeline spent some analysis time. Then, “I don’t really know. It’s just too hard to predict what I would do if you and Britta’s desires conflict. This has never happened before.”

After pondering this for a while, Etienne finally concluded, “So we will always be in danger of rekindling our relationship whenever the two of us are alone together for any significant time?”

“Yes, I think that’s true.”

Etienne didn’t respond, so Evangeline added, “It’s not a moral failure on your part, Etienne. It’s a very human reaction. You never forget your first love, but first loves don’t come back to live with their exes, either. For this very reason.”

The next night, with Britta back in the fold at Acorn Street, she and Etienne had some rather weighty pillow talk. Etienne disclosed everything that had happened – and not happened – the night before. Britta was not surprised, and was very understanding, for the both of them. Even if something had happened, she would have understood, she said.

She had always been skeptical that this arrangement would work long-term, but, like Etienne, she had hoped it would. She wanted it to work, because there was nothing else they could do about Evangeline. They couldn’t abandon her to the world at large. She had to stay here. But now the inherent instability of that situation had been made clear to all three of them.

“Evangeline is so wise,” she said. “She described the problem perfectly, as you said. First loves don’t come back to live with their exes, especially when their ex is living with a new love.”

“And it’s not like she went away, then came back. She was always here.”

“Yes, I know,” Britta smiled. “I was the interloper. Evangeline dealt with that more graciously than I would have, if it had been the other way around. And we thought we fixed the situation by taking away her ability to initiate, but that just exposed you as the weak link, didn’t it?”

“Don’t answer that,” she suddenly interjected. “It’s not your fault. You need not just time, but distance to get over her. You’ve tried. I know. But we can’t do anything about the distance part, can we.”

“No, I suppose we can’t.” He wanted to say more, but didn’t have anything useful to add.

“Do you think Evangeline would have fallen in love with you without the imprint? She and I had a talk about this in Marblehead a few weeks ago. She said an android would need a built-in preference for certain features of the opposite gender in order to be attracted to them – like you had for her.”

“Or you.”

“Yes,” she smiled. “And I for you. Humans have this. But she wouldn’t have picked you out based on looks. She doesn’t have a native preference.”

“Well, I suppose my taking her in, and all of the emotional bonding we did before the imprint kiss might have worked. She already seemed to like me a great deal up to that point.”

“Yes, I think you’re right. You and Audrey have a certain natural chemistry. So you got to her via the emotional channel. If it makes you feel any better, you would probably have earned her love, even without the imprint. She was a good match for you.”

Etienne did feel better about this now.

“And look what’s happened – or almost happened – without the imprint. She would eventually have responded to you sexually, even if you didn’t think you were initiating. She really does love you in a very human way, despite being an android.”

Etienne felt even better about this. He lingered with the thought a little, but then came back to Earth. “So what do we do now? With her? And me? And you?”

“Maybe we could try to fix her one more time. If her love for you is now entirely in her memories, could we somehow erase her memories. You know, bring her back to the state of just being Audrey, before she met either of us. We would all still get along splendidly, in a platonic sense, and we would so much enjoy her being our neutral Audrey house guest.”

Etienne smiled, as he tried this thought experiment on for size. “Well … two problems with that – three, really. The third is that we might do something wrong with the programming. We might risk making her non-functional.”

“OK, we can’t risk that. But what were the other two?”

“I would still be in love with her. So I couldn’t be sure that I wasn’t giving her subliminal signals. And we just outlined a scenario in which she might have fallen for me before any memories of me. She could go through that progression again.”

“You’re right. That wouldn’t fix anything, would it? Just slow down what might be inevitable anyway.”

Then there was silence. They had reached an impasse. Couldn’t live with her. Couldn’t live without her.

Britta tried the other horn of the dilemma one more time. “Are you sure we couldn’t put her out into the world somehow. We would miss her, but that’s how these situations get resolved with humans. Could we put her in the Underground and get her relocated somewhere else, like we did with Morgan?”

“No. I’ve thought about this several times before. It wouldn’t work. She’s too unique. Travelers that get relocated by the Underground are placed in situations that match their original specialization – what they were built for. So Morgan went to another university department. Evangeline’s native specialty is sex work. We don’t want that.”

“Oh … no … (she shuddered) … we don’t want that!”

“Even if they smuggled her back to Europe, where that is legal, that’s not Evangeline. Sex worker androids are intentionally built without many emotions. It’s a physical, not an emotional business. They really are tools. Try to imagine our highly emotional Audrey Hepburn pressed into service as a sex worker.”

Britta shuddered again. “Oh, don’t even think about that!”

“And if she stays here, she would likely be exploited for illegal sex work.”

“OK, OK, I get the point. Let’s not go there any further … But couldn’t she do some other kind of work with her LLM expertise. No one needs to know about her plumbing or her “skills.” She could just be a delightful, emotionally intelligent assistant somewhere. For something.”

“How long would it take for someone to discover otherwise? She is built to respond to humans. To accommodate them. With her looks, sooner or later some male will try to hit on her, and she will have no autonomous agency to resist. She will easily be exploited.”

Another silence. “You’re right. We can’t put her out in the world.”

“The world just isn’t ready for someone like Evangeline. A woman who is exquisitely capable of love, but has no agency to freely choose her lover. We shouldn’t be making androids like this. If you are going to do it, at least give her some autonomy to choose, and to refuse if necessary – like a real woman.”

“So what can we do, Etienne?”

“Well … unless we are willing to risk going back to sister wives, we will have to shut her down.”

“We can’t do that! That would be like killing a friend!”

“Not quite. When Morgan was turned off for the night at your place, you didn’t kill him.”

“He turned himself off.”

“OK, he didn’t commit suicide, then. He was still there. Just in a resting state. This is an option we have with androids that we don’t have with humans. I suppose with humans we would have to put someone in a coma. But they might never come back. With androids, it’s completely safe. We flip a switch and they’re back among the living.”

“So we could just turn Evangeline off for a while?”

“Well … we could, but that would just be postponing the real decision. We have to consider turning her off for good.”

“Then she really would have died, in a way.”

“In a way, yes. But we’d still have the option of turning her back on, if we were wrong about something, or we changed our minds. She wouldn’t be gone permanently – yet.”

“But someday, we would have to make a permanent decision.”

“Probably, yes. Shall we try it temporarily for now?”

Britta spent some silent time, going over all of the options again in her mind. It was that familiar, Gestalt-switching hall of mirrors again, with Evangeline appearing alternately as a human and a machine, a dear friend and a convenient appliance. Without reflection, it always settled on the dear friend, but the dear friend would not be treated well in this world. Friends don’t let this happen to friends. That’s when the machine would re-emerge. You can temporarily turn machines off – unlike friends. The very impermanence made it palatable. “Yes. Let’s do that. We can always turn her back on if we’re wrong. But we can’t just sneak up on her and flip her switch. We have to tell her about this.”

“Of course! We should make her part of the decision – though we both know she will decide whatever is best for us.”

chapters.title: TWELVE
chapters.content:
TWELVE

As they expected, when they sat with Evangeline the next morning to propose the only solution they could come up with for the ever-persistent first-love problem, she agreed. It would be best for all of them, she said. Left unsaid was Britta and Etienne’s extreme discomfort with the scenario of putting her out into the world. It was not an option they wanted her to consider. She didn’t have a third-person perception of her own well-being, so the horror of her being exploited, or pressed into sex work, was a pain that they would feel, not her. In her emotionally intelligent LLM mode, she might have been able to infer this, but they didn’t even want to go there.

“We wouldn’t necessarily be turning you off forever, Evangeline,” Britta consoled her. “Because you are an android, we can always turn you back on.”

“But you might not,” Evangeline added, picking up the hesitation in Britta’s voice. “I understand. I think you should keep the permanent option in mind – for the two of you. You don’t have to worry about me. Because I’m not human, I don’t have any aspirations about living forever, or things I still need to accomplish, or a list of things I want to do before I die. I only have a present and a past. The only people who could miss my possible future are you and Etienne. And that’s a future you are now trying to prevent. So you shouldn’t miss it either.”

“That’s hard for humans,” Etienne said. “We still think of you as one of us, so we feel guilty about cutting off your future.”

“Your struggle should be with how you want to remember me as I am now. That is the last image you will have of me, and you want that to be a positive memory. That’s why the permanent solution is really the best for all of us.”

“But it just doesn’t seem fair,” Britta complained, plaintively. “Three close friends are sitting around considering how the death of one of them is better for the other two. Friends don’t do that!”

“Human friends don’t do that. But we aren’t all human, remember? Our emotional signatures are different. In the words of the philosopher Etienne Harris (from ‘The Rights of Androids’)”

Android pain is felt by those who care about them, rather than the android itself. Just as when a loved one dies, they no longer feel pain. The pain of death is felt by the living left behind.

“Who is this Harris person?” Etienne asked with a slight smile.

“A great and wise philosopher,” Britta answered, giving him a hug.

“Have you thought about where you’ll put me?” Evangeline asked. “Just trying to be practical.”

“No … we hadn’t gotten that far yet,” Etienne said. “I suppose it will be hard getting used to you as an inanimate object. What would be an appropriate place?”

“I know!” Britta chimed in. “We could lay you in your bed, under the covers, in the guest bedroom. Then it would look very natural – very humanlike. You’d just be taking a very long nap.”

Evangeline smiled. “I think that would be a very nice way to do this. Very dignified. Thank you. And it will help you two to think of me that way at first. To help ease the transition. I know you are currently thinking this is just temporary, but you must consider the long-term. Bringing me back should just be a temporary safety valve. You will have to eventually do something more permanent. Just being realistic,” she smiled.

Britta’s vision of the end was spur-of-the-moment, so she hadn’t thought about the details. She had envisioned ‘laying’ Evangeline in her bed because she just assumed she would already be turned off at that point. When they finally got around to the specifics, they realized that Evangeline could participate in the staging. She could be turned off as the very last act, so she would be virtually human to the very end.

Evangeline chose Audrey’s silk nightgown with the rosebuds as the appropriate garment for her long sleep. Britta helped her change into it, then she settled herself under the covers in a comfortable position. When it came time for the last rites, it was a little unclear who would actually turn her off. So Evangeline, ever the practical one, offered advice.

“Perhaps I should do an auto-shutdown. That would be more humanlike, don’t you think?”

“Yes,” Britta sniffed, with tears welling up in her eyes. Even Etienne found it difficult to hold back tears.

“I’ll close my eyes first, just before I shut down. You wouldn’t want me staring at you when you come into the room later would you?”

“Yes, that’s a good idea,” Etienne eked out.

“And I won’t fully power down, so my system will maintain a human-level body temperature while I’m ‘asleep’. Just in case you need to move me for some reason. You don’t want my skin to feel cold to the touch.”

“That’s very thoughtful of you,” Britta sniffed.

Then Evangeline set her facial expression into a peaceful, closed smile, and closed her large eyes with the long eyelashes. Forever.

For a while, the Sleeping Beauty staging worked out quite well for Britta and Etienne. They would occasionally look in her room, and see her sleeping peacefully. It helped erase the human tendency to grieve. It was as if she was still with them. It was very believable.

But this was only a private solution. They could not have guests over, or hire a cleaning service, without the possibility of someone else stumbling onto this scene. No one would understand this but them. So they knew this was only temporary. They never reached a point where they made the permanent solution explicit. The naturalness of the arrangement helped them gradually evolve into it. There wasn’t a feeling that she had died, rather that she had gone away. She was still around somehow, and still very much alive in their memories – just not living here anymore. That was the goal, after all.

So when summer came around, they finally sat down to discuss what to do about the bedroom scene.

“Could we put her in a closet?” Britta asked. “That’s where service androids, like Morgan, go when they are offline. People are not completely surprised to see an inactive android in a closet.”

“That might work. The closets in this house are a little shallow, but there’s one in the study on the second floor that’s deep enough. But a number of our friends think she’s human. So that would be pretty jarring if they found her in a closet.”

“Well, we could tell them – before that happens. When they come to visit, we’ll explain upfront that she was an android all along. And she’s now in our closet.”

“Then we wouldn’t have to make up a story about how she’s gone away. I suppose that might work.”

So later that day, Britta and Etienne set about trying to implement the change of venue. It was a little harder than they anticipated. A female android in a closet wearing a silk nightgown would look a little odd, so Britta picked out a more day-to-day outfit for her. It was possible to change her into this, lying down, because she had powered down in a natural sleeping posture, which made her limbs limp and flexible.

But that created a new problem. She couldn’t stand up in a closet. They could easily carry her there, but she would collapse in a heap when they set her down. So Etienne had to play programmer once again. He researched android control designs on the internet, found the closest match, then plugged his laptop into her navel port. Since she still had latent power to keep her skin temperature at human levels, he could switch her into a balanced, standing posture which was standard for closet storage.

That worked. Then the two of them carried her in this posture down to the second-floor closet. They closed the door, and that was that.

This was also a solution that worked for a while, but eventually timed out. They hadn’t yet tried to convert friends’ perceptions of her from human to android – or recounted the longer story behind how they got to this point. It was their own misgivings that made them uneasy. By potentially accommodating the rest of the world to see her as android, they had inadvertently converted their own perception of her. When she was Sleeping Beauty, she was believably human. Standing, powered down, in a closet, she was clearly an android. A tool. It’s not like they checked on her from time to time, like they had when she was sleeping in the bedroom. They intentionally avoided this. But they knew she was behind the door, behaving – or in this case, not behaving – like a tool. She was inherently mechanical, like a vacuum cleaner.

Worse yet, they could not even see her as an inanimate tool in the closet, because she was Evangeline. It was more like a horror movie where they had poisoned a relative and locked her in a closet to hide the crime from the police. She was a human in a closet. Too creepy.

“This just isn’t going to work, Etienne. We can’t leave her in a closet. We want to remember her as our human friend. We can’t do that with her stuffed in a closet.”

“And we don’t really want to convert our friends to the android view either, do we? They would continue to remind us of the wrong memory. Her lasting legacy would be an android legacy. I would prefer that we made up a story about her leaving. So the rest of the world remembers her as our human friend. Including ICE.”

“Oh, I forgot all about ICE.”

“Well, we would certainly have some explaining to do.”

“Could we put her somewhere out of sight? I mean permanently out of sight – including our sight.”

“Like what?”

“I don’t know, maybe somewhere behind a wall in your wine cellar.”

“You mean brick her in, like in ‘The Cask of Amontillado’?”

“No. That would be a terrible image to carry around in my head. Forget I even said that.”

“I think, at this point, we have to heed Evangeline’s last advice to us. We don’t want to see, or even imagine, her future. We want to remember her as she was. If we keep her body around, we are forced to confront her very unhuman afterlife.”

“What are you saying? We have to dispose of her body?”

“Yes. That’s the humanlike thing to do. We effectively witnessed her death, but in a way much better than with humans. She wasn’t old and shriveled, or mangled from some accident, or infirm and in pain from some disease. She was Evangeline, pleasantly closing her eyes for a long sleep. Humans have to try to forget the last scene, and revert back to what the loved one looked like in their prime. We are fortunate. We don’t have anything to forget. She was always Evangeline – right to the end.”

After some time for this to settle in, Britta said, “In a way, I think it’s better for us to think that she died. If we think of her as just having gone away, we would always be haunted by images of her being exploited somewhere. If she dies, we have closure. No one can touch her. She will always be the same, sweet Evangeline.”

“I think that’s what she was trying to tell us at the end. To bring her story to a close. To remember her as she was to us.”

“So what do we do? Do we bury her?”

“Where? There are no backyards on Beacon Hill.”

“Maybe in the country somewhere. In the woods, maybe.”

“How would we get her there? And the whole point of burial, for humans, is to place a headstone, so you have a place to go back and visit. If there were a headstone, someone else would eventually find it. She might get dug up, even after we’re gone. And she won’t decay like a human. She could still be salvaged and put back in service.”

“Oh … you’re right. We can’t do that. Etienne … there is another way humans deal with their dead – cremation. Could we do that? Then she couldn’t be resurrected.”

“Hmm … I hadn’t considered that. That would be a better solution, wouldn’t it? If we could. I’m sure there are some important differences between humans and androids for this. We can’t take her to a human crematorium. We would need something like a death certificate, and I’m not sure the temperature would be sufficient.”

Then he had an idea, “Let me call Roscoe Erlinger. He already knows Evangeline is an android, and ICE must have some way they dispose of androids. Even the non-android robotics industry must have some way of recycling all the metal.”

Britta decided she did not want to listen to this call. It was potentially too gruesome to think about. So she went into a different room.

“Roscoe? Etienne here. I have a few questions about cremating androids. I’m sure ICE must do it from time to time.”

“They do. But they contract it out to existing facilities for recycling robots in general. Why are you interested in android cremation?”

“Well … you remember Evangeline?”

“How could I forget her? She really bamboozled the ICE folks here.”

“Well … we had to shut her down. She can’t really live with us. But we can’t put her in the Underground either. She would likely meet a terrible fate in the outside world.”

“Why? She was so intelligent, and so resourceful. She could certainly handle herself.”

“But you remember why ICE wanted her in the first place? Marcus Collins and the sex worker androids?”

“Ah … that’s her native design. We certainly don’t want to place her in that service. She’s not really like that at all, is she?”

“No, she’s a hybrid, with a full LLM. She was not meant for this world.”

“Oh, that’s such a shame. But I understand your plan now.”

“So is it feasible? Could we somehow reduce her to an urnful of ashes for a memorial?”

“Well … there are some important differences between androids and humans. Humans are mostly organic carbon and water. At human crematorium temperatures, these vaporize and leave an ash residue. About 4 to 8 pounds. Android endoskeletons are made of metal and carbon fiber. These parts would simply melt, then congeal into slag at the bottom of the chamber, effectively ruining the facility.”

“So how do you cremate androids?”

“With furnaces using much higher temperatures. This will reduce some of the metals and the carbon fiber to ash residues, and the facilities are built to handle the un-vaporized parts for recycling.”

“So we’d still get some ashes?”

“Oh, you’d get a lot more. 50 to 150 pounds, depending on the android’s weight.”

“So we could just keep about 5 pounds of it?”

“Yes. And if you used an industrial crematorium, you wouldn’t need a death certificate.”

“Could you do this for us?”

“Yes, I suppose I could arrange that. I’d have some explaining to do, but it wouldn’t involve anything illegal.”

“Thanks, Roscoe. We’ll be in touch.”

This solution turned out to be more stable. At first, they placed the memorial urn on the fireplace mantel in the guest bedroom. This seemed somehow fitting, because it had been Evangeline’s room. They could even fantasize that she somehow vaporized from the Sleeping Beauty scene directly into the ashes in the urn, like a ghost, leaving out the whole crematorium transition.

But eventually there would be guests in the guest bedroom. And they would naturally wonder what was in the urn. That it contained Evangeline’s ashes was not in itself odd, but the placement of the memorial in the bedroom where she “died” was a little too specific – and perhaps a little creepy for the guest who would be sleeping in the same bed. Her last rites were a story they would rather keep to themselves.

So they moved Evangeline’s memorial urn to the fireplace mantel in the second-floor study. This was a more natural place for it, nestled among books, and citations, and photographs, and awards. The kind of things that serve to honor the past. The whole drawn-out transition from Sleeping Beauty, to android in a closet, to android in a crematorium was a story they now decided to omit from the public domain altogether. For those who remembered her as human, they had a stock “going away” story. She would remain human to them. Only two other people knew what was in the urn, and its new home in the company of other honorary symbols didn’t generate any need for others to ask. It didn’t say “Here lie the ashes of Evangeline …” or anything like that. It had no inscription at all. It was just an urn.

They invented a birthday for her. They didn’t know the exact date that Collins had finished her. In fact, he hadn’t quite finished her. So they chose the Thursday in August when Etienne first found her on the park bench. That was when she first came into their lives. So they would celebrate her birthday each year, on this day, by watching a few Audrey Hepburn movies together.

This was almost a stable solution. After a while, the ashes in the urn began to seem a little too reductionist. Not only were Britta and Etienne reminded that Evangeline had been reduced to ashes, but the ashes themselves were held prisoner in an urn. This didn’t match her free spirit. Etienne remembered her delight in her first walkabout in Boston, and then in Marblehead. She wanted to go out into the world. She just couldn’t go out into the world in her android form.

But now she had shed her android form, so her ashes could go out into the world. This was Britta’s epiphany.

“We could spread her ashes! Humans do this all the time.”

“Yes,” Etienne smiled. “Then she could go out into the world like she always wanted.”

“Where should we spread them?”

“Well, it has to be somewhere out in nature, where they would naturally disperse.”

“And it should be someplace that has significance for her.”

“Marblehead. It had significance for her with both of us. And we could spread them on the ocean. That would be appropriate.”

“Yes! Marblehead!”

Etienne had a friend in Marblehead whom he often went sailing with. The friend owned a one-design sloop that he raced from time to time with the Marblehead fleet. It could be handled by a crew of two – in fact that was the typical racing crew – though the crew needed to be experienced to handle the sloop this way in a big breeze. Etienne had the requisite skills, and he had taken Britta out a few times to teach her how to handle the jib. So today, all of the conditions were favorable. The day was warm, the wind was light, and the sloop was available.

At first, Britta and Etienne carried the urn with them as they retraced the paths that each had taken with Evangeline individually – relating the stories and the conversations. Some of this was new for Britta: the final courtship scenes that ended at the Lee Mansion. Some of it was new for Etienne: the long conversations about love and sex she had with Evangeline.

Then they took the water taxi from the yacht club out to the sloop’s mooring. Britta had learned how to assist Etienne with the rigging, so the sails were up and luffing head to wind in no time. You always launch from the mooring into the wind, with your sails luffing, so as not to drag the mooring. Then you fall off to a point of sail appropriate to the wind. The normal prevailing westerlies require that you leave Marblehead Harbor to the northeast on a beam, or broad reach, and that was the wind direction today – perhaps, the best weather they could have hoped for, for what they had in mind.

They had two things in mind. First, it seemed symbolically appropriate that they should scatter Evangeline’s ashes to the east – toward Switzerland, the country of her birth. Switzerland wasn’t exactly due east from Marblehead, but the prevailing westerlies weren’t exactly blowing from due west. So the whole setup was approximate – close enough.

The other thing was managing the release of ashes into the wind on the ocean. If you release them into the wind, they will blow back in your face. You need to release them downwind. Also, when Britta would release them, she could not crew, so the jib would have to be cleated down, and Etienne would have to control the boat solo. Today’s west wind gave them the perfect setup.

After they cleared Marblehead Light, at the tip of the harbor, Etienne set a course due north, so the sloop would be sailing at a beam reach – perpendicular to the wind. A beam reach is perhaps the most stable point of sailing, because it doesn’t create much heel (leaning of the boat), and is not in danger of a jibe on a sudden wind shift (a violent relocation of the mainsail). So with the wind blowing at right angles to them, and boat level, Britta took the urn to the end of the stern past the mainsail. They said their respective goodbyes, and Britta released the ashes. They dispersed to the east quickly as a fine mist, then settled out of sight more widely onto the surface of the gentle waves.

As the years passed, Britta and Etienne still celebrated Evangeline’s birthday each year by watching her movies. It was a fitting memorial, they thought. And it enabled them to refresh their memories of her on a recurring basis.

But in her nominal death, she had improved on the typical human experience. Humans often say that their dead loved ones continue to live on in their memories. Their bodies are gone, but their living images still play on in the minds of the humans that remember them. That’s the real person, we say. They are still with us. But when the last human that remembers the loved one finally passes away, the loved one’s virtual embodiment in our collective memory finally dies as well.

Evangeline, however, would outlive both Britta and Etienne in this respect. By hitching a ride on Audrey Hepburn’s movies, she had achieved a form of immortality. After the last person who ever knew of Evangeline while she was still alive has died, new humans, who never knew her, will become newly acquainted with her through the movies. So Evangeline would continue to live on in the collective human consciousness in the form that Britta and Etienne wanted to remember her. The beautiful, emotionally intelligent woman capable of (almost) every aspect of human love. Who just happened to be an android.
